hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. Be sure to scout areas prior to the season and to get your baits put out as early as legally possible. It typically only takes a few days for bears to find your bait station. Bears have a great sense of smell, so using strong smelling bait will help bring bears in. Talk to your local bakery about getting day-old pastries to use as bait. Once you have a bear coming into bait, be sure to watch for any cubs that may be present. It is illegal to harvest a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. The majority of the region has a good deal of road access. This hunt unit offers some areas that are closed to vehicle access. These areas hold bears but can be difficult to hunt and don't receive as much pressure. The Meadow Creek WMA, and parts of the Bitter Creek WMA are two of these areas.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the fall the bears are trying to optimize there foraging strategy around pine nuts, remaining berries and acorns. hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder mountain has a good bear population but is a rugged, large, tough place to hunt. Vehicle access is limited and the steep, rocky terrain makes it a challenging experience. The DWR has several GPS tracking collars on female bears and would ask that hunters not harvest a bear with a collar on this unit. These individuals provide important information for the unit and often have cubs with them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please don't harvest our radio collared bears! Boars usually prefer the higher elevations on the Boulder and sows with cubs often don't leave the oak/mountain brush zones around the mountain. All parts of the mountain have populations of bears and pre-season scouting and hiking will help hunters find good areas. There are many lakes and streams on the Boulder and these are areas where bears like to feed and lounge. When trailing bears with hounds, hunters can expect to cover lots of country through thick vegetation while pursuing. Spot and stalk style hunting on this unit is incredibly difficult due to the topography and thick conifer stands covering the unit that prohibit hunters from being able to see far with optics. Hunting with a guide on the Boulder is a good idea for some hunters.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Boulder is a tough place to hunt. Take plenty of water and always tell someone where you plan to hunt. Be prepared to spend the night in the backcountry in case your hunt goes south on you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is unpredictable and can change suddenly. Snow can fall anytime of the year especially at high elevations. Nights can be very cold.

hunt_bio_general_information: The San Juan has one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the fall, focus on areas with berry patches or oak stands. Later in the season, bears will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet. They will look for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, along with scavenging dead carcasses. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear, suggesting that she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. When hunting with bait, use caution when entering your bait station area. If using a tree stand, use a safety harness. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Plan for all types of weather conditions. Flash floods are common in this area, so pay attention to what the sky is doing miles away from you.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt allows the use of any legal Weapon. This hunt does not allow the use of bait, including early baiting. Spot and stalk and the use of dogs are allowed for this hunt. No more than 16 dogs may be used to pursue a bear at any given time.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bears are found across the entire unit. Hunters are encouraged to locate baits in areas not previously hunted if they are looking for a large boar. Harvesting bears in the same locations each year leads to over harvest of mature adults in that area. Be aware of thermal air current flow as you pick your hunting spot. Cold air travels down hill in the morning and evenings and warm air rises up hill during the day. Bears have amazing noses and can wind hunters easily and then will likely only come to the bait after dark when it is not legal harvest them. Hunter success using the Spot & Stalk method has been very low on this unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This hunt now allows legal firearms to be used. Be certain of your target before pointing your weapon. Rifle scopes should never be used as binoculars. Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather during this season is normally warm with cool mornings. Unexpected weather is always possible during this season. Be prepared for hot and dry conditions or wet and cold.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the fall, focus on areas with berry patches or oak stands. Later in the season, bears will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet. They will look for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, along with scavenging dead carcasses. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear that suggests she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. You should be ready for anything from rain and sleet, to dry and hot conditions. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_general_information: Spring:The majority of harvest occurs the last 10 days of the hunt. Be prepared to cover several miles every day cutting tracks, and looking for sign. This area can be difficult to access in early April depending on the severity of the winter. There is no baiting during this hunt. If you find any illegal baits please contact the UDWR in Vernal (435) 781-9453. I would focus my efforts in areas where I have good visual vantage points. I have seen bears in the spring at the top ends of the canyons on grassy benches. They seem to prefer the grassy aspen stands relatively close to water. Be prepared to ride and hike in vertical, rocky terrain. The snow can cause delays in accessing certain parts of this unit. I would hunt later when the bears are more likely to be covering more country. Be prepared for a tough hunt. Bait Hunt:This hunt unit is in a very remote location and can be difficult to access to replenish baits. The unit offers a high bear density. Look for scat piles and tracks on the trails. There are several riparian areas and springs the bears will be accessing. Make sure you give yourself plenty of time to get your bait sites approved before your hunt starts. As soon as you can start baiting I would. There will also be archery deer and elk kills that bears will be visiting during this time.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The bear's diet in the spring generally consists of grass, and forbs. They will be relatively close to water sources (creeks, or springs) in the spring, summer and fall. In the late summer fall they will switch to carbohydrates like: pine nuts, acorns, and berries. They move the most during the early morning hours and the evening. The boars are more likely to come out of there dens first. They will continue to increase their movements as the hunt progresses. Their mating season takes place around the second week of June and can last several weeks.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote area with no vehicle access. Every year sportsmen injure horses and themselves while riding in the rough terrain. Be prepared for adverse weather, and limited cell phone coverage.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be prepared for hot/dry/cold conditions, with occasional thunder storms. The trails can get extremely slick and dangerous.

hunt_bio_general_information: Please reference the Black Bear Guide Book and be familiar with the rules and regulations concerning hunting bears in Utah. The summer hunt allows you to hunt over bait, or you can spot & stalk hunt. For the summer hunt, the use of dogs to track or pursue bears and 'early baiting' prior to the opening of the hunt is not permitted. If you find any illegal baits during the Spring or fall hunts please report them promptly to the UDWR. Desirable bait site locations are almost always away from roads and atv trails and where there are denser conifer stands with water nearby. With that in mind do not violate Utah Code § 23-20-3 and Utah Admin. Rule R657-33-14: You may not place bait in either of the following areas: Within 100 yards of water, a public road or a designated trail. Or within a half-mile of any permanent dwelling or campground. There may be additional bait-placement restrictions, depending upon historical human and bear activity-especially nuisance complaints within any given area. The site that you choose to place a bait should not put other people using that same area at risk. Seek other suitable locations if other campers or resource users are nearby. Oftentimes, multiple bears will come into a bait station and hunters need to know how to tell whether it is a male or female. Be sure of the bear you are shooting, that it does not have cubs of the year with it or evidence that it is a female that has cubs. A female with new cubs is illegal to pursue or harvest. The required black bear orientation course can be found here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html If you find any illegal baits, please report them to the UDWR promptly. Apply early for a certificate of registration (COR) to run a bait station which a can take upwards of ten days.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: You can find resources on black bear habitat, diet, behavior, and natural history on the division's black bear hunting website here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html Hunting bears on or near sheep allotments on the south Manti is encouraged to help decrease the number of bears taken by Wildlife Services- Dept. of AG each year for killing domestic sheep. Not all bears kill sheep, but if sportsmen take some of the bears that do, there will be more opportunity for sportsmen to harvest bears. These allotments are generally higher in elevation reaching to Skyline Drive. Other areas on the S. Manti include Huntington and Cottonwood canyons and the following mountains: East, Trail, Candland, Heliotrope, Ferron, and the White Mtn area. Another area not to be overlooked is along the Price River between Woodside and Cedar Mountain; we have had a number of reports of black bear sign along this river corridor.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: You can find resources on safety in black bear country on the division's website here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service, it also allows a designated person with internet service to track you. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Expect muddy roads and cool springtime conditions at high elevations in June. Depending on winter conditions there may be snowdrifts that persist at high elevations along Skyline Drive into July. If using a tree stand, it is a good idea to wear a safety strap.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the spring, focus on areas with green, grassy meadows. This typically means following the snowline up and glassing south facing hills. Bears will feed on the green grass soon after coming out of their dens. Later in the season, their diet will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet, looking for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, and then berries and acorns later on. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear, suggesting that she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. For those using bait, be cautious when entering your bait station area. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. During the early and late portion of the hunt rain and snow may be possible. You should also be prepared for hot, dry conditions throughout the hunt. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is not known for producing large bears, however, hunters can expect to see multiple bear tracks during their hunt. Due to the forest service road closures, this unit does not get hunted very heavily during the spring harvest objective season. The fall limited entry season overlaps several deer and elk hunts. This unit receives heavy hunting pressure and camping use.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas to hunt: Greendale Junction, Eagle Creek, Meadow Park, Carter Creek, Goslin Creek, Mustang Ridge/Bare Top, Summit Spring
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, wind, heat, and lightning. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Roads can become very muddy, and sometimes impassable, after spring storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The bear population on the Panguitch Lake/Zion unit has been slowly increasing over the past few years. The Panguitch Lake portion of the unit is primarily public land and the Zion portion is primarily private land. Make sure you have written permision before you access private land. If you are planning to use bait and not dogs remeber to apply for your baiting Certificate of Registration early. Don't wait until a few days before the hunt to apply. You will be delayed in beginging your hunt. If you are planning to hunt on private land you still have to register your bait station. Make sure to bring a copy of your written permision to submit with your COR application.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunters will find bears primarily in the oak brush to mixed conifer habitats. Bear numbers and are increasing on the unit and bears can be found primarily from about the 7,000-9,500 foot elivations all around the unit. Hunters can choose to use dogs, spot and stalk, or use bait on this hunt. If you choose to use bait during this hunt, please make sure to follow the rules do not apply for a bait station near homes/cabins, campgrounds and water sources. Also, if you end up using dogs, do not start them on a bear track within a several miles of your bait station. Sweet baits and meats that are very aromatic seems to work best for bear. Make sure to clean up after you self when you are done hunting or after you harvest. If you choose to use dogs please be respectfull of other public land users. There are several other big game hunts going on, in this unit during this hunts during the fall time frame. In the spring you will most likely encounter turkey hunters.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Make sure somebody at home knows where you are going and when you plan to return. Please be prepared with plenty of food and water if you plan to be out for an extended period of time.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Daytime temps should be mild to warm during this season during the summer and early fall portions of the season. In April, May and November you should expect cold temps and snow. Night time temps can still be below freezing at the the higher elevations but are typically in the high 30's to low 40's. It can and will still snow in May, June and September at the higher elevations on this unit.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder mountain has a good bear population but is a rugged, large, tough place to hunt. Vehicle access is limited and the steep, rocky terrain makes it a challenging experience. The DWR has several GPS tracking collars on female bears and would ask that hunters not harvest a bear with a collar on this unit. These individuals provide important information for the unit and often have cubs with them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please don't harvest our radio collared bears! Boars usually prefer the higher elevations on the Boulder and sows with cubs often don't leave the oak/mountain brush zones around the mountain. All parts of the mountain have populations of bears and pre-season scouting and hiking will help hunters find good areas. Game cameras can help bait hunters identify promising areas to select for bait sites and evaluate age class and sex of bears frequenting the area. There are many lakes and streams on the Boulder and these are areas where bears like to feed and lounge. When trailing bears with hounds, hunters can expect to cover lots of country through thick vegetation while pursuing. Spot and stalk style hunting on this unit is incredibly difficult due to the topography and thick conifer stands covering the unit that prohibit hunters from being able to see far with optics. Hunting with a guide on the Boulder is a good idea for some hunters.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Boulder is a tough place to hunt. Take plenty of water and always tell someone where you plan to hunt. Be prepared to spend the night in the backcountry in case your hunt goes south on you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is unpredictable and can change suddenly. Snow can fall anytime of the year especially at high elevations. Nights can be very cold.

hunt_bio_general_information: The San Juan has one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the spring, focus on areas with green, grassy meadows. This typically means following the snowline up and glassing south facing hills. Bears will feed on the green grass soon after coming out of their dens. Later in the season, their diet will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet, looking for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, and then berries and acorns later on. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear, suggesting that she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. For those using bait, be cautious when entering your bait station area. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. During the early and late portion of the hunt rain and snow may be possible. You should also be prepared for hot, dry conditions throughout the hunt. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit receives a lot of public use throughout the hunts, including camping. During the spring hunt, expect forest service roads to be closed for most of the hunt. The fall hunt coincides with the bull elk and buck deer archery hunts and several other hunts, including muzzleloader elk and general season deer. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas on Diamond Mountain: Marshall Draw, Mail Draw, Warren Draw, Little Hole
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting seasons. Be prepared for snow, rain, wind, heat, and lightning. Dogs are allowed March 30 - May 27, Aug. 1 - Aug. 31 & Nov. 4 - Nov. 10, 2024. You may not place bait in either of the following areas: •Within 100 yards of water, a public road or a designated trail. •Within a half-mile of any permanent dwelling or campground. Fore more information refer to the Utah Bear hunting guide book. https://wildlife.utah.gov/guidebooks/bear_guidebook.pdf
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are bears across the whole unit. Look for areas away from campgrounds, roads, trails, and areas frequented by the general public. The more remote the area the better. Bears like areas close to water and cover. Streams flowing by conifers are good places to start. Use some kind of attractant such as anise oil or liquid fish fertilizer. Place attractant high in a tree so as to have the sent loft out. Bears can smell a mile away. Trail cameras are a good tool to use to find information on bears sex, age and time of day visiting the area. Make sure to follow all rules regarding the use of Trail cameras. Some areas to look at are Strawberry valley, Sheep Creek, Diamond Fork, Hobble Creek, American Fork Canyon, but bears can be found in most all areas on the unit.. Hunters are encouraged to locate baits in areas not previously hunted if they are looking for a large boar. Harvesting bears in the same locations each year leads to over harvest of mature adults in that area. Be aware of air current flow as you pick your hunting spot. Bears have amazing noses and can wind hunters easily and then may only come to the bait after dark when it is not legal harvest them. Hunter success using the Spot & Stalk method has been very low on this unit

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the spring, focus on areas with green, grassy meadows. This typically means following the snowline up and glassing south facing hills. Bears will feed on the green grass soon after coming out of their dens. Later in the season, their diet will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet, looking for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, and then berries and acorns later on. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear that suggests she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. For those using bait, be cautious when entering your bait station area. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. During the early and late portion of the hunt rain and snow may be possible. You should also be prepared for hot, dry conditions throughout the hunt. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Mt. Carmel Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located west and northwest of Orderville, Utah. It is divided into three parcels and each parcel is associated with Muddy Creek. The south pracel occurs on both sides of Muddy Creek, ranging from 5200 feet to 5500 feet. The higher elevation on this south part is around 5800 feet. The middle parcel is the smallest and is on both sides of Muddy Creek, ranging from 5600 feet to 6000 feet. The high elevation on this parcel is 6100 feet. The north parcel is the largest and occurs mostly to the west of Muddy Creek. On this parcel Muddy Creek ranges from 6100 feet to 6800 feet. The high elevation on this parcel is around 8200 feet. The most common elevation is 7200 feet but ranges from 5300 feet to 8300 feet with an elevation difference of 3000 feet. Fifty-four percent (54%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6300 feet and 7300 feet an elevation difference of 1000 feet. The two (2) dominate land cover types on the Mt. Carmel Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) are Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) and Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36). There are a many land cover types (33 types), but they make up a small parts of the total cover. One of the Mt. Carmel Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ORDERVILLE (426534), is 1.2 km east of the east edge of the CWMU. ORDERVILLE has ninety-eight (98) years of records, 1910 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.78 inches, but it can be as high as 11.32 inches or as low as 0.54 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 12 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is also 1 day with precipitation greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 2.4 inches but can be as high as 17.0 inches. FALL temperature at ORDERVILLE averages 53.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 100.0 degrees F. or as low as -1.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 35 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

It would be advisable to hunt in a manner that will not attract attention to yourself as to minimize any negative public perceptions that could occur with wounded animals, gutpiles in people's yards etc.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: It is hot in August and September. hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is designed to reduce deer numbers on a depleted winter range and reduce deer moving into Tooele City. The hunt is in a popular recreation area near Tooele City. The terrain is steep and rugged. Habitat consists of Gambel's oak forests and sagebrush slopes, with pockets of conifers and aspen trees. Hunters will be required to pay any applicable fees at the Tooele County fee booths.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is a hunt to control deer numbers on depleted winter range and in Tooele city. This hunt is primarily in Settlement Canyon. Access will generally be through the county recreation gates near settlement canyon reservoir and middle canyon. Any other access points may involve passing through private land and permission will be needed by the landowner. Settlement Canyon is a recreation area for hiking, horseback, camping and fishing. Expect to see other recreational activities and people enjoying the outdoors. Be aware of camps and private land.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Expect to see hikers, bikers, horseback, camps in the area. Be aware of private land and Tooele City limits.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The hunt is in August and September. It will be hot with the possibility of severe thunderstorms and lightning. Be prepared to move quick to cover or to take proper care of game in hot temperatures.

hunt_bio_general_information: After numerous complaints from residents, the town council of Oak City convened and supported a city-wide archery hunt as an option to mitigate problems caused by urban mule deer. The weapon type is archery only. There are empty lots and other open spaces in between residential areas where hunters can safely harvest does with archery equipment. Hunters will need written permission from landowners. This hunt is specifically designed to target resident mule deer living within the city limits of Oak City. There is no public land within this hunt boundary. Hunters should not apply unless they have access secured to a private property within the boundary that has mule deer present. The season dates are purposely set early in the fall to ensure there is no harvest of migratory does that will come off the Oak Creek mountains later in the year.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: All archery hunters should be extremely careful about what shots they're willing to take. This hunt though will require an extra level of conscientiousness to determine safe shots given the density of people in the area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Temperatures will be hot and could range anywhere from approximately 70 to 110 degrees. Depending on the year, we sometimes get monsoon rains during this timeframe. Monsoon moisture can bring a lot of rain, but if we don't get rain it'll likely be hot and dry.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt encompasses primarily private land. Do not apply for this hunt unless you have previously obtained permission from a private landowner, or you have access to private land. This hunt was designed to help alleviate depredation deer issues in town, and help decrease deer vehicle collisions. The DWR hopes to target valley deer and not harvest migratory deer. Please consider management principle while hunting on this unit. This hunt can be a great management tool to help decrease the negative impacts of a growing mule deer herd in the Ashley Valley, and Ouray Valley. Please do not call the office or biologist to ask if there are landowners that are willing to allow hunting on their property. Landowners frown on us giving out their personal information.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Valley deer can be patterned and if you put the time in you can place a tree stand or a ground blind in high traffic areas to increase your success. You can not bait for this hunt. The mule deer in the Ashley Valley are mostly resident deer and don't migrate. Please avoid shooting migratory deer on this hunt. It is designed to harvest valley deer that are causing damage to vehicles and agricultural land.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is an archery hunt, please be cautious of shot placement. Consider the ethics and public perception when a wounded doe has an arrow protruding out of its body in town. Do your best to ensure the animal dies on the property you have permission to be on. Be mindful of hunting out of tree stands and take the appropriate safety gear with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The season dates cover the end of summer to the start of winter. Be prepared for anything.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt can be a very enjoyable experience for hunters and those who make their way to the mountain to help scout and tend camp. There is great country to see and lots of opportunity to glass up trophy deer. Bison are sometimes at higher elevations and there may be opportunities to see them while out scouting for deer. The Henry's deer unit is managed as a premium limited entry unit with a 40-50 buck:doe ratio. Over 70% of harvested bucks are 5 years or older. Generally most hunting occurs either on Mt. Ellen, Mt. Pennell, or Mt. Hillers. All have good access and places to get away from roads. Most harvest occurs above 7000'. Mt Ellen attracts most hunters because you can see and glass a lot of different bucks around the loop road but there is also good opportunity to find older age class bucks on Mt. Hillers and Mt. Pennell. There is private land on Mt. Ellen and on Mt. Hillers so be aware that you will need to have written permission to hunt there.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of deer will be found at mid-higher elevations on all three mountains; Mount Ellen, Mount Pennell, and Mount Hillers. These areas are accessible by vehicle and bucks are easily glassed. There are also areas on the northern portion of Mt Ellen and to the southern side of Pennell that you can hike into away from roads. Tarantula Mesa has a deer population and occasionally a nice deer is harvested there. The Little Rockies have a small mule deer herd that live on and around the mountain and canyons but it is rarely hunted. Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Henry's leave the higher mountain elevations during late fall after the rut for the winter range on the lower slopes, draws, hills, and mesas of the unit. In late spring they typically follow green-up of grasses/forbs and migrate back to higher elevations on the Henry Mountain range. Water and high value habitat is available at mid to high elevations through the fall. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is managed as a premium limited entry unit with a 40-50 buck:doe ratio. Over 70% of harvested bucks are 5 years or older. Generally most hunting occurs either on Mt. Ellen, Mt. Pennell, or Mt. Hillers. All have good access and places to to get away from roads. Most harvest occurs above 7000'. Mt Ellen attracts most hunters because you can see and glass a lot of different bucks around the loop road but there is also good opportunity to find older age class bucks on Mt. Hillers and Mt. Pennell. There is private land on Mt. Ellen and on Mt. Hillers so be aware that you will need to have written permission to hunt there.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of deer will be found at mid-higher elevations on all three mountains; Mount Ellen, Mount Pennell, and Mount Hillers. These areas are accessible by vehicle and bucks are easily glassed. There are also areas on the northern portion of Mt Ellen and to the southern side of Pennell that you can hike into away from roads. Tarantula Mesa has a deer population and occasionally a nice deer is harvested there. The Little Rockies also has mule deer that live on and around the mountain and canyons but it is rarely hunted. Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Henry's leave the higher mountain elevations during late fall after the rut and winter on the lower slopes, draws, hills, and mesas of the unit. In late spring they typically follow green-up of grasses/forbs and migrate back to higher elevations. Water and high value habitat is available at mid to high elevations through the hunts. After the rut, and the onset of shorter days and increased snowfall, mule deer will move down to lower elevations. Scouting Tips: Spend enough days in the fall to get familiar with where the deer are on the Henry's. Use good, clean, high-power optics especially if you are hunting on the Management Hunt. Deer are easy to glass at higher elevations on the open slopes, ridges and burned areas. They will generally stay in the areas they are found unless they are spooked. If enough time is spent observing them you can pattern their movements and habitat use, they could change their patterns/movements and leave their home range with increasing hunting pressure. Behavior: Mule deer are most active in the early morning and later before sunset. During the hunt bucks are often in bachelor groups of 3 or more and feed and bed down near each other. They are habitual and have predictable movements along trails within their home range. Water is a limiting factor of habitat selection so the home range is partially determined by the proximity to water. They will likely drink morning and evening and can travel up to 1.5-3 miles depending on free water and succulent vegetation. The mule deer rut usually runs from mid November-mid December. Occasionally a buck that has been seen on one mountain has been known to move to another mountain leading up to the rut.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Use common sense. Let others know where you will be hunting, camped, etc. Some have been stranded by flat tires, very muddy conditions, flash floods, etc. Carry a survival kit. Most areas have no cell phone coverage, others are spotty. Consider hand held radios and a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. On later season hunts high mountain roads can become iced up and unsafe to proceed (chains may help to get you where you want to be). On rare occasion a bear is seen on the mountain. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. Click on the following link for more information http://wildlife.utah.gov/learn-more/bear-safety.html. There has never been a conflict with a bear on the Henry's but if you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Southeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435-613-3700), or call the local dispatch center (435-637-0893).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be prepared for inclement weather. Keep abreast of the weather forecast. Expect and prepare for unfavorable weather conditions such as high temperatures, intense thunder storms, flash floods, early mountain snows, and muddy roads that are difficult to travel even with chains.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt can be such an enjoyable experience for hunters and those who make their way to the mountain to help scout and tend camp. There is great country to see and lots of opportunity to glass up trophy deer. Bison are sometimes at higher elevations and there may be opportunities to see some while out scouting for deer. The Henry's deer unit is managed as a premium limited entry unit with a 40-50 buck:doe ratio. Over 70% of harvested bucks are 5 years or older. Generally most hunting occurs either on Mt. Ellen, Mt. Pennell, or Mt. Hillers. All have good access and places to get away from roads. Most harvest occurs above 7000'. The loop road around Mt Ellen attracts many hunters because you can see and glass a lot of different bucks but there is also good opportunity to find older age class bucks on Mt. Hillers and Mt. Pennell. There is private land on Mt. Ellen and on Mt. Hillers so be aware that you will need to have written permission to hunt there.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Purpose of the Management Buck Hunt: The definition of a management buck is "any buck deer with 3 points or less on at least one antler above and including the first fork in the antler. A point means a projection longer than one inch, measured from its base to its tip. The eye guard is not counted as a point." The purpose of the hunt is to manage the buck to doe ratio following the targets in the Henry Mountain mule deer management plan, and provide more opportunity to hunt on the Henry Mtn unit and harvest a management buck. Its purpose is not to improve herd genetics, which would not be possible with this hunt. There is a kicker point or "crab claw" point gene that is widespread in the herd. Often these points are close to an inch so it is critical that you pay attention to the shorter crab claw or kicker points on the Henry's bucks. If they are over an inch they are counted as a point. Don't take chances on these bucks, take your time and glass from different angles to make sure that there are not any of these short points hiding on the antler where they cannot be seen from your vantage point. You will fare better to let bucks go that have these points than to take a chance on a measurement made through your optic. Being within 100 yards and using an 80 power scope will increase your chances of not making a mistake. Take care to not make long shots or shots in heavy brush where the points can be mistaken for branches. If you harvest a buck deer, you are required to check the deer in with DWR personnel within 48 hours after the date of kill. This inspection will include gathering hunter information, harvest location, antler configuration, and extracting teeth for aging. There is a class of buck between what is a legal management buck and a trophy class buck normally sought after on the premium limited entry hunt. For example a 25 inch buck having a 4x3 framed rack with a 1-3/4 inch kicker on the 3 point side making it an illegal 4x4 management buck by definition, but arguably still perceived as a management buck. Many ideas have been floated about how to harvest these "lesser quality" bucks, but the difficulty is where to draw the line between what one person thinks is a management buck and what another thinks is a trophy buck. In the previously mentioned example there is a difference of opinion between a 25 inch rack and a 30 inch rack. A number of premium hunters would be satisfied with a 3x4 that was 30 inches wide. Until there can be some consensus on the matter these "lesser" bucks will continue to be there for the management hunter to see but not harvest. From the outset you should know going in that this is not an easy hunt even though you've probably heard of or seen many impressive "management bucks". Since the opening of the management hunt in 2009 most of the older bucks have been harvested, younger bucks have taken their place so there are fewer trophy management bucks. This is expected, we also expect some smaller, younger deer will also be included in the harvest. Regardless of age class however, added harvest helps to lower the buck:doe ratio and meet the Management Plan targets. For most hunters this is still a quality hunt, they like being on the Henry's and being able to see plenty of deer, especially the older class trophy bucks. For others it's not what they expected for a Henry's hunt. Gathered from many conversations from disappointed hunters, here's why: It is a short 5 day hunt in the middle of the week. You are competing with other hunters for fewer and often the same 'trophy' management bucks. This can pressure some hunters to hurry a shot and misjudge their intended target and what they thought was a legal management buck. Rushed to beat another hunter they did not get close enough or take long enough to confirm their choice, it happens every year. Some hunters' feel that the hunt is too crowded. Many hunters have friends and family helping scout and share in their Henry's deer hunt and make memories. As big as the Henry's Mountains are there are only so many roads and with many having their own transportation you're looking at a lot of vehicles traversing the mountain. For some it's a great hunt but it's not the ideal hunt for everyone. If you haven't already, spend enough time scouting to know the buck potential and check out the management hunt for yourself before applying. You may have a lot of points on the line so please keep these things in mind and adjust expectations accordingly when applying for the Henry Mountains management buck permit. Location of harvest: The majority of deer will be found at mid-higher elevations on all three mountains; Mount Ellen, Mount Pennell, and Mount Hillers. These areas are accessible by vehicle and bucks are easily glassed. There are also areas on the northern portion of Mt Ellen and to the southern side of Pennell that you can hike into away from roads. Tarantula Mesa has a deer population and occasionally a nice deer is harvested there. The Little Rockies have a small mule deer herd that live on and around the mountain and canyons but it is rarely hunted. Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Henry's leave the higher mountain elevations during late fall after the rut for the winter range on the lower slopes, draws, hills, and mesas of the unit. In late spring they typically follow green-up of grasses/forbs and migrate back to higher elevations on the Henry Mountain range. Water and high value habitat is available at mid to high elevations through the fall. After the rut, and the onset of shorter days, colder temperatures, and increased snowfall, mule deer will move down to lower elevations. Scouting Tips: Spend a enough days, particularly a few days before your hunt, to get familiar with where the deer are on the Henry's. Use good, clean, high-power optics, especially if you are hunting on the Management Hunt. The Henry's deer are easy to glass at higher elevations on the open slopes, ridges and burned areas. Deer are somewhat habitual and have predictable movements within their home range; they will generally stay in the areas they are found unless they are spooked. If enough time is spent observing them you can pattern their movements and habitat use. However with increasing hunting pressure you can expect these patterns to change. Behavior: Mule deer are most active in the early morning and later before sunset. Bucks are habitual and have predictable movements along trails within their home range but expect their patterns to begin to change with increasing hunting pressure and the approaching rut in mid-November. Water is a limiting factor in habitat selection so the home range is partially determined by the proximity to water. They will likely drink morning and evening and will travel 1-3 miles depending on free water and succulent vegetation. Occasionally a buck that has been seen on one mountain has been known to move to another mountain leading up to the rut. The mule deer rut usually runs from mid November-mid December.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Henry Mountain range is remote and services are many miles away. Have good tires with extra spares, the roads are known for flat tires and it is not uncommon to have a couple flats. Flash floods are common during the monsoon season or later fall storms in this region. Roads can be washed out from storms many miles away from surrounding drainages leaving you with few exit points so be prepared. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges. On later season hunts high mountain roads can become iced up and unsafe to travel (chains may help to get you where you want to be). Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but will not always connect. Consider hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Use common sense. Be prepared to spend the night out if you get stuck or for some reason can't make it back to camp. Carry a survival kit. It's always a good idea to let someone know where you plan to camp and when you will return. On rare occasion a bear is seen on the mountain. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. Click on the following link for more information http://wildlife.utah.gov/learn-more/bear-safety.html. There has never been a conflict with a bear on the Henry's but if you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Southeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435-613-3700), or call the local dispatch center (435-637-0893).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Storms can cause muddy impassable road conditions with or without chains. Flash floods are common during the monsoon season or later fall storms in this region. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area.

hunt_bio_general_information: Most hunters are able to locate 20-40 bucks a day. The Book Cliffs has one of the highest success rates for archery hunters in the state. Some hunters are disappointed in the quality of bucks so I would suggest trying to spend some time in the area to become familiar with the quality of bucks, and the steep terrain. There are not many 30" bucks on this unit. The average buck harvested on this unit is a 22" 4 point or 3 x 4. This area provides challenging terrain in a remote part of the state. There are other hunts that coincide with the archery deer hunt. They are: limited entry elk, limited entry bear, bear pursuit, and upland game hunts. In the past deer hunters have had negative experiences with bear hunters in the area. Please be aware that everyone has an equal right to hunt this area. The Book Cliffs is an incredibly large area, but during summer and early fall most of the animals are congregated in a small area. If you really want to get away from ATV and vehicle traffic I would plan on hunting in the Little Creek WMA (roadless area). Primary Access Points: There are several access points to the Book Cliffs. From the north side there are two main roads that take you to the Book Cliffs. Utah State Road 88 located between Vernal and Roosevelt. As you follow it south it turns into the Seep Ridge Road. Hwy 45 or the Bonanza Hwy is located east of Vernal. It takes you towards the east side of the Book Cliffs. After you cross the White River you come to the Dragon or Duck Rock intersection. The Dragon Rd will take you south to the Book Cliffs. The Hay Canyon Rd is the main access road on the south side of the Book Cliffs. You can access it from I-70. It is a hard packed dirt/gravel road. The roadless area has two access points, a north and a south. The north access is called the Ten Mile Knoll trailhead. It is located at the start of Steer Ridge. There is a parking area, but it can fill up in a hurry with trucks and horse trailers. The south trail head starts at the top of Sego Canyon. The road starts at Thompson Springs in Grand County and continues up the Sego Canyon Rd; follow it to the end of the road. There is a water trough at the trailhead, but it is not always full of water. This trailhead can also fill up with vehicles, and trailers. There are no bathrooms or other facilities at either of these trailheads, so plan accordingly.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: You will find the majority of the deer located along the Divide Road. The Book Cliffs range divides the north from the south with a long ridge that runs east to west. The Seep Ridge Rd becomes the Divide Rd and runs east to Colorado and West to Steer Ridge. The Book Cliffs has limited summer range. The majority of the deer are going to be located along the Divide Rd. The deer will be relatively close to water sources. There are numerous springs in the heads of the steep canyons. The local ranches keep small ponds and reservoirs full, but don't rely on them to always be full of water. Some of the areas where hunters have harvested in the past are: Rat Hole Ridge and Canyon, Rail Road Canyon, Black Horse and Saddle Horse Ridge, PR Springs, Horse Point, Moon Ridge, Cherry Mesa, Rock Springs Mesa, Cedar Camp, Steer Ridge, and Little Creek Ridge. The elevation plans a key role in where you will find deer during this time of year. I suggest if you are not seeing deer to change your elevation. Migration Patterns: The mule deer migrate to the higher elevation in late spring. They fawn on their summer range and most of the bucks stay on the summer range until they strip their velvet. The Book Cliffs is limited by summer range which can make the archery hunt a very successful hunt. By mid-October the deer start to migrate to their winter range and can be found in the transitional zone. There is a large transitional area where the deer can hole up until winter storms start to move them to their winter range. From past biological studies we have found that approximately two thirds of the deer migrate to the north and approximately one third of the population migrates to the south. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. I would scout the higher ridges where oak brush is prominent. Your preseason scouting can really pay off on this hunt. The deer won't start to leave the high country until mid-October. The bucks might not be on the same ridge, but I would expect them to stay with-in a five mile radius. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset. There are several recovering burned areas along the Divide. The oak brush is starting to get more established and creates great habitat for mule deer. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings. Their behavior is dictated by the weather as well. Rain provides more areas for them to drink, and can eliminate a need to travel more sustainable water sources. The bucks will still be in bachelor groups of three to as many as ten in a group. They will often bed down together so it can be difficult to close the distance. They will tend to use the same game trails and with good pre-scouting you might be able to pattern a bucks movements. I would expect their behavior to change after all of the hunting pressure from opening weekend.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs has a high bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or call the local dispatch center (435 789-4222). The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with trying not to get there meat to spoil in the heat. I would plan on hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Dolores Triangle typically leave the higher elevations of Colorado during mid to late fall and head for their Utah wintering range at lower elevations. Weather conditions in Colorado highly affect how many deer migrate into Utah, and when they come. Winter range occurs throughout the unit, but deer tend to head South and West on the range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in mid-late October. Most deer will be traveling to the Triangle at this time and you will be able to get an idea of what kind of bucks are typical on the unit. The amount and severity of winter storms will increase the number of deer that winter on the unit, numbers can change weekly. Early season scouting in the Glade Park area of Colorado may also give you some idea as to what kind of bucks to expect on the hunt. Once the rut starts, look for does, bucks will be around them. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. this can be of great benefit to hunters on these late hunts. Recommended areas for the La Sal, Dolores Triangle subunit: Dolores Triangle - The unit is not that big, all of the mesa tops should have deer on them during these late hunts, especially if there is any accumulation of snow. Late season snow storms can settle in on this unit, causing some roads to be impassible.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: This is a late season hunt. Weather on this hunt unit tends to be cold with snow conditions, but can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit is managed as a trophy limited entry unit for deer and elk. There is a Landowner Association on the unit and the private property comprises about 35% of the total acreage. This unit encompasses pine, aspen, and open sagebrush in the higher elevations and desert scrub in lower elevation wintering habitat. The private property is posted and a GPS showing private/public property boundaries is recommended. Even though the unit has private property, there is still 65% public land that is huntable. Don't expect to gain access to hunt the private property. The average buck taken is a 24 inch 4x4.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer on this unit are typically on the top of Diamond Mountain during all three hunting seasons. The top of Diamond Mountain is where the majority of the water and food is during the fall. After the rut, mule deer will move north to Browns Park and south to the Diamond Rim and lower elevations during the winter, depending on snow depth. The migration is mostly to either the north or south. Scouting Tips: Deer are pretty habitual until the rut starts. Scouting trips are recommended, especially for the archery and muzzleloader hunts. The bigger, more mature bucks are sometimes harder to find and scouting trips are recommended if you wish to take a bigger mature buck. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Deer do have areas they like and stay in but they can move if they get spooked. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November to mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas on Diamond Mountain: Deer are found throughout much of the unit, depending on time of year. During all three hunts, deer are typically found higher in elevation and haven't moved to their wintering habitat yet, which includes Browns Park and south of Diamond Rim. There are a lot of roads in the bottom of the draws on this unit so deer can be seen easily from vehicles. Good public land areas to hunt include Wild Mountain, Diamond Rim, Top of Crouse Canyon, Marshall Draw, Warren Draw, Mail Draw, and Little Hole. Most of the ridges on this unit are public land and are accessible through public lands, although not always easily. Most of the public land on Diamond Mountain is BLM and DWR-owned lands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty in the mountains on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past in this unit. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, wind, and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Typically, the weather is warm throughout the archery season.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Book Cliffs offers a challenging landscape. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. Most of the canyons and ridges have roads or ATV trails to provide access. There are plenty of areas to hike and get away from the main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend. There are two roads that allow you to drive across the majority of the Book Cliffs. The Kings Well Rd starts at the Seep Ridge Rd on the west side, and it can take you all the way to the Dragon Rd on the east side. The Indian Ridge Road starts at the Seep Ridge Rd and goes through the bottom of Sweet Water, top of McCook Ridge, Bitter Creek, and to Big Park. It is a great road to locate deer during this time of year. Most hunters are able to locate 20-40 bucks a day. The Book Cliffs has one of the highest success rates for rifle hunters in the state. Some hunters are disappointed in the quality of bucks so I would suggest trying to spend some time in the area to become familiar with the steep terrain and the quality of bucks. There are not many 30" bucks on this unit. The average buck harvested on this unit is basically a 23" 4 point or 3 x 4. This area provides challenging terrain in a remote part of the state. There are other hunts that coincide with the any weapon deer hunt. They are: limited entry bear, bear pursuit, and upland game hunts. In the past deer hunters have had negative experiences with bear hunters in the area. Please be aware that everyone has an equal right to hunt this area. If you really want to get away from ATV and vehicle traffic I would plan on hiking in the more remote areas. A Book Cliffs deer committee was formed to come up with a solution to the buck to doe problem on this unit. The southern side of the unit consistently has a higher buck to doe ratio than the north. It was proposed by the committee to split the rifle hunt to harvest more bucks on the south, side to bring the buck to doe ratio into compliance with the management plan. The Wildlife Board accepted the proposal and now we have two hunt units for the any weapon hunt. The reason we didn't split the other hunts was because the deer are concentrated along the Divide Ridge during the archery and muzzle loader hunts. This unit offers more road access, and more total deer than the southern unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The deer will be relatively close to water sources until it snows. There are numerous springs in the heads of the steep canyons. The local ranches keep small ponds and reservoirs full, but don't rely on them to always be full of water. There are four main drainages that have streams. They are: Willow Creek, Sweet Water, Bitter Creek, and Evacuation Creek. The deer will be congregated around these areas because they are key water sources while they migrate off higher elevations. The east side of the Book Cliffs borders Colorado, and there are several deer later in the hunt that migrate down from Colorado. Some of the areas where hunters have harvested in the past are: Flat Rock, Agency Draw, Willow Creek, Wood Canyon, Indian Ridge, PR Springs, McCook Ridge, Bitter Creek, Big Park, Wolf Den, Atchee Ridge, Three Mile Canyon, Evacuation Creek, Park Canyon, and Rabbit Mountain. The elevation plays a key role in where you will find deer during this time of year. I suggest if you are not seeing deer to change your elevation. Migration Patterns: The mule deer migrate to the higher elevation in late spring. The does fawn on the summer range, and most of the bucks stay on the summer range until they strip their velvet. The Book Cliffs has limited by summer range. By mid-October the deer start to migrate to their winter range and can be found in the transitional zone. This is a large area where the deer can hole up until storms start to move them to their winter range. This area is made up of a lot of pinyon/juniper trees, mahogany, bitter brush, sage brush and grasses. From past biological studies we have found that approximately two thirds of the deer migrate to the north. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. During this time the bucks are not likely to stay in the same general area. It would be best to come out a few days before the hunt opener to find the elevation where the majority of the bucks are located. I would scout the transitional areas. I would not plan on scouting during the late summer or early fall for this hunt. The deer will start to leave the high country until early to mid-October. I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset. There are several recovering burned areas on McCook Ridge. Behavior: Like other wildlife, deer are most active in the early mornings and evenings. Their behavior is dictated by the weather as well. As the hunt progresses I would expect to see the bucks become more active during the day. Rain and snow provides much needed drinking water for deer, and can eliminate a need to travel to more sustainable water sources. The bucks will be breaking up from their bachelor groups. I would expect their behavior and routine to change after all of the hunting pressure from opening weekend
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice. The Book Cliffs has a high bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or call the local dispatch center (435 789-4222).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and snow. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a Limited Entry hunt unit and is managed for 25-35 bucks per 100 does. These are late season hunts, during the rut, 150 inch bucks are not uncommon. Hunters should be aware of the Utah/Colorado state line boundary. Utah hunters are not permitted to hunt in Colorado.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Dolores Triangle typically leave the higher elevations of Colorado during mid to late fall and head for their Utah wintering range at lower elevations. Weather conditions in Colorado highly affect how many deer migrate into Utah, and when they come. Winter range occurs throughout the unit, but deer tend to head South and West on the range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in mid-late October. Most deer will be traveling to the Triangle at this time and you will be able to get an idea of what kind of bucks are typical on the unit. The amount and severity of winter storms will increase the number of deer that winter on the unit, numbers can change weekly. Early season scouting in the Glade Park area of Colorado may also give you some idea as to what kind of bucks to expect on the hunt. Once the rut starts, look for does, bucks will be around them. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Mule Deer Rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. this can be of great benefit to hunters on these late hunts. Recommended areas for the La Sal, Dolores Triangle subunit: Dolores Triangle- The unit is not that big. All of the mesa tops should have deer on them during these late hunts, especially if there is any accumulation of snow. Access is almost entirely restricted to coming in from the Colorado side, through Glade Park. Limited/seasonal access to the unit is available on the Western point of the unit, near Robert's Bottom.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell phone service is very limited on this unit. It is a good idea to let someone know where you are and when you will return. I would recommend having a four-wheel drive vehicle during this hunt, with tire chains or a tow strap, just in case. Late season snow storms can settle in on this unit, causing some roads to be impassible.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: This is a late season hunt. Weather on this hunt unit tends to be cold with snow conditions, but can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a Limited Entry hunt unit and is managed for 25-35 bucks per 100 does. The average harvested age of bucks on the unit is around 4.5 yrs old. Given these two variables, there should be opportunity for mature bucks to be harvested. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on Elk Ridge typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range, but deer tend to head South and West from the range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the San Juan, Elk Ridge subunit: Elk Ridge - Any weapon hunters should focus on mid to low elevation areas. If any snow accumulates, deer will start heading for lower elevations consisting of oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, intermixed with pinyon/juniper stands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the Abajos. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.
