hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit is managed as a trophy limited entry unit for deer and elk. There is a Landowner Association on the unit and the private property comprises about 35% of the total acreage. This unit encompasses pine, aspen, and open sagebrush in the higher elevations and desert scrub in lower elevation wintering habitat. The private property is posted and a GPS showing private/public property boundaries is recommended. Even though the unit has private property, there is still 65% public land that is huntable. Don't expect to gain access to hunt the private property. The average buck taken is a 24 inch 4x4.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer on this unit are typically on the top of Diamond Mountain during all three hunting seasons. The top of Diamond Mountain is where the majority of the water and food is during the fall. After the rut, mule deer will move north to Browns Park and south to the Diamond Rim and lower elevation during the winter, depending on snow depth. The migration is mostly to either the north or south. Scouting Tips: Deer are pretty habitual until the rut starts. Scouting trips are recommended, especially close to the start of the hunt. The bigger, more mature bucks are sometimes harder to find and scouting trips are recommended if you wish to take a bigger mature buck. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Deer do have areas they like and stay in but they can move if they get spooked. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not typically affect this hunt. Recommended areas on Diamond Mountain: Deer are found throughout much of the unit, depending on time of year. During all three hunts, deer are typically found higher in elevation and haven't moved to their wintering habitat yet, which includes Browns Park and south of Diamond Rim. There are a lot of roads in the bottom of the draws on this unit so deer can be seen easily from vehicles. Good public land areas to hunt include Wild Mountain, Diamond Rim, Top of Crouse Canyon, Marshall Draw, Warren Draw, Mail Draw, and Little Hole. Most of the ridges on this unit are public land and are accessible through public lands, although not always easily. Most of the public land on Diamond Mountain is BLM and DWR-owned lands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty in the mountains on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past in this unit. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable or very muddy.

As the hunt progresses, the bucks begin to enter a pre-rut phase and will become more visible. If the unit gets some snow, the hunting improves greatly and hunters may see more bucks. hunt_bio_general_information: Most hunters are able to locate 20-40 bucks a day. The Book Cliffs has one of the highest success rates for archery hunters in the state. Some hunters are disappointed in the quality of bucks so I would suggest trying to spend some time in the area to become familiar with the steep terrain and the quality of bucks. There are not many 30 in bucks on this unit. The average buck harvested on this unit is basically a 22" 4 point or 3x4. This area provides challenging terrain in a remote part of the state. There are other hunts that coincide with the muzzleloader deer hunt. They are: limited entry elk, limited entry bear, bear pursuit, and upland game hunts. In the past, deer hunters have had negative experiences with bear hunters in the area. Please be aware that everyone has an equal right to hunt this area. The Book Cliffs is an incredibly large area, but during summer and early fall most of the animals are congregated in a small area. If you really want to get away from ATV and vehicle traffic I would plan on hunting in the Little Creek WMA (roadless area). The Ute Tribe as agreed to allow sportsmen to access this area across Ute Tribal trust lands. Once you leave the Sego Trailhead parking area and start down the Went Ridge trail you are on Tribal land for the first few miles. There are signs indicating that you have permission from the Tribe to use this route. We ask that you please keep this area clean and stay on the main trail until you are off of Ute Tribal land. This is a privilege and abuse of this area could lead to sportsmen losing this access permit. This hunt excludes all Ute Tribal lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: You will find the majority of the deer located along the Divide Road. The Book Cliffs range divides the north from the south with a long ridge that runs east to west. The Seep Ridge Rd becomes the Divide Rd and runs east to Colorado and West to Steer Ridge. The Book Cliffs has limited summer range. The majority of the deer are going to be located along the Divide Rd. The deer will be relatively close to water sources. There are numerous springs in the heads of the steep canyons. The local ranches keep small ponds and reservoirs full, but don't rely on them to always be full of water. Some of the areas where hunters have harvested in the past are: Rat Hole Ridge and Canyon, Rail Road Canyon, Black Horse and Saddle Horse Ridge, PR Springs, Horse Point, Moon Ridge, Cherry Mesa, Rock Springs Mesa, Cedar Camp, Steer Ridge, and Little Creek Ridge. The elevation plans a key role in where you will find deer during this time of year. I suggest if you are not seeing deer to change your elevation. Migration Patterns: The mule deer migrate to the higher elevation in late spring. The does fawn on the summer range, and most of the bucks stay on the summer range until they strip their velvet. The Book Cliffs has limited by summer range. By mid-October the deer start to migrate to their winter range and can be found in the transitional zone. This is a large area where the deer can hole up until storms start to move them to their winter range. This area is made up of a lot of pinyon/juniper trees, mahogany, bitter brush, sage brush and grasses. From past biological studies we have found that approximately two thirds of the deer migrate to the north. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. I would scout the higher ridges where oak brush is prominent. Your preseason scouting can really pay off on this hunt. The deer won't start to leave the high country until mid-October. The bucks might not be on the same ridge, but I would expect them to stay with-in a five mile radius. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset. There are several recovering burned areas along the Divide. The oak brush is starting to get more established and creates great habitat for mule deer. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings. Their behavior is dictated by the weather as well. Rain provides more areas for them to drink, and can eliminate a need to travel more sustainable water sources. The bucks will still be in bachelor groups of three to as many as ten in a group. They will often bed down together so it can be difficult to close the distance. They will tend to use the same game trails and with good pre scouting you might be able to pattern a bucks movements. I would expect their behavior to change after all of the hunting pressure from opening weekend.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice. The Book Cliffs has a high bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or call the local dispatch center (435 789-4222).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and snow. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

Hunters should be aware of the Utah/Colorado state line boundary. Utah hunters are not permitted to hunt in Colorado.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Dolores Triangle typically leave the higher elevations of Colorado during mid to late fall and head for their Utah wintering range at lower elevations. Weather conditions in Colorado highly affect how many deer migrate into Utah, and when they come. Winter range occurs throughout the unit, but deer tend to head South and West on the range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in mid-late October. Most deer will be traveling to the Triangle at this time and you will be able to get an idea of what kind of bucks are typical on the unit. The amount and severity of winter storms will increase the number of deer that winter on the unit, numbers can change weekly. Early season scouting in the Glade Park area of Colorado may also give you some idea as to what kind of bucks to expect on the hunt. Once the rut starts, look for does, bucks will be around them. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. this can be of great benefit to hunters on these late hunts. Recommended areas for the La Sal, Dolores Triangle subunit: Dolores Triangle - The unit is not that big, all of the mesa tops should have deer on them during these late hunts, especially if there is any accumulation of snow. Access is almost entirely restricted to coming in from the Colorado side, through Glade Park. Limited/seasonal access to the unit is available on the Western point of the unit, near Robert's Bottom.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell phone service is very limited on this unit. It is a good idea to let someone know where you are and when you will return. I would recommend having a four-wheel drive vehicle during this hunt, with tire chains or a tow strap, just in case. Late season snow storms can settle in on this unit, causing some roads to be impassible.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: This is a late season hunt. Weather on this hunt unit tends to be cold with snow conditions, but can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Anthro Subunit Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation towards the end of October and first part of November. Most of the wintering areas are on Tribal Land and private lands Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Anthro subunit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer. Because the density is so low, if you do find any bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. There is a lot of area East of Antelope Canyon all the way to the Green River, with even lower deer densities, while hunting these areas your best chance is finding water. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Nutter's Ridge - USFS higher elevation, a few large aspen stands, very accessible Jeep Trail Ridge - USFS just East of Nutter's Ridge, large canyons with a few aspens, several water sources Wire Fence Ridge - USFS rough road, biggest aspen stands on Anthro, good burned side hills Alkaline/Choke Cherry - USFS very open country, few deer, East of Jeep Trail Wells Draw - BLM lands, low elevation pinyon/juniper, low density Cottonwood Ridge - USFS difficult access, higher elevation, many timbered hill sides Range Creek Subunit There are higher deer densities on the Range Creek subunit than the Anthro subunit. There is however an abundance of private land in much of the optimal habitat. The advantage of the late season muzzleloader hunt is that some of these deer will migrate off of high elevation private lands on to public lands in November. Popular hunting areas on primarily public lands on the Range Creek Subunit include; Harmon Canyon, Cottonwood Ridge, Cold Springs Ridge, Cedar Ridge, and lower Range Creek. Deer can also be found on the benches north and east of Price along the airport road and near the mouths of Coal and Soldier Creeks. These latter areas are at lower elevations (5500 - 6500 feet) so will only have large amounts of deer if there has been some snow.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

The Pine Valley Unit is 90% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Most deer on this hunt should be on their winter ranges.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. This hunt is pre-rut but the bucks are definitely staging for the rut and will be in close proximity to the large congregations of does. Recommended areas to hunt: The Pine Valley Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several livestock tanks, springs and guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: North end of Beaver Dam Mtns - BLM and SITLA lands west of St. George. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Deer movement into this area can vary from year to year depending on migration. Tobin Bench to Motaqua - BLM and SITLA with some small private lands in the Motaqua area. Deer migration is more reliable in this area with increasing numbers on the second weekend of the hunt. Above Dameron and Diamond Valley- BLM, Forest Service and SITLA lands at higher elevations above Dameron and Diamond Valley. Enterprise North Hills and New Castle- BLM, Forest Service, Private and SITLA lands. Deer begin moving into these areas about the second week of October. Most deer will be in the agricultural fields at night and then available on Public Lands during the day. Bumblebee and Sweat Hills -BLM, Forest Service and SITLA lands West and South of Cedar City. Some deer may remain high on Bumblebee Mtn. until heavier snow storms drive them down.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions. Day time tempretures should be in the 60's and the morning will be below 32 degrees.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Thousand Lakes unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit has some great deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced an increase in the deer population and an increase in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good for those willing to hunt away from roads and ATV trails. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters have been noticing an increasing number of mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be in parts of the unit where aspen habitat is available. The southern portion of the unit is drier, and has fewer deer. During the Muzzleloader season most of the deer still tend to be in the higher elevations though some have began to move down a little. Hunter densities are not as high and the weather is often pleasant. Remember that Capitol Reef National Park is on the eastern portion of this unit and the park is closed to hunting and ATV travel.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the Muzzleloader season deer are scattered over the entire unit. Much of the buck movement is dictated by weather conditions. Bucks tend to remain higher in elevation than does until the rut gets underway. The table is above 11,000 ft elevation and generally most deer move off the Table by late September. Most of the deer tend to be at the intersection of the conifer/aspen habitats and the aspen/mountain brush/sage habitats. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some very remote areas on this unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms often occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit is managed as a trophy limited entry unit for deer and elk. There is a Landowner Association on the unit and the private property comprises about 35% of the total acreage. This unit encompasses pine, aspen, and open sagebrush in the higher elevations and desert scrub in lower elevation wintering habitat. The private property is posted and a GPS showing private/public property boundaries is recommended. Even though the unit has private property, there is still 65% public land that is huntable. Don't expect to gain access to hunt the private property. The average buck taken is a 24 inch 4x4.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer on this unit are typically on the top of Diamond Mountain during the muzzleloader hunt. The top of Diamond Mountain is where the majority of the water and food is during the fall. After the rut, mule deer will move north to Browns Park and south to the Diamond Rim and lower elevations during the winter, depending on snow depth. The migration is mostly to either the north or south. Scouting Tips: Deer are pretty habitual until the rut starts. Scouting trips are recommended, especially for the muzzleloader hunt. The bigger, more mature bucks are sometimes harder to find and scouting trips are recommended if you wish to take a bigger mature buck. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Deer do have areas they like and stay in but they can move if they get spooked. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas on Diamond Mountain: Deer are found throughout much of the unit, depending on time of year. During all three hunts, deer are typically found higher in elevation and haven't moved to their wintering habitat yet, which includes Browns Park and south of Diamond Rim. There are a lot of roads in the bottom of the draws on this unit so deer can be seen easily from vehicles. Good public land areas to hunt include Wild Mountain, Diamond Rim, Top of Crouse Canyon, Marshall Draw, Warren Draw, Mail Draw, and Little Hole. Most of the ridges on this unit are public land and are accessible through public lands, although not always easily. Most of the public land on Diamond Mountain is BLM and DWR-owned lands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty in the mountains on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past in this unit. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable or very muddy.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year some nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The unit includes the High Uintas Wilderness area. The Wilderness can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also less deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. Almost all of the deer will be moved down out of the wilderness area before this hunt. Road access on much of the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain. Migration: Deer on this unit move down in elevation for the winter and they winter primarily on Ute Tribal Lands and on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. The deer also move down towards the Tribal Land boundary as soon as they get much hunting pressure. There is very little hunting pressure on the Tribal Lands so some deer have learned to go there as soon as hunting pressure starts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt gets close to the the mule deer rut that usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Yellowstone: During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for deer. Every canyon across the South Slope, Yellowstone has deer and they are of similar quality. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: North Fork of the Duchesne- limited road access Blind Stream- limited road access, tribal land down low, popular area Log Hollow- must cross Tribal Lands to access, rough roads Rock Creek- paved road access, steep areas Pigeon Water- popular area but hunters must be aware of tribal boundary Bear Wallow- hunters must be aware of tribal boundary, steep terrain Lake Fork/Moon Lake- paved road access, some private property along the paved road. Yellowstone- rough roads, need to be aware of Tribal boundary 77 Flat/Burnt Mill- gravel roads, a little flatter area, be aware of Tribal boundary Dry Gulch- very rough road, steep terrain, be aware of Tribal boundary on the east. Uinta Canyon- Tribal lands down low, steep Terrain Elk Horn Loop- gravel roads that go almost to the summit of the Uintas, lots of opportunity to scatter out. Whiterocks Canyon- Whiterocks river is the eastern unit boundary, steep terrain.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for warm & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or snowy conditions. Early snow storms occur often during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Southwest Desert is a very large unit with a small population of deer that are widely spread. This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. On years with good pinion nut production the deer may spend more time in the pinion tree areas and be harder to spot.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation towards the end of October and first part of November. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Southwest Desert unit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer because the density is so low. When you do find bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. The higher elevation areas above the thick pinion and juniper are the best for locating deer. South Wah Wah Range - BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range - BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Black Hills - BLM and SITLA lands located southwest of Minersville. Baboon Peak, Dry Willow Peak and Little Horse Valley areas. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas to hunt: There are numerous areas to hunt on this unit. The areas surrounding Strawberry Reservoir and Currant Creek Reservoir are excellent for deer hunting. They are easy to access with many roads and trails and camping areas. This of course leads to many people hunting these areas. There are very few areas on this unit without a road in the general area. There is far less hunting pressure on the Avintaquin unit, but that is because the overall deer density is much lower and the terrain is more rugged. This unit has very large aspen stands that hold a lot of deer in the early fall. Many of the best bucks taken each year come from these aspen stands. In the summer there are deer in the more open higher areas, but once they get pressured by hunters they will move into the lower, thicker aspen stands. These areas are difficult to hunt, because of the leaves on the trees and fewer open areas to glass with optics. There are also many lower areas with several different browse species, including; oak brush, service berry, mountain mahogany, bitter brush, snow berry, sage brush, etc. These areas also have deer in them during the hunt, but at a lower density. The deer on this unit tend to migrate from the higher elevations in the West to the lower elevations in East. With the later season dates for this hunt, many of the deer will be starting their migration. Some areas to hunt include the following: Currant Creek Reservoir Area - high elevation, large aspen stands, very accessible, high deer density for the unit. Low Pass Creek- near Currant Creek Reservoir, rough road, great for ATV's, great for glassing up high. West Fork of the Duchesne- limited ATV access, but open to trucks. Chicken Creek/Race Track- popular area, but holds a lot of deer and bucks CO-OP Creek -Very Popular area, near Highway 40, great camping, large aspen stands Trout Creek- many bucks taken here opening weekend Wildcat WMA - good access, flat on top, a lot of pressure, many yearling bucks taken here. North Fork of Deep Creek - borders private land, limited access by road, great horse area Tabby Mountain - great for ATV's, better after snow storms, mostly public land. Coleman Basin/Red Creek Mtn- SITLA land, some areas without roads, rough roads Reservation Ridge -fewer deer, but fewer people Strawberry Peak- High elevation, large areas near by with no road access, Cow Hollow, Slab Canyon, low deer density Timber Canyon/Long Ridge- low deer density, rough terrain, better after storms, rough roads. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is comprised primarily of sagebrush in the lower elevations, transitioning into juniper woodlands. The higher elevations have serviceberry, snowberry and bitterbush, with pockets of chokecherry, aspen and conifer. This unit is primarily the Sheeprock and Simpson Mts. This area is very accessible, with many dirt roads. Spend some time in the area to become familiar with the steep terrain, access points and the quality of bucks. Because this is a desert unit, precipitation affects antler growth a lot from one year to the next. If you hope to get away from other hunters you will need to go places ATV's can't go. This area is patrolled quite frequently by DWR personnel. Keep this in mind when you are transporting your game. Try to make it easy to access the permit and tag on the animal.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most of the deer are found on the Sheeprock and Simpson Mountains. Few deer are on Desert and Keg Mountains during the hunting season. The average buck harvested on this unit is a 24" wide four point, which means half the bucks harvested are smaller than this. A hunter will have to spend a lot of time and effort to harvest a buck larger than 25" wide. Most of the deer are associated with mountain brush (buckbrush) communities, including serviceberry and snowberry. Concentrate your efforts in the highest elevations and near water sources. Deer can also be found in agricultural areas, written permission is needed to hunt these areas. Most muzzleloader hunters are able to locate 10 or more bucks a day. This unit could experience a wide range of weather events.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "In-reach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunderstorms can cause muddy road conditions and rare flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with keeping their harvest meat cool. Plan on hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Zion unit is an area that has had good mule deer production and the population is generally at or over the objective in the management plan. The unit is also over the general season buck objective of 18-20 bucks per 100 does. This has resulted in the opportunity to hunt mule deer during this late season muzzleloader hunt to provide opportunity and harvest additional bucks to reach the unit objectives. High deer densities can be found across winter range. The highest densities can be found on the southeastern portion of the unit including areas along and south of SR9 and east of Zion National Park. Landmark areas include Poverty Flat, Elephant Gap, and the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park. There is no hunting allowed in Zion. Substantial numbers of wintering deer may also be found south of Cedar City along I-15, south to the New Harmony exit. Additionally, good mule deer winter range exists south of Zion National Park on Smith Mesa and the surrounding drainages.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of hunters tend to hunt on public lands managed by the BLM and SITLA. Typically hunters are successful if they are certain where public lands and access roads exist within the hunt boundary, so study some property boundary maps. A 4WD or ATV will be useful to for access at this time of year. Migration Patterns: The migratory segments of this population may begin their fall movements in late September and October. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Most deer will be on winter range during this hunt. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars will be helpful. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens since deer are still moving and will be in or close to the rut. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points. Behavior: Mule deer should be in rut and preparing for winter during this hunt and therefore may be found in large groups. They should be in a high level of activity feeding and in rutting behaviors.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Zion unit offers substantial truck and ATV access. Cellular phone coverage within this hunt boundary can be spotty. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, as well as winter conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: Most hunters are able to locate 20-40 bucks a day. The Book Cliffs has one of the highest success rates for archery hunters in the state. Some hunters are disappointed in the quality of bucks so I would suggest trying to spend some time in the area to become familiar with the steep terrain and the quality of bucks. There are not many 30 in bucks on this unit. The average buck harvested on this unit is basically a 22" 4 point or 3x4. This area provides challenging terrain in a remote part of the state. There are other hunts that coincide with the muzzleloader deer hunt. They are: limited entry elk, limited entry bear, bear pursuit, and upland game hunts. In the past, deer hunters have had negative experiences with bear hunters in the area. Please be aware that everyone has an equal right to hunt this area. The Book Cliffs is an incredibly large area, but during summer and early fall most of the animals are congregated in a small area. If you really want to get away from ATV and vehicle traffic I would plan on hunting in the Little Creek WMA (roadless area). The Ute Tribe as agreed to allow sportsmen to access this area across Ute Tribal trust lands. Once you leave the Sego Trailhead parking area and start down the Went Ridge trail you are on Tribal land for the first few miles. There are signs indicating that you have permission from the Tribe to use this route. We ask that you please keep this area clean and stay on the main trail until you are off of Ute Tribal land. This is a privilege and abuse of this area could lead to sportsmen losing this access permit. This hunt excludes all Ute Tribal lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: You will find the majority of the deer located along the Divide Road. The Book Cliffs range divides the north from the south with a long ridge that runs east to west. The Seep Ridge Rd becomes the Divide Rd and runs east to Colorado and West to Steer Ridge. The Book Cliffs has limited summer range. The majority of the deer are going to be located along the Divide Rd. The deer will be relatively close to water sources. There are numerous springs in the heads of the steep canyons. The local ranches keep small ponds and reservoirs full, but don't rely on them to always be full of water. Some of the areas where hunters have harvested in the past are: Rat Hole Ridge and Canyon, Rail Road Canyon, Black Horse and Saddle Horse Ridge, PR Springs, Horse Point, Moon Ridge, Cherry Mesa, Rock Springs Mesa, Cedar Camp, Steer Ridge, and Little Creek Ridge. The elevation plans a key role in where you will find deer during this time of year. I suggest if you are not seeing deer to change your elevation. Migration Patterns: The mule deer migrate to the higher elevation in late spring. The does fawn on the summer range, and most of the bucks stay on the summer range until they strip their velvet. The Book Cliffs has limited by summer range. By mid-October the deer start to migrate to their winter range and can be found in the transitional zone. This is a large area where the deer can hole up until storms start to move them to their winter range. This area is made up of a lot of pinyon/juniper trees, mahogany, bitter brush, sage brush and grasses. From past biological studies we have found that approximately two thirds of the deer migrate to the north. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. I would scout the higher ridges where oak brush is prominent. Your preseason scouting can really pay off on this hunt. The deer won't start to leave the high country until mid-October. The bucks might not be on the same ridge, but I would expect them to stay with-in a five mile radius. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset. There are several recovering burned areas along the Divide. The oak brush is starting to get more established and creates great habitat for mule deer. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings. Their behavior is dictated by the weather as well. Rain provides more areas for them to drink, and can eliminate a need to travel more sustainable water sources. The bucks will still be in bachelor groups of three to as many as ten in a group. They will often bed down together so it can be difficult to close the distance. They will tend to use the same game trails and with good pre scouting you might be able to pattern a bucks movements. I would expect their behavior to change after all of the hunting pressure from opening weekend.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice. The Book Cliffs has a high bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or call the local dispatch center (435 789-4222).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and snow. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a Limited Entry hunt unit and is managed for 25-35 bucks per 100 does. The average harvested age of bucks on the unit is around 4.5 yrs old. Given these two variables, there should be opportunity for mature bucks to be harvested. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on Elk Ridge typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range, but deer tend to head South and West from the range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the San Juan, Elk Ridge subunit: Elk Ridge - For the archery hunt, focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. These areas consist of large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding. Muzzleloader hunters may find bucks in the high country, but should also focus on mid elevations. Any weapon hunters should focus on mid to low elevation areas. If any snow accumulates, deer will start heading for lower elevations consisting of oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, intermixed with pinyon/juniper stands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the Abajos. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit is managed as a trophy limited entry unit for deer and elk. There is a Landowner Association on the unit and the private property comprises about 35% of the total acreage. This unit encompasses pine, aspen, and open sagebrush in the higher elevations and desert scrub in lower elevation wintering habitat. The private property is posted and a GPS showing private/public property boundaries is recommended. Even though the unit has private property, there is still 65% public land that is huntable. Don't expect to gain access to hunt the private property. The average buck taken is a 24 inch 4x4.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer on this unit are typically on the top of Diamond Mountain during all three hunting seasons. The top of Diamond Mountain is where the majority of the water and food is during the fall. After the rut, mule deer will move north to Browns Park and south to the Diamond Rim and lower elevations during the winter, depending on snow depth. The migration is mostly to either the north or south. Scouting Tips: Deer are pretty habitual until the rut starts. Scouting trips are recommended, especially for the archery and muzzleloader hunts. The bigger, more mature bucks are sometimes harder to find and scouting trips are recommended if you wish to take a bigger mature buck. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Deer do have areas they like and stay in but they can move if they get spooked. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas on Diamond Mountain: Deer are found throughout much of the unit, depending on time of year. During all three hunts, deer are typically found higher in elevation and haven't moved to their wintering habitat yet, which includes Browns Park and south of Diamond Rim. There are a lot of roads in the bottom of the draws on this unit so deer can be seen easily from vehicles. Good public land areas to hunt include Wild Mountain, Diamond Rim, Top of Crouse Canyon, Marshall Draw, Warren Draw, Mail Draw, and Little Hole. Most of the ridges on this unit are public land and are accessible through public lands, although not always easily. Most of the public land on Diamond Mountain is BLM and DWR-owned lands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty in the mountains on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past in this unit. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable or very muddy.

hunt_bio_general_information: The majority of land is managed by the BLM and forest Service. There is also a significant amount of private land. This unit does have a Landowner Association. There is private land and some of it is accessible through the DWR's Walk-in-Access Program (http://wildlife.utah.gov/walkinaccess/).
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is primarily the Sheeprock and Simpson Mts.. I would not spend precious time/gas (unless you something different) on Desert or Keg Mts. The average buck has been near a 24 inch/4x4. Last year the average slipped down a little but there is still good bucks out there. Archery: hunters should expect this unit to provide a spot and stalk type archery hunt. Hunter will find bucks to be high in elevation and near stream habitat. Expect dry conditions and monsoon seasons. Weather can change in a heartbeat so be prepared for a down pour. Waterholes may not be a productive hunt method if these conditions occur. Bucks will frequently change up their routine. Muzzleloader: hunters tend to see many bucks in the canyons the first few days. Expect mid season buck movements to change. Bucks start moving and may not be where you've seen them before. Keep looking. I've had many reports over the years that bucks are gone the second weekend. They are still there but moved to other canyons or areas. Any Weapon: hunters should expect changes in weather and possible muddy roads. This unit could experience a wide range of weather events. If it snows I would still expect bucks to remain higher in elevation. Some bucks will transition over to the south side. If the weather is bad expect bucks to be hid in brush and cover. The Sheeprock and Simpson mountain ranges are remote areas in Utah. There are few service stations. Gas is available in Vernon, Eureka, and Lynndyl. Bring plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice. The west or south side is desert and dirt road. Private land holdings limit access to canyons. If you want to hunt those canyons attain permission or go over the top from the other side.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road conditions and rare flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with trying not to get there meat to spoil in the heat. I would plan on hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced small decreas in the deer population and in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters have been noticing good numbers of mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced a decrease in the deer population and in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters have been noticing an increased number of mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer. Limited Entry Muzzleloader Season: In late October and early November the deer on the Fish Lake unit tend to be very spread out. On much of the unit some of the deer have moved onto or near their winter range. Snow levels permitting, there are also some deer on the highest peaks. Hunters should use scouting just prior to the season to locate deer concentrations. Hunters often concentrate in areas where deer are easily seen near agricultural areas. Migration Patterns: Some of the deer on Fish Lake unit begin to migrate to or closer to their winter range in mid-October. By the time this early November hunt arrives a sizable portion of the herd is often in the transitional ranges between their winter and summer ranges. However many deer also stay as high as they can until heavy snows push them lower. Most of the migration is rather simple, the deer just move up or down in elevation. However there are some deer that move from their summering areas on the north and central parts of the unit to the southern, eastern, and western parts of the unit closer to their winter range. Mule Deer Rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid December. For this hunt expect bucks to be just beginning to rut. Many of the bucks will be with the does but some will not. Recommended Areas to Hunt on the Fish Lake Unit: There are deer spread across the entire Fish Lake unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. During this early November muzzleloader hunt the deer will be very spread out unless there have been significant snow storms. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want. If deer numbers are not significant at you elevation try lower or high elevations depending on the snow.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a large area and cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. During the archery season hunters should be prepared to cool harvested game quickly due to warm temperatures.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is a migration study underway to look at timing and routes of migration for North Slope deer. We ask that collared deer are not killed. If one is, DO NOT CUT THE COLLAR; remove the collar by loosening the lock nuts and call the number on the collar or the local biologist. This unit encompasses lodgepole pine, open sagebrush, and desert scrub. Hunters should expect to see other deer and elk hunters and other public land users. This hunt coincides with a limited entry elk hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer in the High Uintas do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the west side of the North Slope to the east end of the North Slope for the winter. During the winter, deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats all along the North Slope. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the general rifle hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country. During warm, dry falls deer stay up higher longer. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November to mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the North Slope: Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Depending on weather conditions, most of the deer on the Summit portion get pushed down into Wyoming before the Any Weapon hunt begins. Also, high country deer are typically pushed down out of the High Country by mid-October if any early season snow storms hit. The majority of the deer in the 3 Corners portion of the unit stay up high on Bear Mountain, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, and Bender Mountain until later in October/early November when deer start showing up in Browns Park for the winter. This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure during the regular season hunts, especially in Browns Park, Goslin Mountain, South Valley, Dowd Mountain, and along Hwy 44. Areas with highest harvest success include Dowd Mountain, Death Valley, South Valley, Greendale Junction (along Highway 44 and 191), Red Creek Flat, Clay Basin, Goslin Mountain, and 3 Corners. Hunters that receive written permission from private landowners in Manila also do well.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the fall. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure. Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Most higher elevation Raft River Mountains deer will remain high on the range until snow depths push them down into the sagebrush flats. Access to higher elevations is through One Mile Canyon, George Creek Canyon, Johnson Canyon, and Wildcat Canyon. Deer are plentiful and hunting opportunities exist up every canyon. Deer along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range can be found up Kimbell Creek, Red Banks, and Keg Springs along the west side and near Devil's Playground and Rocky Pass on the east side. Mule deer in the higher elevations do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the Raft River Mountains to the southeast end of the Grouse Creek Mountains for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats from Kelton to Devil's Playground. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country.

A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This is a very productive unit with one of the largest deer herds in the state. Muzzleloader hunters will find most success hunting on summer habitats at 7,500 feet and above. In some years hunting on water sources can be productive but water is generally not limiting on the Manti portion of this unit. Migration Patterns: There is very little deer migration during the muzzleloader hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches east of SR-89 on the west and the sagebrush benches west of SR-6 and SR-10 on the east side of the mountain. There is very little seasonal movement of deer on the San Rafael portion of the unit. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: Upper Fish Creek and it's tributaries. The tributaries include Gooseberry Creek, Silver Creek, C Canyon, and the Straight Fork. This is a roadless area on the north end of the unit. This area has had some prescribed fires recently that has improved deer habitat. It can be accessed from North Skyline Drive on the west or from Scofield Reservoir on the east. The bottom two miles of Upper Fish Creek is privately owned and in a CWMU Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge These ridges have roads going down them. They are northwest of Scofield Reservoir. The bottom 2 miles of these ridges are privately owned. This is excellent habitat in the Pondtown Creek drainage on the north end of the unit. It is best accessed from North Skyline Drive. Trough Spring Ridge This is accessed off of SR-264 southwest of the town of Scofield. It is just above the Skyline Coal Mine. This is the ridge on the east side of Electric Lake. There are some small pockets of private land that are posted well but the majority of the acreage is Forest Service. Much of this ridge burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 which has improved the deer habitat in this area. Gentry Mountain. This is accessed from SR-10 just north of the town of Huntington at Huntington Reservoir. Part of this mountain is privately owned and part of it burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 West of Skyline Drive All the small towns along the west face of the Central Mountains Manti Unit has a canyon road to connect to Skyline Drive. Some roads are fairly rough going with the better access up from Fairview, Ephraim and Mayfiled. Concentrate on side roads and trails from the main canyon roads to get to the more likely areas to find deer. The higher elevations in aspen and sagebrush meadows with water in close proximity will hold some of the mature bucks. hunt_bio_general_information: This is a pre-rut/early rut hunt that highly depends on weather factors. If weather conditions are warm and/or there hasn't yet been a substantial snow storm bucks may be found solitary or in bachelor groups still at high elevations. Snow and cool temperatures may initiate deer migration to lower elevations as well as early rut behavior with bucks being found grouped up with does in transitional mountain brush habitats or winter range. Be flexible in hunting strategies for greatest chance of success.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This is a very productive unit with both road access to high elevations and backcountry hunting opportunities. If the weather has been mild throughout October then most hunters will find most success hunting on summer habitats at 7,500 feet and above. If there has been a few snowstorms then deer will often begin their fall migration and hunters find success on sagebrush and mid-mountain brush type habitats. Migration Patterns: Fall migration is very weather dependent on this unit. Most migration occurs in late November when significant snowfall typically occurs. However, big snowstorms in late October have prompted migration during the any weapon hunt. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to benches on both the east and west sides of the mountain. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. but pre-rut and early rut behaviors may be observed during this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: Nebo Loop, Loafer Mtn, Spencer Fork, and Mona and Santaquin Benches on the north Nebo, Chicken Creek, Log Hollow, Red Ledges, and Sage Flats on the Sanpitch Mtns are good places to start looking. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer. Find a high vantage point and glass a lot of terrain. If you find does with no bucks grouped up with them, keep checking on the area periodically as bucks will begin to group up with does more and more as the hunt goes on.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, snow, and cold. Early winter storms can create muddy or snowy roads and trails.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the La Sals typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Using quality binoculars or spotting scopes will be very valuable to you. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas for the muzzleloader hunt: Muzzleloader hunters will find bucks in the high country, but should also focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. Look for oak patches with intermixed sagebrush meadows and a healthy forbe component.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is managed as a General Season deer hunt and is not necessarily managed for trophy bucks, but every year a few nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The Uintah Mountain range can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also less deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. There are several four wheeler roads and dirt roads that provide a lot of access on much of the unit. The Bonanza unit has very low deer densities.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and tend to stay on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. Mule Deer rut: This hunt gets close to the the mule deer rut that usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Vernal: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. There is a variety of habitat to hunt during this late muzzleloader hunt. There is pinyon/juniper, sage brush savanna, thick lodge pole pine and areas above timber line. The larger openings on the forest are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and rocky terrain. During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for deer. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: Whiterocks Canyon- Whiterocks River is the western unit boundary, steep terrain. Paradise Park- Higher forest terrain, steep forested canyons. Mosby Mountain- High aspen forest, with large sagebrush bowls, excellent habitat. Red Cloud Loop Rd- Long road that starts in Dry Fork Canyon (west of Vernal). It takes you all the way through the Vernal unit, and comes out on Hwy 191.. Taylor Mountain- Great vantage points. Excellent area to glass and locate animals from far distances. Colton Ranger Station- Aspen/conifer mix forest. Limestone, Little V, and Range Study- These areas are east of Hwy 191 and border the Diamond Mountain limited entry deer and elk unit, know the boundary and your location.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: There is spotty cell service in some of the lower elevation hunting areas and typically on the faces overlooking the Uinta Basin. However, there are many areas with no phone service so let someone know where you are going and when you will be back.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for warm & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or snowy conditions. Early snow storms occur often during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: General Considerations: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. There are many CWMUs on this unit and a list of these can be found on the UDWR webpage. Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from East to West, with most of the deer wintering on Wallsburg WMA, Sheep Creek and Diamond Fork canyons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. There are many CWMUs on this unit and a list of these can be found on the UDWR webpage. Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from East to West, with good numbers of deer wintering on Wallsburg WMA, Sheep Creek and Diamond Fork canyons and the Wasatch face. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. After the general season deer hunt is over, bucks will begin to look for does to breed. Start looking on winter ranges as deer start to migrate at lower elevations at this time of year. Recommended areas to hunt: There are numerous areas to hunt on this unit. The areas surrounding Strawberry Reservoir, Sheep Creek, Diamond Fork, Hobble Creek, American Fork canyons, Mt. Timpanogos are excellent for deer hunting. They are easy to access with many roads and trails and camping areas. There are very few areas on this unit without a road in the general area. This unit has very large aspen stands, oak brush can hold a lot of deer in the early fall. In the summer there are deer in the more open higher areas, but once they get pressured by hunters they will move into the lower, thicker tree stands. These areas are difficult to hunt because of the leaves on the trees and fewer open areas to glass with optics. There are also many lower areas with several different browse species, including; oak brush, service berry, mountain mahogany, bitter brush, snow berry, sage brush, etc. These areas also have deer in them during the hunt, but at a lower density. All ways look for areas that deer are watering in. Some areas to hunt include the following: Strawberry Reservoir area- Try Indian canyon, Clyde Creek, Mud Creek, Squaw Creek, Horse Creek, Main canyon and Strawberry ridge. Sheep Creek area- Try any of the waters ( First to Sixth) along Ray's Valley road. Sheep Creek is a good winter range, Diamond Fork- Diamond Fork is a mixture of public and private and is a good winter range. Hobble Creek- Right Hand fork is mostly public land, Left Hand Fork is mostly private land. American Fork Canyon/Mt. Timpanogos-This area is steep and rugged. Timp WMA-This area is real brushy but can be good hunting. Wallsburg WMA-This WMA is mostly open sagebrush. Hunting can be good as the rut begins
