hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located just south of the Idaho - Utah state-line with State Highway 150 forming much of the east boundary. The high elevation is around 9100 feet. The Hayden Fork (7800 feet to 8400 feet) and the West Fork (7800 feet to 9000 feet) of the Bear River cut the Unit on the east. Two major drainages flowing into the Bear River and its forks are Mill City Creek (8400 feet to 9200 feet) and Deer Creek (8300 feet to 9100 feet). On the west side of the Unit, Yellow Creek, ranging from 7700 feet to 8800 feet, cuts the unit. The most common elevation is 8900 feet but ranges from 7500 feet to 9600 feet with an elevation difference of 2100 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 8100 feet and 8900 feet an elevation difference of 800 feet. The Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) land cover is dominated by two (2) types in almost equal proportions, Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) and Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Rocky Mountain Subalpine-Montane Riparian Shrubland (77) is also a prominent land cover type on the Unit. There is also a large patch of Rocky Mountain Lodgepole Pine Forest (29) in the southeast corner that contributes to the land cover mix. One of the Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, COALVILLE (421590), is about 14.2 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. COALVILLE has thirty-four (34) years of records, 1974 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.71 inches, but it can be as high as 7.09 inches or as low as 1.68 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 19 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.8 inches but can be as high as 32.0 inches. FALL temperature at COALVILLE averages 43.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 87.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 61 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Wallsburg Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located east of Wallsburg, Utah. The higher elevations are on the east side of the Unit, ranging from 8900 feet in the south to 8400 feet in the north. Maple Creek or Maple Canyon cuts the Unit in the southwest, ranging from 6200 feet to 8400 feet. In the north Boomer Canyon cuts the Unit, ranging from 7000 feet to 8400 feet. Near forty percent (40%) of the Wallsburg Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). This Aspen Forest and Woodland is all on the eastside of the unit. On the westside of the unit it is a mixture of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed MontaneShrubland (41). One of the Wallsburg Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, DEER CREEK DAM (422057), is 12.1 km west of the west edge of the CWMU. DEER CREEK DAM has forty-nine (49) years of records, 1959 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.54 inches, but it can be as high as 7.69 inches or as low as 0.60 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 4.4 inches but can be as high as 30.0 inches. FALL temperature at DEER CREEK DAM averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 97.0 degrees F. or as low as -12.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 54 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a great late season buck deer hunt. It is managed by an operator who is honest and fair. They have harvested some great trophy bucks off this unit. The boundaries are well marked and there is plenty of landscape to cover on foot or from a vehicle. There are several vantage points were you can locate your quarry. The range is perfect for using optics. It is comparable to certain parts of the moon. The access is great for ATV's, trucks, or hiking. There are some areas that remote but most of it is accessible by ATV's. There are some sections of BLM, and SITLA mixed in with the private. You can drive every road on the whole unit in a day, but you cannot hunt the entire unit in a day. The hunt historically has only gotten better as it progresses.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are very few stands of trees. Most of the deer bed down in the grease wood bottoms during the day and feed out of them in the evenings. Water is limited and some of the deer will travel to willow creek to access water, or drink out of small reservoirs/ponds. The season dates are ideal for hunting trophy bucks. This hunt can be very dependent on weather. The bucks are in the pre-rut, and can travel long distances searching for does in estrus. You will find new bucks showing up each day. The more does that start to move down to this winter range the better chance of harvesting a trophy buck. Winter weather helps kick their migration off, but some does will start to trickle down onto the unit by mid-October. It can be difficult to pattern a buck this time of year because of these pre-rut movements.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote area and you will not always have cell phone reception. I would make sure you have good tires, and emergency equipment with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: I would prepare for fair to cold weather conditions. The roads can be affected by rain and snow. There is a fair amount of oil field traffic that helps keep the roads open.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Woodruff Creek South Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located southwest of Woddruff, Utah. High elevations in the east are 7900 feet and 8400 feet in the west. Woodruff Creek (6800 feet to 7300 feet) forms the north border along with Woodruff Reservoir (6800 feet) and approximates the west Unit border. Meachem Canyon (7000 feet to 7700 feet) forms the south border. One primary drainage, Road Hollow, flowing east to west cuts the Unit, ranging from 7200 feet to 7800 feet. The most common elevation is 7800 feet but ranges from 6900 feet to 8500 feet with an elevation difference of 1600 feet. Fifty-four percent (54%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7400 feet and 8000 feet an elevation difference of 600 feet. Almost seventy-five percent (75%) of the Woodruff Creek South Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). The only other major land cover types is Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). This Aspen Forest and Woodland are in large patches in the middle and towards the west of the Unit. On the westside Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland occur in several large patches. One of the Woodruff Creek South Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, WOODRUFF (429595), is about 14.6 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. WOODRUFF has one hundred eleven (111) years of records, 1897 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.64 inches, but it can be as high as 5.18 inches or as low as 0.64 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.7 inches but can be as high as 29.2 inches. FALL temperature at WOODRUFF averages 40.8 degrees F. but can be as high as 111.0 degrees F. or as low as -26.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 73 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 6 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Jacobs Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is west of Morgan, Utah on the Morgan County side of the Davis - Morgan County boundaries. Higher elevation are on the west side of the Unit, ranging from 9200 feet in the north to 9300 feet in the middle, then dropping to 9000 feet in the south. Jacobs Creek is a drainage in the northern part of the Unit. It ranges from 8600 feet to 5000 feet. Petersen Creek flows west to east and has three forks. The Right Fork starts about 8800 feet elevation, 7500 feet for the Middle Fork, and 7600 feet for the Left Fork. Petersen Creek exits the Unit at 5000 feet. Another west to east drainage that has three forks is Dalton Creek. The Right Fork of Dalton Creek starts at 7400 feet, the Middle Fork at 7700 feet and the Left Fork at 7500 feet. After converging into Dalton Creek the forks exit the Unit at 5500 feet. Two other drainages are Smith Creek ( 8200 feet to 6600 feet) and Line Creek ( 8700 feet to 6800 feet) drain the Unit. The most common elevation is 5700 feet but ranges from 4900 feet to 9300 feet with an elevation difference of 4400 feet. Fifty percent (50%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6300 feet and 8400 feet an elevation difference of 2100 feet. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is the dominant land cover typeon the Jacobs Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). It is mostly located onthe north and east sides of the Unit. Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) is another major land cover type on the Unit, it runs down the middle and toward the west side of the Unit. In between the Shrubland and Forest and Woodland are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30), and Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (28) add to the Forest and Woodland character of the Unit. Rocky Mountain Lower Montane Riparian Woodland and Shrubland (79) intermixes with lower elevation Forest and Woodland types. One of the Jacobs Creek Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, FARMINGTON (422721), is 6.6 KM west of the west edge of the CWMU. FARMINGTON has seventy-two (72) years of records, 1893 - 1965. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 4.61 inches, but it can be as high as 7.83 inches or as low as 1.18 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 17 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day with precipitation greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 6.8 inches but can be as high as 20.5 inches. FALL temperature at FARMINGTON averages 51.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 98.0 degrees F. or as low as -1.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 30 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 2 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Iron Spring Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located west of Cedar City between the Swett Hills and Three Peaks. It is one block of land that ranges from 5400 feet to 5700 feet. The vegetation ranges from a Pinion Juniper Shrubland on the east of the unit to a Desert Grassland on the west. Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. There may be a few resident deer in the area around the agricultural pivot earlier in the season. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. So it usually does not affect this hunt. On years with cooler weather some of the larger bucks will start into some pre rut behavior in the last week of October. Recommended areas to hunt: The majority of the deer will be found adjacent to the agricultural field that is included in this unit. The unit is managed as a limited entry unit but does not guarantee success. CWMUs are managed separately from the larger units of which they are a part, but management objectives are the same. Specific information related to this CWMU should be directed to the CWMU operator before applying for the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The 5S Land & Livestock Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located in the East Canyon Wildlife Management Unit near the town of Morgan, Utah. Elevation ranges from 5800 feet to 8300 feet elevation. The topography varies across the CWMU from deep canyons and slopes to more gentle open slopes providing year round seasonal habitats for wildlife. Lower elevations of the CWMU include agricultural land. The dominant vegetative cover found on the CWMU is composed mainly of big sagebrush, but also includes bitterbrush, service berry, oak and aspen/conifer woodlands.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Except for about 750 hectares around the town of Alton, Utah; the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) surrounds the town. To the northeast of Alton (7500 feet), mountains rise from 8500 to 9000 feet. These mountains slope down toward the Sevier River at an elevation of around 7200 feet on the north. On the the south, these mountains slope down to the Kanab River which parts the Alton CWMU on the southeast. The most common elevation is 7400 feet but ranges from 6400 feet to 9000 feet with an elevation difference of 2600 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7300 feet and 8200 feet an elevation difference of 900 feet. Lower elevations on the Unit are around 6800 feet. Towards the southwest of the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWM), there are extensive areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36). A co-dominant land cover type is Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). This Shrubland occurs throughout the Unit except for the extreme north. In the extreme north and towards the middle of the Unit are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are also large patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). The Alton CWMU also has large patches of Rocky Mountain Ponderosa Pine Woodland (34) and Agriculture (114) is scattered throughout the Unit. One of the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ALTON (420086), is about 1.0 km from the middle of the CWMU. ALTON has eighty-three (83) years of records, 1915 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 4.14 inches, but it can be as high as 11.35 inches or as low as 0.36 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch of perciptiation. Total FALL snowfall averages 7.6 inches but can be as high as 41.7 inches. FALL temperature at ALTON averages 47.3 degrees F. but can be as high as 91.0 degrees F. or as low as -5.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 44 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This CWMU occurs on the Nine Mile deer unit in southern Carbon County and northern Emery County. It is a new CWMU beginning in 2022. Most of this property was formerly part of the Patmos Ridge CWMU. Elevation on the CWMU ranges from about 7,000 to 9,000 feet. Although there are some resident deer, this CWMU is likely transitional habitat for deer in the fall and spring. Deer densities are likely not very high. Pinyon-Juniper forest predominates at lower elevations with Douglas-fir more prevalent at higher elevations. This area is extremely steep and rugged with very limited road access. Significant water and habitat improvement projects are planned and are underway on this property. In general, buck:doe ratios tend to be high on the surrounding Nine Mile unit due to the predominance of private land.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure. Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Most higher elevation Raft River Mountains deer will remain high on the range until snow depths push them down into the sagebrush flats. Access to higher elevations is through One Mile Canyon, George Creek Canyon, Johnson Canyon, and Wildcat Canyon. Deer are plentiful and hunting opportunities exist up every canyon. Deer along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range can be found up Kimbell Creek, Red Banks, and Keg Springs along the west side and near Devil's Playground and Rocky Pass on the east side. Mule deer in the higher elevations do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the Raft River Mountains to the southeast end of the Grouse Creek Mountains for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats from Kelton to Devil's Playground. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This is a very productive unit with one of the largest deer herds in the state. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches east of SR-89 on the west and the sagebrush benches west of SR-6 and SR-10 on the east side of the mountain. There is very little seasonal movement of deer on the San Rafael portion of the unit. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: Upper Fish Creek and it's tributaries. The tributaries include Gooseberry Creek, Silver Creek, C Canyon, and the Straight Fork. This is a roadless area on the north end of the unit. This area has had some prescribed fires recently that has improved deer habitat. It can be accessed from North Skyline Drive on the west or from Scofield Reservoir on the east. The bottom two miles of Upper Fish Creek is privately owned and in a CWMU Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge These ridges have roads going down them. They are northwest of Scofield Reservoir. The bottom 2 miles of these ridges are privately owned. This is excellent habitat in the Pondtown Creek drainage on the north end of the unit. It is best accessed from North Skyline Drive. Trough Spring Ridge This is accessed off of SR-264 southwest of the town of Scofield. It is just above the Skyline Coal Mine. This is the ridge on the east side of Electric Lake. There are some small pockets of private land that are posted well but the majority of the acreage is Forest Service. Much of this ridge burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 which has improved the deer habitat in this area. Gentry Mountain. This is accessed from SR-10 just north of the town of Huntington at Huntington Reservoir. Part of this mountain is privately owned and part of it burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 West of Skyline Drive All the small towns along the west face of the Central Mountains Manti Unit has a canyon road to connect to Skyline Drive. Some roads are fairly rough going with the better access up from Fairview, Ephraim and Mayfield. Concentrate on side roads and trails from the main canyon roads to get to the more likely areas to find deer. The higher elevations in aspen and sagebrush meadows with water in close proximity will hold some of the mature bucks. Down low in the agricultural valleys many younger bucks will use the alfalfa fields in the evenings and early morning. Much of the adjacent property along the agriculture is either Forest Service or State lands and there will be a good opportunities there. hunt_bio_general_information: The Nebo unit has some very rough terrain. I tell hunters that "the Nebo is either straight up or straight down" so be prepared for some very hard work. ATV use is not allowed on the north Nebo and horses or mules are recommended. At the very least hunters should be in very good physical condition.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: In the past the harvest has been distributed throughout the entire portion of the Nebo. The higher elevations can be good places to start looking for more mature bucks but the younger bucks can be found at lower elevations, especially associated with agriculture areas. Don't limit yourself to a few areas. They can be found anywhere on the mountains. Some of the areas to concentrate on are Nebo Creek, Page Fork, Hop Creek, and Mahogany Knoll. Other good places are off the Nebo Loop Road around Payson Lakes and the Summit Trail. The south Nebo (Sanpitch Mts.), that portion of the Nebo Unit that is south of SR 132, may be more accessible since ATV use is allowed by the USFS. However there is private property further south as well as a CWMU deer unit. Water sources are good places to find deer. Most archery hunters have the most success early in the hunt sitting at remote water holes and canyons with perennial water. Migration Patterns: There is very little deer migration during the archery and muzzleloader hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches which is usually after the rifle hunt. However, heavy snow fall during the hunt may cause deer to migrate to lower elevations early. Scouting Tips: Good hunters will scout and find their own "honey hole". A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of deer. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Depending on the season be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road and trail conditions. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat especially during the archery season so in anticipation of hot weather plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fillmore unit has great deer habitat and has had an increase in the buck/doe ratio over the last few years. Although the hunt boundary extends onto the west side of I-15, the Pahvant Mountain Range (east side of I-15) receives most of the hunting pressure.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Deer: Deer can be found across the entire unit, on both the east and west sides, with most of the deer being found at higher elevations. It is common to see bucks off of the main roads which results in those roads receiving a high amount of hunting pressure. Walking out ridges and away from roads can be a great strategy in finding deer and seeing fewer hunters. Water: The Pahvant is relatively dry. There are creeks in the bottoms of some of the canyons and a few springs and stock ponds on top. Water sources can be productive areas for finding deer during the archery hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreationists. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. After heavy rain storms, many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage is good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Temperatures are high during the archery hunt and you may experience rain and thunderstorms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal Mountains unit is one of the most beautiful places that you will ever encounter. The unit has high alpine peaks, above 12,000 ft. and goes down to low desert valleys around 4,000 ft. This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit however, every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is good road access throughout the unit, however there are also many places that hunters can hike into and get away from the crowds. Hunters should be aware of the CWMU's and private lands on the unit and learn the boundaries. There are 2 CWMUs on this unit and a list is available on the UDWR webpage: http://wildlife.utah.gov/maps/public/list_cwmus.php
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the La Sals typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Using quality binoculars or spotting scopes will be very valuable to you. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas for the archery hunt: For the archery hunt, focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. These areas consist of large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding. Some bucks will be above timberline in very remote areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is extremely limited throughout most of the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sals. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms. Dirt roads on this unit can become extremely muddy, very quick. Be attentive and use caution when traveling during stormy weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced a decrease in the deer population and decrease in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good. Typically hunters experience a high success rate. Deer populate the entire Monroe unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be on central and northern parts of the unit. The southern portion of the unit is narrower, drier, as has fewer deer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the past couple of years the Monroe unit has experienced reduced fawn production and survival, primarily due to both drought and harsh winter conditions. This has caused a reduction in the overall deer population and decreased buck/doe ratios. Hunting is still good, but buck permits have been reduced to reflect the current population status. During the archery season most of the deer are concentrated above 8,000 feet in elevation. Several peaks on the unit are above 11,000 ft elevation but most of the unit consists of moderate elevation hunt areas. There are deer on the highest peaks however most of the deer tend to be at the intersection of the conifer/aspen habitats and the aspen/mountain brush/sage habitats. Archers on the Monroe generally enjoy a good hunt with good success rates. There are deer spread across the entire Monroe unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want. Great deer range exists in the Northern part of the unit, productive areas include above the towns of Glenwood and Annabella including the Hunter's Flat, Thompson Basin, and Big Lake areas. On the East side of the unit deer hunting can be good in the Mormon Mountain area (much of this is private) and in the hills above Burrville. Good road access and prime deer habitat are located in the following areas: Box Creeks, Indian Peak, Monroe Peak, Greenwich Creeks, and the Dairies areas. There is some private property in these areas so make sure you know where you are. Most of these areas are aspen and mountain brush habitats. On the West side of the unit good places to find deer include Poverty Flat, the canyons surrounding Marysvale peak, and the area around Barney Lake. The South end of the unit contains deer in the Forshea Mtn, Langdon Peak areas. The sage flats West of Angle have some deer during the rifle season.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This unit is has a high buck/doe ratio primarily due to an abundance of private land where hunting pressure is generally light. This is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The key to this unit is finding public lands. Most of the public lands are at the fringes of the good summer and fall deer habitat as most of the high elevation acreage is privately owned. Migration Patterns: Most deer on the Tavaputs Plateau migrate to the east toward the Green River to spend the winter months. This includes the lower ends of Ceder, Cottonwood, and Flat Iron Ridges as well as the area near Prickly Pear Canyon. Deer on the western part of the unit tend to migrate to the southwest to the foothills just north and east of Price near the Price Airport, Coal Creek, and Soldier Creek. Generally there is no migration during the archery hunt and most deer are on top of the mountain. Mule Deer Rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Cold Springs WMA provides good public land access on high elevation summer habitat and transitional fall habitat near Bruin Point. There is a county road through the middle of the WMA with over 2500 acres of public lands available. Much of the property is walk-in only to maintain quality deer hunting in the area. This area can be accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside or if the weather is bad from Nine Mile Canyon and up Cottonwood Canyon. There is an abundance of wild horses on this part of the mountain. Upper Patmos Ridge/Range Creek - There are 5 sections of BLM land that are surrounded by private lands just south of Bruin Point and North of the Preston Nutter Ranch gate. This provides good deer habitat at high elevations on steep timber covered terrain with ample water. This is accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside. Harmon Canyon/Prickly Pear Canyon - This is good transitional habitat especially if there has been some snow. It is accessed via Nine Mile Canyon then you can drive up the Harmon Canyon road which is about 30 miles east of Wellington Utah. These are sagebrush/PJ habitats at about 7500 feet in elevation. Cottonwood/Ceder Ridge. This is good transitional habitat in sagebrush at elevations of 6500 to 8000 feet. There are private lands to the west but plenty of public lands as you go down the ridges. These areas are accessed via Nine Mile Canyon and then Cottonwood Canyon 45 miles east of Wellington. Anthro Subunit Recommended areas to hunt: The Anthro subunit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer. Because the density is so low, if you do find any bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. There is a lot of area East of Antelope Canyon all the way to the Green River, with even lower deer densities, while hunting these areas your best chance is finding water. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Nutter's Ridge - USFS higher elevation, a few large aspen stands, very accessible Jeep Trail Ridge - USFS just East of Nutter's Ridge, large canyons with a few aspens, several water sources Wire Fence Ridge - USFS rough road, biggest aspen stands on Anthro, good burned side hills Alkaline/Choke Cherry - USFS very open country, few deer, East of Jeep Trail Wells Draw - BLM lands, low elevation pinyon/juniper, low density Cottonwood Ridge - USFS difficult access, higher elevation, many timbered hill sides
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in August and September are generally pretty mild with warm days and cold nights. There is rarely snow on the ground during the archery hunt and most deer are still found on high elevation summer ranges. Roads are generally in good shape. Be prepared for cold nights and occasional rainstorms which can make the roads muddy. August is the wettest month of the year in the Price area as monsoon rainstorms in the afternoon are quite common. This can disrupt hunting and deer behavior as well as the ability to hunt on a water source.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is a migration study underway to look at timing and routes of migration for North Slope deer. We ask that collared deer are not killed. If one is, DO NOT CUT THE COLLAR; remove the collar by loosening the lock nuts and call the number on the collar or the local biologist. This unit encompasses lodgepole pine, open sagebrush, and desert scrub. Hunters should expect to see other deer and elk hunters and other public land users.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer in the High Uintas do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the west side of the North Slope to the east end of the North Slope for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats all along the North Slope. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is after this hunt ends so it does not affect the hunt. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the North Slope: Deer are found throughout much of the unit. During the archery hunt, deer will be higher in elevation, although there are some that stay year-round in the sagebrush habitat on Dowd Mountain, Death Valley, and Red Creek Flat. Depending on weather conditions, most of the deer on the Summit portion get pushed down into Wyoming before the Any Weapon hunt begins. Also, high country deer are typically pushed down out of the High Country by mid-October if any early season snow storms hit. The majority of the deer in the 3 Corners portion of the unit stay up high on Bear Mountain, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, and Bender Mountain until later in October/early November when deer start showing up in Browns Park for the winter. This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure, especially in Browns Park, Goslin Mountain, South Valley, Dowd Mountain, and along Hwy 44. Areas with highest harvest success include Greendale Junction (along Highway 44 and 191), Sheep Creek Lake, Long Park, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, and 3 Corners. Hunters that receive written permission from private landowners in Manila also do well. Recommended areas include along Highway 44 and 191, Sheep Creep Lake, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, 3 Corners, Henry's Fork, Bridger Lake and along the North Slope Road.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Pine Valley Unit is 90% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Deer on the Archery hunt are spread out across their summer ranges deer densities are higher in some areas than they are in other. Some high deer density areas also have higher numbers of hunters and can result in some hunter crowding. Please be aware of other hunters and be courteous. Day time temperatures during the archery hunt can still reach into the low 90's. On years with good monsoonal moisture the deer may be spread out more across their range.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Migration should not be a factor on this hunt. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. So it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Pine Valley Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several livestock tanks, springs and guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Bull Valley Mountains - Forest Service and small tracts of private land South and West of Enterprise. This area is very accessible by vehicles. Deer densities decrease as you move further west towards the Nevada state line. Hunting is best in oak brush and service berry near water sources. Bumblebee Mtn. - BLM, USFS, and SITLA SW of Cedar City. The higher elevation areas in the oak brush best for locating deer. Access is limited to a few main roads and ATV trails. Hunters will do better if they get out and do some hiking and spotting deer. Paradise and Pine Valley Wilderness - Forest Service land from Pace Draw NW of New Harmony to the south face of the Pine Valley Mtn. This area is remote and has little to no vehicle access. There are several foot and horse trails into the area. Some access points are the Anderson and Comanche trail head in the New Harmony area, The Grants Ranch trail head between New Harmony and Pinto, The Paradise trail head near Pinto, The Mill Canyon and Water Canyon trail heads south of the Town of Pine Valley in Grass Valley, The Whipple and Forsyth trail heads in Pine Valley. The further you are willing to hike in the better the hunting may become. Atchison and Harrison Peak - Forest Service land Between Mountain Meadow and Grass Valley. Mostly sagebrush and serviceberry habitat with some scattered pinion and juniper. This area has limited access and with a few ATV trails. Hiking in a ½ mile plus from the roads will increase success in finding the bucks.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: It can be very hot during this season. Please be prepared with plenty of water. Make sure friends and family know where you area going and when you will return. Be aware of rattle snakes!
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder/Kaiparowits unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit has some excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced an increase in the deer population and an increase in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters have been noticing an increasing number of mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be on the Boulder part of the unit. The southern portion of the unit, the Kaiporowits, is drier and has fewer deer. During the Archery season most of the deer tend to be in the higher elevations near water. Hunter densities are not high.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the Archery season deer are scattered over the entire unit. Much of the buck movement is dictated by weather conditions. Bucks tend to remain higher in elevation than does. The Boulder Top is above 11,000 ft elevation and generally most deer move off the top by late September. Most of the deer tend to be at the intersection of the conifer/aspen habitats and the aspen/mountain brush/sage habitats. Hunters who want to hunt the Kaiparowits portion of the unit need to be prepared to see few deer and experience very difficult hunting conditions. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some very remote areas on this unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms often occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer. Archery Season: During the Archery Season most of the deer will be above 8,000 ft. The heaviest populations tend to be in the aspen/oak habitats. There are some deer and some good mature bucks that use the highest elevations. These deer are spooked easily and when disturbed may drop down into more secure cover. Scouting before the season is key in finding where bucks are hanging out. Heavy hunting pressure will be near the good camping areas and roads. Muzzleloader Season: During the Muzzleloader season most of the deer still tend to be in the mid to higher elevations though some have began to move down a little. This season is a great time to hunt the Fish Lake, hunter densities are not high and the weather is often pleasant. Deer will be spread out across the unit. Any Weapon Season: In late October the deer on the Monroe unit tend to be very spread out. On much of the unit, some of the deer have moved onto or near their winter range. Snow levels permitting, there are also some deer on the highest peaks. Hunters should use scouting just prior to the season to locate deer concentrations. Hunters often concentrate in areas where deer are easily seen near agricultural areas. Migration Patterns: Some of the deer on Fish Lake unit begin to migrate to or closer to their winter range in mid-October. By the time the rifle hunt arrives a sizable portion of the herd is often in the transitional ranges between their winter and summer ranges. However many deer also stay as high as they can until heavy snows push them lower. Most of the migration is rather simple, the deer just move up or down in elevation. However there are some deer that move from their summering areas on the North and Central parts of the unit to the Southern, Eastern, and Western parts of the unit closer to their winter range. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it generally does not affect the general deer hunts. Recommended areas to hunt on the Fish Lake unit: There are deer spread across the entire Fish Lake unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather Conditions: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. During the archery season hunters should be prepared to cool harvested game quickly due to warm temperatures.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Abajos typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the San Juan, Abajo subunit: Abajo Mountain - For the archery hunt, focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. These areas consist of large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the Abajos. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

Fifty percent of the deer habitat is public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Large blocks of the best deer habitat on this unit are private lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. On years with cooler weather some of the larger bucks will start into some pre rut behavior. Recommended areas to hunt: The Zion Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. During the archery hunt most deer are still in their summer habitat. Most deer will be at the middle to higher elevations from oak brush to the aspen and mixed conifer zone. About 59% of deer summer habitat on the Zion unit is on private lands. The northern portions of the unit south of Highway 14 are the best places for public access onto Forest Service land. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Webster's Flat and Deep Creek - Forest Service land From Woods Ranch area in Cedar Canyon to just east of the Zion Overlook. The Deep Creek area is a USFS roadless area. Access can be found at the trail head a short distance above the turn off to Webster's Flat on Highway 14. Midway - USFS land from the turn off to Cedar Breaks east to Navajo Lake. The old clear cut logging areas and meadows in the Deer Valley area usually have a fair amount of deer use. Strawberry Ridge and Harris Flat- USFS land between Strawberry Cabins area and east to Stout Canyon. This is a ponderosa pine are that has a good understory of bitterbrush. There is good access in to this area with several OHV trails and old logging roads. This area has several wildlife and livestock water catch ponds. This area has several cabin communities and hunters should be careful of private lands and how close they hunt to cabins. Stout Canyon and School Wash - USFS land with some larger blocks of private land. This is a ponderosa pine habitat with a good understory of bitterbrush. There are a few OHV trails and logging roads that cut through this area. Private land - Some of the best deer habitat on the Zion unit is on private lands. This unit is unusual for Southern Utah because of its large parcels of private lands that have several different land owners. Obtaining permission to hunt these areas can be difficult, but is not impossible.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure. Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Most higher elevation Raft River Mountains deer will remain high on the range until snow depths push them down into the sagebrush flats. Access to higher elevations is through One Mile Canyon, George Creek Canyon, Johnson Canyon, and Wildcat Canyon. Deer are plentiful and hunting opportunities exist up every canyon. Deer along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range can be found up Kimbell Creek, Red Banks, and Keg Springs along the west side and near Devil's Playground and Rocky Pass on the east side. Mule deer in the higher elevations do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the Raft River Mountains to the southeast end of the Grouse Creek Mountains for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats from Kelton to Devil's Playground. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.

Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Nebo unit has some very rough terrain. I tell hunters that "the Nebo is either straight up or straight down" so be prepared for some very hard work. ATV use is not allowed on much of the north Nebo and horses or mules are recommended. At the very least hunters should be in very good physical condition.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: In the past the harvest has been distributed throughout the entire portion of the Nebo. The higher elevations can be good places to start looking for more mature bucks but younger bucks can be found at lower elevations, especially associated with agriculture areas. Recent fires do not seem to have significantly affected deer populations or distributions. Closures due to fire have restricted access to some popular hunting areas. However, all state Wildlife Management Areas are still open, and there are still good places to hunt deer. The areas around Loafer and Santaquin Peaks on state property, Willow Creek, Hop Creek/Pole Canyon, Nebo Mtn, Bear Canyon, Mahogany Hill, and Spencer Fork WMA all hold deer and are currently accessible, albeit some areas only on foot. The south Nebo (Sanpitch Mtns), that portion of the Nebo Unit that is south of SR 132, is not under closure and may be more accessible since ATV use is allowed by the USFS. Deer concentration on the Sanpitch Mtns. is higher on the north end than the south end. Water sources are good places to find deer. Most archery hunters have the most success early in the hunt sitting at remote water holes and canyons with perennial water. Migration Patterns: There is very little deer migration during the archery and muzzleloader hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches which is usually after the rifle hunt. However, heavy snow fall during the hunt may cause deer to migrate to lower elevations early. Scouting Tips: Good hunters will scout and find their own "honey hole". A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of deer. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Depending on the season be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road and trail conditions. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat especially during the archery season so in anticipation of hot weather plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Deer: Deer can be found across the entire unit, on both the east and west sides. Deer can be found at all elevations during this hunt. Most of the deer will still be on the mountain but more will have moved onto winter range than what was found during the archery and muzzleloader. Most of the hunting pressure will still be up high and along main roads and easily glassible canyons.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreationists. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. After heavy rain storms, many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage is good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather can change quickly and you may see early large snowstorms during this hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are no CWMUs on this unit. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. Hunters are reminded that bears often frequent the area. Campers and hikers should maintain a bear-safe campsite and dispose of trash properly. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Meat and garbage should be stored inside a vehicle or hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most deer are scattered throughout higher elevations, in remote areas away from major roads and ATV trails. Deer may begin to migrate to lower elevations in early October due to winter weather conditions or hunting pressure. Hunters are encouraged to do their pre-season scouting on the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area and can make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal Mountains unit is one of the most beautiful places that you will ever encounter. The unit has high alpine peaks, above 12,000 ft. and goes down to low desert valleys around 4,000 ft. This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit however, every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is good road access throughout the unit, however there are also many places that hunters can hike into and get away from the crowds. Hunters should be aware of the CWMU's and private lands on the unit and learn the boundaries. There are 2 CWMUs on this unit and a list is available on the UDWR webpage: http://wildlife.utah.gov/maps/public/list_cwmus.php
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the La Sals typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Using quality binoculars or spotting scopes will be very valuable to you. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas for the any weapon hunt: Any weapon hunters should focus on mid to low elevation areas. If any snow accumulates, deer will start heading for lower elevations consisting of oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, intermixed with pinyon/juniper stands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is extremely limited throughout most of the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sals. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms. Dirt roads on this unit can become extremely muddy, very quick. Be attentive and use caution when traveling during stormy weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter, the unit has experienced an decrease in the deer population and a decrease in the buck/doe ratio. Buck permits have been decreased to reflect this change in the herd status. Deer hunting has still been good. Typically hunters experience a high success rate. Deer populate the entire Monroe unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be on central and northern parts of the unit. The southern portion of the unit is narrower, drier, as has fewer deer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Any Weapon Season: In late October the deer on the Monroe unit tend to be very spread out. On much of the unit some of the deer have moved onto or near their winter range. Snow levels permitting, there are also some deer on the highest peaks. Hunters should use scouting just prior to the season to locate deer concentrations. Hunters often concentrate in areas where deer are easily seen near agricultural areas. Some of the deer on Monroe begin to migrate to or closer to their winter range in early October. By the time the rifle hunt arrives a sizable portion of the herd has moved down in elevation, often concentrating their foraging activities in Agricultural areas. However many deer also stay as high as they can until heavy snows push them lower. Most of the migration is rather simple, the deer just move up or down in elevation. However there are some deer that move from their summering areas on the North part of the unit to some winter range near the town of Angle. Usually this movement is after the rifle hunting season.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather Conditions: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot, dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms occur often during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has seen good deer numbers over recent years. Hunters have reported seeing more bucks and more mature bucks have been harvested in the last couple years. This unit has several areas that have no vehicle access. Hunters that hike into some of these areas, or use horses have good success at harvesting deer. Before snow falls on the unit you can access the top of the mountain from Antimony, or Cottonwood Creek in Johns Valley. Deer in the summer can be found across the unit in higher and lower elevations. There is good access on most of the BLM lands across the unit, but a lot of the forest service has limited access. There is good access on the south end of the unit in the Hunt Creeks, and often holds deer year round. There was a large fire that burned on the unit in 2002. This made it very good for glassing long distances. There is a lot of pinon and juniper in the lower elevations with Aspen, and mixed conifer stands at higher elevations. During summer months find water and hunt areas around it. During this hunt deer have started moving towards lower elevations for wintering. If the hunt is warm focus on areas around water.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: A lot of roadless areas on the unit expect backcountry hunting conditions

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit has a high buck/doe ratio primarily due to an abundance of private land where hunting pressure is generally light. This is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The key to this unit is finding public lands. Most of the public lands are at the fringes of the good summer and fall deer habitat as most of the high elevation acreage is privately owned.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most deer on the Tavaputs Plateau migrate to the east toward the Green River to spend the winter months. This includes the lower ends of Ceder, Cottonwood, and Flat Iron Ridges as well as the area near Prickly Pear Canyon. Deer on the western part of the unit tend to migrate to the southwest to the foothills just north and east of Price near the Price Airport, Coal Creek, and Soldier Creek. Deer tend to be moving on to transitional habitats during the any weapon deer hunt each year by midweek. Hunting is much better if the weather is bad and generally poor if we have had mild weather. Mule Deer Rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended Areas to Hunt: The Cold Springs WMA provides good public land access on high elevation summer habitat and transitional fall habitat near Bruin Point. There is a county road through the middle of the WMA with over 2500 acres of public lands available. Much of the property is walk-in only to maintain quality deer hunting in the area. This area can be accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside or if the weather is bad from Nine Mile Canyon and up Cottonwood Canyon. Lots of wild horses on this part of the mountain. Upper Patmos Ridge/Range Creek - There are 5 sections of BLM land that are surrounded by private lands just south of Bruin Point and North of the Preston Nutter Ranch gate. This provides good deer habitat at high elevations on steep timber covered terrain with ample water. This is accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside. Harmon Canyon/Prickly Pear Canyon - This is good transitional habitat especially if there has been some snow. It is accessed via Nine Mile Canyon then you can drive up the Harmon Canyon road which is about 30 miles east of Wellington Utah. These are sagebrush/PJ habitats at about 7500 feet in elevation. Cottonwood/Ceder Ridge - This is good transitional habitat in sagebrush at elevations of 6500 to 8000 feet. There are private lands to the west but plenty of public lands as you go down the ridges. These areas are accessed via Nine Mile Canyon and then Cottonwood Canyon 45 miles east of Wellington. Airport Road/Coal Creek/Soldier Creek - These are the low elevation benches that concentrate deer if there has been a significant snowstorm in October. They are the foothills just north and east of the towns of Price and Wellington. Hunting is generally poor if the weather is mild and can be good after a snowstorm. They are mostly public lands. Anthro Subunit Recommended Areas to Hunt: The Anthro subunit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer. Because the density is so low, if you do find any bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. There is a lot of area East of Antelope Canyon all the way to the Green River, with even lower deer densities, while hunting these areas your best chance is finding water. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Nutter's Ridge - USFS higher elevation, a few large aspen stands, very accessible Jeep Trail Ridge - USFS just East of Nutter's Ridge, large canyons with a few aspens, several water sources Wire Fence Ridge - USFS rough road, biggest aspen stands on Anthro, good burned side hills Alkaline/Choke Cherry - USFS very open country, few deer, East of Jeep Trail Wells Draw - BLM lands, low elevation pinyon/juniper, low density Cottonwood Ridge - USFS difficult access, higher elevation, many timbered hill sides
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: If there is an early snow, the Bruin Point area east of Sunnyside may not be accessible. However, if there are early snows it generally makes the hunting on public lands much better as it pushes deer off of high elevation summer ranges on private lands to transitional and winter habitats that are generally on public lands. Be prepared for snow, rain, cold or hot. There is a little of everything on this unit.
