hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is a migration study underway to look at timing and routes of migration for North Slope deer. We ask that collared deer are not killed. If one is, DO NOT CUT THE COLLAR; remove the collar by loosening the lock nuts and call the number on the collar or the local biologist. This unit encompasses lodgepole pine, open sagebrush, and desert scrub. Hunters should expect to see other deer and elk hunters and other public land users.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer in the High Uintas do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the west side of the North Slope to the east end of the North Slope for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats all along the North Slope. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the North Slope: Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Depending on weather conditions, most of the deer on the Summit portion get pushed down into lower elevations after the Any Weapon hunt begins. Also, high country deer aren't typically pushed down out of the High Country until mid to late October if any early season snow storms hit. The majority of the deer in the 3 Corners portion of the unit stay up high on Bear Mountain, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, and Bender Mountain until later in October/early November when deer start showing up in Browns Park for the winter. This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure, especially in Browns Park, Goslin Mountain, South Valley, Dowd Mountain, and along Hwy 44. Areas with highest harvest success include Dowd Mountain, Death Valley, South Valley, Greendale Junction (along Highway 44 and 191), Red Creek Flat, Clay Basin, Goslin Mountain, and 3 Corners. Hunters that receive written permission from private landowners in Manila also do well.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Deer habitat includes a lot of public land but there is substantial habitat on private lands throughout the unit. Hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Panguitch Lake unit has a healthy deer population. Expect to see several bucks each day, with the majority probably being young deer. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. During the rifle hunt most deer are in transition to their wintering habitat. Some deer will still be higher on Forest Service and Private lands, but many may be on the lower elevation BLM and private lands. The eastern portion will still have good numbers of deer on USFS lands and will generally see the heaviest hunting pressure. Some good areas to hunt include Hatch Mountain, Pole Hollow/5 Mile, 3 Mile Creek, Bear Valley, Buckskin Valley, Cottonwood, and all areas along I-15. Migration Patterns: The migratory segments of this population may begin their fall movements in late September and October. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars can be helpful if you are unfamiliar with the area. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Pine Valley Unit is 90% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Deer on the rifle hunt are beginning to congregate onto their winter ranges so hunters can be expected to be following which will result in some hunter crowding. Please be aware of other hunters and be courteous. Day time temperatures during the rifle hunt can still reach into the low 80's. On years with good monsoonal moisture the deer may be spread out more across their range.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Pine Valley Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several livestock tanks, springs and guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: North end of Beaver Dam Mtns - BLM and SITLA lands west of St. George. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Deer movement into this area can vary from year to year depending on migration. Tobin Bench to Motaqua - BLM and SITLA with some small private lands in the Motaqua area. Deer migration is more reliable in this area with increasing numbers on the second weekend of the hunt. Above Dameron and Diamond Valley- BLM, Forest Service and SITLA lands at higher elevations above Dameron and Diamond Valley. Enterprise North Hills and New Castle- BLM, Forest Service, Private and SITLA lands. Deer begin moving into these areas about the second week of October. Most deer will be in the agricultural fields at night and then available on Public Lands during the day. Bumblebee and Sweat Hills -BLM, Forest Service and SITLA lands West and South of Cedar City. Some deer may remain high on Bumblebee Mtn. until heavier snow storms drive them down.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunter crowding can be a spot in localized areas. Make sure you where your hunter orange and know what is beyond your target before shooting.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter, this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival, resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer. Any Weapon Season: In late October the deer on the Fish Lake unit tend to be very spread out. On much of the unit, some of the deer have moved onto or near their winter range. Snow levels permitting, there are also some deer on the highest peaks. Hunters should use scouting just prior to the season to locate deer concentrations. Hunters often concentrate in areas where deer are easily seen near agricultural areas. Migration Patterns: Some of the deer on Fish Lake unit begin to migrate to or closer to their winter range in mid-October. By the time the rifle hunt arrives a sizable portion of the herd is often in the transitional ranges between their winter and summer ranges. However many deer also stay as high as they can until heavy snows push them lower. Most of the migration is rather simple, the deer just move up or down in elevation. However there are some deer that move from their summering areas on the North and Central parts of the unit to the Southern, Eastern, and Western parts of the unit closer to their winter range. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it generally does not affect the general deer hunts. Recommended areas to hunt on the Fish Lake unit: There are deer spread across the entire Fish Lake unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a large area and cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. During the archery season hunters should be prepared to cool harvested game quickly due to warm temperatures.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit however, every year a few nice bucks are taken. The unit population has been increasing over the past few years, along with the buck to doe ratio. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are 3 CWMUs on this unit, which general season permits are not permitted. A list of all CWMUs is available on the UDWR webpage: http://wildlife.utah.gov/maps/public/list_cwmus.php
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Abajos typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the San Juan, Abajo subunit: Abajo Mountain - Any weapon hunters should focus on mid to low elevation areas. If any snow accumulates, deer will start heading for lower elevations consisting of oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, intermixed with pinyon/juniper stands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the Abajos. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The Uintah Mountain range can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also less deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. There are several four wheeler roads and dirt roads that provide a lot of access on much of the unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and tend to stay on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Vernal: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. There is a variety of habitat to hunt during the rifle hunt. There is pinyon/juniper, sage brush savanna, thick lodge pole pine and areas above timber line. The larger openings on the forest are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and rocky terrain. During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for deer. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks River is the western unit boundary, steep terrain. Paradise Park - Higher forest terrain, steep forested canyons. Mosby Mountain - High aspen forest, with large sagebrush bowls, excellent habitat. Red Cloud Loop Rd - Long road that starts in Dry Fork Canyon (west of Vernal). It takes you all the way through the Vernal unit, and comes out on Hwy 191.. Taylor Mountain - Great vantage points. Excellent area to glass and locate animals from far distances. Colton Ranger Station - Aspen/conifer mix forest. Lime Stone, Little V, and Range Study - These areas are east of Hwy 191 and border a limited entry deer and elk unit. Diamond Mountain.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The unit includes the High Uintas Wilderness area. The Wilderness can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also less deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. Road access on much of the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain. Weather Conditions: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms occur often during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit move down in elevation for the winter and they winter primarily on Ute Tribal Lands and on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. The deer also move down towards the Tribal Land boundary as soon as they get much hunting pressure. There is very little hunting pressure on the Tribal Lands so some deer have learned to go there as soon as hunting pressure starts. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Yellowstone: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. The Wilderness Area can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also less deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. Deer in the Wilderness are generally found above tree line or in small pockets of openings in the lodge pole cover. The larger openings are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and lots of rocks. During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for deer. Every canyon across the South Slope, Yellowstone has deer and they are of similar quality. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: Soapstone area - high elevation, but more road access, closer to the Wasatch Front. North Fork of the Duchesne- limited road access Blind Stream - limited road access, tribal land down low, popular area Log Hollow- must cross Tribal Lands to access, rough roads Rock Creek - paved road access, steep areas Pigeon Water - popular area but hunters must be aware of tribal boundary Bear Wallow - hunters must be aware of tribal boundary, steep terrain Lake Fork/Moon Lake- paved road access, some private property along the paved road. Yellowstone - rough roads, need to be aware of Tribal boundary 77 Flat/Burnt Mill- gravel roads, a little flatter area, be aware of Tribal boundary Dry Gulch- very rough road, steep terrain, be aware of Tribal boundary on the east. Uinta Canyon- Tribal lands down low, steep Terrain Elk Horn Loop - gravel roads that go almost to the summit of the Uintas, lots of opportunity to scatter out. Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks river is the eastern unit boundary, steep terrain.

The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. On years with good pinion nut production the deer may spend more time in the pinion tree areas and be harder to spot.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation towards the end of October and first part of November. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Southwest Desert unit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer because the density is so low. When you do find bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. The higher elevation areas above the thick pinion and juniper are the best for locating deer. South Wah Wah Range - BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range - BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Black Hills - BLM and SITLA lands located southwest of Minersville. Baboon Peak, Dry Willow Peak and Little Horse Valley areas. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.

The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from West to East, with most of the deer wintering on or near Tabby WMA. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: There are numerous areas to hunt on this unit. The areas surrounding Strawberry Reservoir and Currant Creek Reservoir are excellent for deer hunting. They are easy to access with many roads and trails and camping areas. This of course leads to many people hunting these areas. There are very few areas on this unit without a road in the general area. There is far less hunting pressure on the Avintaquin unit, but that is because the overall deer density is much lower and the terrain is more rugged. This unit has very large aspen stands that hold a lot of deer in the early fall. Many of the best bucks taken each year come from these aspen stands. In the summer there are deer in the more open higher areas, but once they get pressured by hunters they will move into the lower, thicker aspen stands. These areas are difficult to hunt, because of the leaves on the trees and fewer open areas to glass with optics. There are also many lower areas with several different browse species, including; oak brush, service berry, mountain mahogany, bitter brush, snow berry, sage brush, etc. These areas also have deer in them during the hunt, but at a lower density. Some areas to hunt include the following: Currant Creek Reservoir Area - high elevation, large aspen stands, very accessible, high deer density for the unit. Low Pass Creek - near Currant Creek Reservoir, rough road, great for ATV's, great for glassing up high. West Fork of the Duchesne - limited ATV access, but open to trucks. Chicken Creek/Race Track - popular area, but holds a lot of deer and bucks CO-OP Creek - Very Popular area, near Highway 40, great camping, large aspen stands Trout Creek - many bucks taken here opening weekend Wildcat WMA - good access, flat on top, a lot of pressure, many yearling bucks taken here. North Fork of Deep Creek - borders private land, limited access by road, great horse area Tabby Mountain - great for ATV's, better after snow storms, mostly public land. Coleman Basin/Red Creek Mtn - SITLA land, some areas without roads, rough roads Reservation Ridge - fewer deer, but fewer people Strawberry Peak - High elevation, large areas near by with no road access, Cow Hollow, Slab Canyon, low deer density Timber Canyon/Long Ridge - low deer density, rough terrain, better after storms, rough roads. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. On years with cooler weather some of the larger bucks will start into some pre rut behavior in the last week of October. Recommended areas to hunt: The Zion Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. During the rifle hunt most deer are in transition to their wintering habitat. Some deer will still be higher on Forest Service and Private lands, but most will be on the lower elevation BLM and private lands. There are several livestock tanks, springs and a few guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: East Zion - BLM and SITLA land East of Zion National Park from Orderville south to the state line. The Sands, Elephant Cove, Poverty Flat are all good areas to find deer in their migration. Be aware of smaller parcels of private land. This unit is unusual for Southern Utah because of its large parcels of private lands that have several different land owners. Obtaining permission to hunt these areas can be difficult, but is not impossible.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure. Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Most higher elevation Raft River Mountains deer will remain high on the range until snow depths push them down into the sagebrush flats. Access to higher elevations is through One Mile Canyon, George Creek Canyon, Johnson Canyon, and Wildcat Canyon. Deer are plentiful and hunting opportunities exist up every canyon. Deer along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range can be found up Kimbell Creek, Red Banks, and Keg Springs along the west side and near Devil's Playground and Rocky Pass on the east side. Mule deer in the higher elevations do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the Raft River Mountains to the southeast end of the Grouse Creek Mountains for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats from Kelton to Devil's Playground. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This is a very productive unit with one of the largest deer herds in the state. Muzzleloader hunters will find most success hunting on summer habitats at 7,500 feet and above. In some years hunting on water sources can be productive but water is generally not limiting on the Manti portion of this unit. Migration Patterns: There is very little deer migration during the muzzleloader hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches east of SR-89 on the west and the sagebrush benches west of SR-6 and SR-10 on the east side of the mountain. There is very little seasonal movement of deer on the San Rafael portion of the unit. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: Upper Fish Creek and it's tributaries. The tributaries include Gooseberry Creek, Silver Creek, C Canyon, and the Straight Fork. This is a roadless area on the north end of the unit. This area has had some prescribed fires recently that has improved deer habitat. It can be accessed from North Skyline Drive on the west or from Scofield Reservoir on the east. The bottom two miles of Upper Fish Creek is privately owned and in a CWMU Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge These ridges have roads going down them. They are northwest of Scofield Reservoir. The bottom 2 miles of these ridges are privately owned. This is excellent habitat in the Pondtown Creek drainage on the north end of the unit. It is best accessed from North Skyline Drive. Trough Spring Ridge This is accessed off of SR-264 southwest of the town of Scofield. It is just above the Skyline Coal Mine. This is the ridge on the east side of Electric Lake. There are some small pockets of private land that are posted well but the majority of the acreage is Forest Service. Much of this ridge burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 which has improved the deer habitat in this area. Gentry Mountain. This is accessed from SR-10 just north of the town of Huntington at Huntington Reservoir. Part of this mountain is privately owned and part of it burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 West of Skyline Drive All the small towns along the west face of the Central Mountains Manti Unit has a canyon road to connect to Skyline Drive. Some roads are fairly rough going with the better access up from Fairview, Ephraim and Mayfiled. Concentrate on side roads and trails from the main canyon roads to get to the more likely areas to find deer. The higher elevations in aspen and sagebrush meadows with water in close proximity will hold some of the mature bucks. Down low in the agricultural valleys many younger bucks will use the alfalfa fields in the evenings and early morning. Much of the adjacent property along the agriculture is either Forest Service or State lands and there will be a good opportunities there. East of Skyline Drive and South of Huntington Canyon There is a considerable amount of access along Skyline Drive, high elevation ridge tops, and lower canyons and valleys. There are also many areas where you can hike to get away from roads, much of it very steep, but where nice bucks hold up. Some preliminary scouting with maps is a great way to familiarize yourself with the unit. hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in late September are generally pretty mild with warm days and cold nights. There is rarely snow on the ground during this hunt and most deer are still found on high elevation summer ranges. Roads are generally in good shape. Be prepared for cold nights and occasional rainstorms which can make the roads muddy. This can disrupt hunting and deer behavior as well as the ability to hunt on a water source.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Nebo unit has some very rough terrain. I tell hunters that "the Nebo is either strait up or strait down" so be prepared for some very hard work. ATV use is not allowed on the north Nebo and horses or mules are recommended. At the very least hunters should be in very good physical condition.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: In the past the harvest has been distributed throughout the entire portion of the Nebo. The higher elevations can be good places to start looking for more mature bucks but the younger bucks can be found at lower elevations, especially associated with agriculture areas. Don't limit yourself to a few areas. They can be found anywhere on the mountains. Some of the areas to concentrate on are Nebo Creek, Page Fork, Hop Creek, and Mahogany Knoll. Other good places are off the Nebo Loop Road around Payson Lakes and the Summit Trail. The south Nebo (Sanpitch Mts.), that portion of the Nebo Unit that is south of SR 132, may be more accessible since ATV use is allowed by the USFS. However there is private property further south as well as a CWMU deer unit. Water sources are good places to find deer. Most archery hunters have the most success early in the hunt sitting at remote water holes and canyons with perennial water. Migration Patterns There is very little deer migration during the archery and muzzleloader hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches which is usually after the rifle hunt. However, heavy snow fall during the hunt may cause deer to migrate to lower elevations early. Scouting Tips: Good hunters will scout and find their own "honey hole". A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of deer. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Depending on the season be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road and trail conditions. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat especially during the archery season so in anticipation of hot weather plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fillmore unit has great deer habitat and had an increase in the buck/doe ratio. Although the hunt boundary extends onto the west side of I-15, the Pahvant Mountain Range (east side of I-15) receives most of the hunting pressure.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Deer Deer can be found across the entire unit with most of the deer still being found at higher elevations during the muzzleloader season. It is common to see bucks off of the main roads which results in those roads receiving a high amount of hunting pressure. Walking out ridges and glassing canyons can be a great strategy in finding deer and seeing fewer hunters. Water The Pahvant is relatively dry. There are creeks in the bottoms of some of the canyons and a few springs and stock ponds on top. Deer can be found on both the east and west sides.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreational users. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. After heavy rain storms, many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage is good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Temperatures are starting to cool down some it is a great time to hunt deer on the Pahvant.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal Mountains unit is one of the most beautiful places that you will ever encounter. The unit has high alpine peaks, above 12,000 ft. and goes down to low desert valleys around 4,000 ft. This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit however, every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is good road access throughout the unit, however there are also many places that hunters can hike into and get away from the crowds. Hunters should be aware of the CWMU's and private lands on the unit and learn the boundaries. There are 2 CWMUs on this unit and a list is available on the UDWR webpage: http://wildlife.utah.gov/maps/public/list_cwmus.php
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the La Sals typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Using quality binoculars or spotting scopes will be very valuable to you. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas for the muzzleloader hunt: Muzzleloader hunters will find bucks in the high country, but should also focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. Look for oak patches with intermixed sagebrush meadows and a healthy forbe component.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is extremely limited throughout most of the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sals. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.

It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter, the unit has has experienced decreased fawn production and survival. This has resulted in a decrease in the deer population and bucks available to hunt. Buck deer permit numbers have been reduced to reflect the current population status. Deer hunting has been good however. Deer populate the entire Monroe unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be on central and northern parts of the unit. The southern portion of the unit is narrower, drier, as has fewer deer. During the Muzzleloader season most of the deer still tend to be in the higher elevations though some have began to move down a little. This season is a great time to hunt the Monroe. Hunter densities are not high and the weather is often pleasant.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are deer spread across the entire Monroe unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want. Great deer range and population exists in the Northern part of the unit, productive areas include above the towns of Glenwood and Annabella including the Hunter's Flat, Thompson Basin, and Big Lake areas. On the East side of the unit deer hunting can be good in the Mormon Mountain area (much of this is private) and in the hills above Burrville. Good road access and prime deer habitat are located in the following areas: Box Creeks, Indian Peak, Monroe Peak, Greenwich Creeks, and the Dairies areas. There is some private property in these areas so make sure you know where you are. Most of these areas are aspen and mountain brush habitats. On the West side of the unit good places to find deer include Poverty Flat, the canyons surrounding Marysvale peak, and the area around Barney Lake. The South end of the unit contains deer in the Forshea Mtn, Langdon Peak areas. The sage flats West of Angle have some deer during the rifle season.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is has a high buck/doe ratio primarily due to an abundance of private land where hunting pressure is generally light. This is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The key to this unit is finding public lands. Most of the public lands are at the fringes of the good summer and fall deer habitat as most of the high elevation acreage is privately owned.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most deer on the Tavaputs Plateau migrate to the east toward the Green River to spend the winter months. This includes the lower ends of Ceder, Cottonwood, and Flat Iron Ridges as well as the area near Prickly Pear Canyon. Deer on the western part of the unit tend to migrate to the southwest to the foothills just north and east of Price near the Price Airport, Coal Creek, and Soldier Creek. Hunting is much better if the weather is bad and generally poor if we have had mild weather. Generally there has been very little migration during the muzzleloader hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Cold Springs WMA provides good public land access on high elevation summer habitat and transitional fall habitat near Bruin Point. There is a county road through the middle of the WMA with over 2500 acres of public lands available. Much of the property is walk-in only to maintain quality deer hunting in the area. This area can be accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside or if the weather is bad from Nine Mile Canyon and up Cottonwood Canyon. Lots of wild horses on this part of the mountain. Upper Patmos Ridge/Range Creek There are 5 sections of BLM land that are surrounded by private lands just south of Bruin Point and North of the Preston Nutter Ranch gate. This provides good deer habitat at high elevations on steep timber covered terrain with ample water. This is accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside. Harmon Canyon/Prickly Pear Canyon This is good transitional habitat especially if there has been some snow. It is accessed via Nine Mile Canyon then you can drive up the Harmon Canyon road which is about 30 miles east of Wellington Utah. These are sagebrush/PJ habitats at about 7500 feet in elevation. Cottonwood/Ceder Ridge This is good transitional habitat in sagebrush at elevations of 6500 to 8000 feet. There are private lands to the west but plenty of public lands as you go down the ridges. These areas are accessed via Nine Mile Canyon and then Cottonwood Canyon 45 miles east of Wellington. Anthro Subunit Recommended areas to hunt: The Anthro subunit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer. Because the density is so low, if you do find any bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. There is a lot of area East of Antelope Canyon all the way to the Green River, with even lower deer densities, while hunting these areas your best chance is finding water. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Nutter's Ridge - USFS higher elevation, a few large aspen stands, very accessible Jeep Trail Ridge - USFS just East of Nutter's Ridge, large canyons with a few aspens, several water sources Wire Fence Ridge - USFS rough road, biggest aspen stands on Anthro, good burned side hills Alkaline/Choke Cherry - USFS very open country, few deer, East of Jeep Trail Wells Draw - BLM lands, low elevation pinyon/juniper, low density Cottonwood Ridge - USFS difficult access, higher elevation, many timbered hill sides
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in late September and early October are generally pretty mild with warm days and cold nights. There is rarely snow on the ground during the muzzleloader hunt and most deer are still found on high elevation summer ranges. Roads are generally in good shape. Be prepared for cold nights and occasional rainstorms which can make the roads muddy.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is a migration study underway to look at timing and routes of migration for North Slope deer. We ask that collared deer are not killed. If one is, DO NOT CUT THE COLLAR; remove the collar by loosening the lock nuts and call the number on the collar or the local biologist. This unit encompasses lodgepole pine, open sagebrush, and desert scrub. Hunters should expect to see other deer and elk hunters and other public land users. There is a muzzleloader doe hunt that coincides with this hunt on a portion of the unit near Manila.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer in the High Uintas do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the west side of the North Slope to the east end of the North Slope for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats all along the North Slope. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after this hunt ends so it does not affect the hunt. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the North Slope: Deer are found throughout much of the unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts, deer will be higher in elevation, although there are some that stay year-round in the sagebrush habitat on Dowd Mountain, Death Valley, and Red Creek Flat. Depending on weather conditions, most of the deer on the Summit portion get pushed down into Wyoming before the Any Weapon hunt begins. Also, high country deer are typically pushed down out of the High Country by mid-October if any early season snow storms hit. The majority of the deer in the 3 Corners portion of the unit stay up high on Bear Mountain, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, and Bender Mountain until later in October/early November when deer start showing up in Browns Park for the winter. This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure, especially in Browns Park, Goslin Mountain, South Valley, Dowd Mountain, and along Hwy 44. Areas with highest harvest success include Greendale Junction (along Highway 44 and 191), Sheep Creek Lake, Long Park, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, and 3 Corners. Hunters that receive written permission from private landowners in Manila also do well. Recommended areas include along Highway 44 and 191, Sheep Creep Lake, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, 3 Corners, Henry's Fork, Bridger Lake and along the North Slope Road.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

This unit has a substantial amount of year-round range that will always have some deer. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Pine Valley Unit is 90% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Deer on the Muzzleloader hunt are spread out across their summer ranges deer densities are higher in some areas than they are in other. Some high deer density areas also have higher numbers of hunters and can result in some hunter crowding. Please be aware of other hunters and be courteous. Day time temperatures during the Muzzleloader hunt can still reach into the mid 80's. On years with good monsoonal moisture the deer may be spread out more across their range.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Migration should not be a factor on this hunt. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Pine Valley Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several livestock tanks, springs and guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Bull Valley Mtns - Forest Service and small tracts of private land South and West of Enterprise. This area is very accessible by vehicles. Deer densities decrease as you move further west towards the Nevada state line. Hunting is best in oak brush and service berry near water sources. Bumblebee Mtn. - BLM, USFS, and SITLA SW of Cedar City. The higher elevation areas in the oak brush best for locating deer. Access is limited to a few main roads and ATV trails. Hunters will do better if they get out and do some hiking and spotting deer. Paradise and Pine Valley Wilderness - Forest Service land from Pace Draw NW of New Harmony to the south face of the Pine Valley Mtn. This area is remote and has little to no vehicle access. There are several foot and horse trails into the area. Some access points are the Anderson and Comanche trail head in the New Harmony area, The Grants Ranch trail head between New Harmony and Pinto, The Paradise trail head near Pinto, The Mill Canyon and Water Canyon trail heads south of the Town of Pine Valley in Grass Valley, The Whipple and Forsyth trail heads in Pine Valley. The further you are willing to hike in the better the hunting may become. Atchison and Harrison Peak - Forest Service land Between Mountain Meadow and Grass Valley. Mostly sagebrush and serviceberry habitat with some scattered pinion and juniper. This area has limited access and with a few ATV trails. Hiking in a ½ mile plus from the roads will increase success in finding the bucks.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: It can be very hot during this season. Please be prepared with plenty of water. Make sure friends and family know where you area going and when you will return. Be aware of rattle snakes!
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer. Muzzleloader Season: During the Muzzleloader season most of the deer still tend to be in the mid to higher elevations though some have began to move down a little. This season is a great time to hunt the Fish Lake, hunter densities are not high and the weather is often pleasant. Deer will be spread out across the unit. Migration Patterns: Some of the deer on Fish Lake unit begin to migrate to or closer to their winter range in mid-October. By the time the rifle hunt arrives a sizable portion of the herd is often in the transitional ranges between their winter and summer ranges. However many deer also stay as high as they can until heavy snows push them lower. Most of the migration is rather simple, the deer just move up or down in elevation. However there are some deer that move from their summering areas on the North and Central parts of the unit to the Southern, Eastern, and Western parts of the unit closer to their winter range. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it generally does not affect the general deer hunts. Recommended areas to hunt on the Fish Lake unit: There are deer spread across the entire Fish Lake unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a large area and cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. During the archery season hunters should be prepared to cool harvested game quickly due to warm temperatures.

The unit population has been increasing over the past few years, along with the buck to doe ratio. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are 3 CWMUs on this unit, which general season permits are not permitted. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Abajos typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the San Juan, Abajo subunit: Abajo Mountain - Muzzleloader hunters may find bucks in the high country, but should also focus on mid elevations. Look for oak-brush stands or sagebrush parks, surrounded by pinyon/juniper communities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the Abajos. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation towards the end of October and first part of November. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Southwest Desert unit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer because the density is so low. When you do find bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from West to East, with most of the deer wintering on or near Tabby WMA. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: There are numerous areas to hunt on this unit. The areas surrounding Strawberry Reservoir and Currant Creek Reservoir are excellent for deer hunting. They are easy to access with many roads and trails and camping areas. This of course leads to many people hunting these areas. There are very few areas on this unit without a road in the general area. There is far less hunting pressure on the Avintaquin unit, but that is because the overall deer density is much lower and the terrain is more rugged. This unit has very large aspen stands that hold a lot of deer in the early fall. Many of the best bucks taken each year come from these aspen stands. In the summer there are deer in the more open higher areas, but once they get pressured by hunters they will move into the lower, thicker aspen stands. These areas are difficult to hunt, because of the leaves on the trees and fewer open areas to glass with optics. There are also many lower areas with several different browse species, including; oak brush, service berry, mountain mahogany, bitter brush, snow berry, sage brush, etc. These areas also have deer in them during the hunt, but at a lower density. Some areas to hunt include the following: Currant Creek Reservoir Area - high elevation, large aspen stands, very accessible, high deer density for the unit. Low Pass Creek- near Currant Creek Reservoir, rough road, great for ATV's, great for glassing up high. West Fork of the Duchesne- limited ATV access, but open to trucks. Chicken Creek/Race Track- popular area, but holds a lot of deer and bucks CO-OP Creek -Very Popular area, near Highway 40, great camping, large aspen stands Trout Creek- many bucks taken here opening weekend Wildcat WMA - good access, flat on top, a lot of pressure, many yearling bucks taken here. North Fork of Deep Creek - borders private land, limited access by road, great horse area Tabby Mountain - great for ATV's, better after snow storms, mostly public land. Coleman Basin/Red Creek Mtn- SITLA land, some areas without roads, rough roads Reservation Ridge -fewer deer, but fewer people Strawberry Peak- High elevation, large areas near by with no road access, Cow Hollow, Slab Canyon, low deer density Timber Canyon/Long Ridge- low deer density, rough terrain, better after storms, rough roads. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

The Deep Creek area is a USFS roadless area. Access can be found at the trail head a short distance above the turn off to Webster's Flat on Highway 14. Midway - USFS land from the turn off to Cedar Breaks east to Navajo Lake. The old clear cut logging areas and meadows in the Deer Valley area usually have a fair amount of deer use. Strawberry Ridge and Harris Flat - USFS land between Strawberry Cabins area and east to Stout Canyon. This is a ponderosa pine are that has a good understory of bitterbrush. There is good access in to this area with several OHV trails and old logging roads. This area has several wildlife and livestock water catch ponds. This area has several cabin communities and hunters should be careful of private lands and how close they hunt to cabins. Stout Canyon and School Wash - USFS land with some larger blocks of private land. This is a ponderosa pine habitat with a good understory of bitterbrush. There are a few OHV trails and logging roads that cut through this area. Private land - Some of the best deer habitat on the Zion unit is on private lands. This unit is unusual for Southern Utah because of its large parcels of private lands that have several different land owners. Obtaining permission to hunt these areas can be difficult, but is not impossible.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunting buck deer in the middle of October is a relatively new thing in Utah. We are accustomed to hunting deer the last week of October when deer are often beginning to rut, and transitioning from summer to winter habitats. During mid October, deer are more likely to be remaining on summer habitats at high elevations. I would focus my efforts on public lands above 7,000 feet in elevation. On the Range Creek subunit, these areas are usually small parcels of public land surrounded by vast areas of private land. Areas to look at would be the small portion of Patmos Ridge that is public land, Cold Springs Ridge, and Cottonwood Ridge. Public land areas occur on Anthro Mountain but deer densities are generally much lower. The Range Creek subunit is also a general season Any Bull unit so expect to see other hunters afield during your deer hunt although elk hunter numbers tend to drop dramatically after the opening weekend. This unit has a high buck/doe ratio. This is due in large part to the large amounts of private land where harvest is conservative.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: A good portion of this hunt unit is in fairly remote country with very little cell coverage. Steep canyons are prone to flash flooding during thunderstorms. Several access roads reach elevations near 10,000 feet where snow can come early in the season
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Fall in Utah. You can expect rain, occasional early fall snowstorms, or warm dry conditions

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is one of two any weapon hunts that take place on this unit. This hunt holds the opportunity to hunt some of the deer on the southern portion of the unit before they migrate to winter ranges, and in some cases off of the unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt was added during the 2019 hunting season as a new hunt. This hunt offers the opportunity to hunt some of the deer on the unit before they migrate from the unit to winter range. Most of the deer on the southern 1/3 of the unit migrate from higher elevation summer ranges to winter ranges, with a good portion of these leaving the unit. Depending on the year the deer may be tricky to find as migration could be occurring during this hunt depending on where you are hunting. If you don't find as many deer as you like, check either higher or lower elevations. You may also want to hunt some of the mid range where migration could be occurring. For the northern 2/3 of the unit slight migration occurs, but it is mainly from higher elevations to mid range, and mountain valleys where ag land and winter range is abundant. There was a significant wildland fire that occurred in the unit in June of 2017. This fire was reseeded, and has taken well as well as a lot of aspen regeneration is occurring. Hunting these burnt areas can now prove to be a good strategy as the feed in these areas is good.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell service is generally good on most of the unit, however their are some dead spots in canyons.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Generally warm temperatures occur during this hunt during the day, but night temperatures could drop into the 30's. There have been many instances over the years that during this week our first snow fall of the year occurs. Check the weather before the hunt, and prepare accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Pine Valley Unit is 90% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Deer on the rifle hunt are beginning to congregate onto their winter ranges so hunters can be expected to be following which will result in some hunter crowding. Please be aware of other hunters and be courteous. Day time temperatures during the rifle hunt can still reach into the low 80's. On years with good monsoonal moisture the deer may be spread out more across their range.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Pine Valley Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several livestock tanks, springs and guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: North end of Beaver Dam Mtns - BLM and SITLA lands west of St. George. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Deer movement into this area can vary from year to year depending on migration. Tobin Bench to Motaqua - BLM and SITLA with some small private lands in the Motaqua area. Deer migration is more reliable in this area with increasing numbers on the second weekend of the hunt. Above Dameron and Diamond Valley- BLM, Forest Service and SITLA lands at higher elevations above Dameron and Diamond Valley. Enterprise North Hills and New Castle- BLM, Forest Service, Private and SITLA lands. Deer begin moving into these areas about the second week of October. Most deer will be in the agricultural fields at night and then available on Public Lands during the day. Bumblebee and Sweat Hills -BLM, Forest Service and SITLA lands West and South of Cedar City. Some deer may remain high on Bumblebee Mtn. until heavier snow storms drive them down.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunter crowding can be a spot in localized areas. Make sure you where your hunter orange and know what is beyond your target before shooting.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.
