hunt_bio_general_information: This can be a very physical hunt, be prepared. Harvest success on this unit has typically been high and with a limited number of permits, there is little competition between hunters. This unit is can be hunted from the bottom along the Chicken Corner Rd and the Lockhart Basin Rd, or from the top from the Canyon Rim Recreation Area (Needles Overlook Rd). This unit offers some of the most scenic viewpoints in Utah. This is a small population of sheep, with the most recent population estimate of ~90 in 2023 with good numbers of younger rams coming into those mature age classes. Mandatory online harvest reporting is required.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Suggested Hunting Areas: This unit can be hunted from below or from the top. Chicken Corner and Lockhart Basin are main access points to below cliff face. The Lockhart Basin Rd can get very rough in spots so an ATV/ OHV is recommended. Canyon Rims Recreation Area (Looking Glass to Anticline) is the main access to hunt from the top. Sheep will work along base of cliff, so if you choose to hunt from the top, be sure you can retrieve the sheep if you harvest. Hurrah Pass, Dripping Spring, Lockhart Basin, below both Needles and Canyonlands Overlook are all great locations to look for sheep. Scouting Tips: It is good to do pre-season scouting to learn the country. However, it is very hot on this unit during the summer months so plan accordingly. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a spotting scope. The unit is dry and rocky/cliffy. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Some of the larger, mature rams will move in with these ewe groups in late October. Do not be overly alarmed if you don't see many mature rams during the summer, they will start looking for the ewe groups in late October as the rut begins. Hunting generally gets better the later you go. The peak of the rut tends to be the mid-late November. Rams will typically move between multiple ewe groups, so it is not uncommon to see different rams with the same group of ewes across multiple days. Sheep will be active throughout the day and are good at finding spots just out of sight. Be patient and let your optics cover visible miles, but make sure to check various vantage points. Behavior: The month of November is during the bighorn sheep rut. Rams are moving between groups of ewes during this time. Rams will butt heads to establish dominance, so it can be helpful to occasionally stop and listen for the sound of butting heads as it can be a good tool for locating sheep that are otherwise difficult to see. Bighorn sheep will not be as tied to water in November as it is generally more available that time of year. They tend to be found on the steep open cliffs and mesa tops and are occasionally feeding on the flat canyon bottoms or benches. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl, even young rams will have a pronounced curl. Mature ewes and yearling rams have similar curl; however, a ewe horn is thin and a yearling ram horn is much heavier especially at the base. The best way to recognize mature bighorn rams is to look for horn mass, particularly out near the tip of the horn. Younger rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. Mature rams that are 6 years and older tend to have thicker horns out near the tips, and thicker bases. Often times if you are close enough you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. The first deep and prominent annuli on a rams horn working from the tip back towards the base is most often the 3.5 yr old ring as it is associated with the ram's first rut. Disease Issues: Bighorn sheep are highly susceptible to infection from respiratory pathogens. Depending on the virulence of respiratory pathogen strain, infection can lead to all age die-offs with continued lamb recruitment suppression for years following an outbreak. Bighorn sheep usually become infected through contact with domestic sheep or goats. These domestic animals carry the bacterium but aren't typically affected by it. This unit has tested positive for Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae, the bacterium most often associated with pneumonia outbreaks in bighorn sheep populations. If you notice any disease symptoms (coughing, sneezing, nasal discharge) While you are out scouting/ hunting please report to the local DWR office.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This unit is steep and rough with very little to no cell coverage. As in most bighorn sheep habitat, hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters will cover many rugged miles and climb/descend thousands of feet in elevation. Be careful working through cliff bands. It can be easy to get yourself onto a ledge with no way beyond that spot, it is advised that you bring extra rope to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is also recommended on this unit. Bring plenty of water as it can be warm in November and there may be very little water on the unit. An InReach can be a useful type of satellite messaging if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in November are variable on this unit. Generally, plan on cold nights with mild days and little to no snow accumulation. Most of the occupied bighorn sheep habitat occurs at lower elevations between 4200 and 6000 feet where snow generally doesn't accumulate. Snow and bad weather is always possible in November. Be cautious of flash flooding during rain storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Dirty Devil bighorn sheep population was last surveyed in 2022 on a 3 year interval. We surveyed a total of 158 sheep; 53 rams, 73 ewes, and 32 lambs. The projected population is 263 sheep. Numbers have improved over the last decade from a low count of 60 sheep in 2014. Lamb production hit a low in 2008 at 10 lambs per 100 ewes but has increased slowly to 44 lambs per 100 ewes in 2022. The ram to ewe ratio increased substantially in 2022 at 73 rams per 100 ewes somewhat due to finding 39 sheep along the upper two-thirds of the unit boundary along the Colorado River in Cataract Canyon and below the Canyonlands National Park boundary. This is a very difficult area to hunt because the canyon bottom is not safely accessibile from the top rim of the canyon. Some hunting has been done with watercraft traveling up river but it is not advised as a water craft was lost in the rapids. As with many other desert sheep units, sheep are spread out over large expanses of habitat, often making them difficult to locate. Plan on scheduling enough time for a lot of scouting and hunting.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Suggested Hunting Area: Sheep are spread out in many areas on this unit. Based upon harvest and observations here are some areas to get you started: Along the Dirty Devil below Sams Mesa and along Happy to Hatch Canyons, Larry's and No Mans Canyons, Gibex Point, Twin Corral, and Sam's Box canyons. Along the Dirty Devil on both sides. The canyons and ridges along SR95 in North Wash including Marinus, Stair, and Butler Canyons, and also including the unnamed canyons, can also hold sheep but we have not counted as many in these areas in recent surveys. The west side of the Dirty Devil from SR95 to the Beaver Canyon area which includes Poison Springs Canyon also is a good place to focus on glassing and looking for sign. Sheep often use cliff bands and the grassy benches between them, the rims of canyons, and the canyon bottoms. They are also often seen in the slick rock areas. Scouting Tips: It's good to be familiar with the area and understand if you have what it will take to find and harvest a mature ram before applying for this permit. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a good spotting scope. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Older rams generally will not move into the area where the ewe groups are until the rut begins in late October. Hunting generally gets better the later you go with more mature rams showing up by November. Rams move a lot in November between ewe groups, so a single group of ewes and lambs can attract different rams from day to day. Behavior: The peak of the rut tends to be the week of Thanksgiving or just prior to it. Rams will be moving from group to group looking for ewes. It is difficult to glass up rams but sometimes you can hear them butting heads as they compete with other rams to breed with the ewes. This can sound like a rifle firing through the canyons if you're close enough. Sheep are generally active throughout the day in November but activity is highest in morning and evening. Bighorn sheep can go long periods without drinking water, acquiring moisture from vegetation that they eat. Bighorn will generally avoid the flat mesa tops where there is tree cover, but not always. Sheep use precipitous canyons and plateaus where the topography is steep with rough rocky outcrops. Between canyon ledges are often wider grassy slopes and shelves where sheep feed and which are corridors to other canyon layers and escape routes. Desert bighorn sheep have cloven hooves with harder sides/edges and softer inner pads. This adaptation allows them to quickly traverse steep rocky terrain to avoid predation. They are good at hiding under tight ledges and rocks. Horn Growth: Both rams and ewes have horns. Mature ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Mature ewes and yearling rams have similar curl; however, a ewe horn is thin and a yearling ram horn is much heavier especially at the base. 2.5 year old rams begin to have a pronounced curl, and rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. The best way to recognize mature trophy class bighorn rams is to look for horns closer to a full curl with horn mass, particularly out near the end of the horn. Mature rams 6 years and older have thicker heavier bases and the horns are thicker out near the ends only because older rams 'broom off' the thinner tips. During the rut horn growth nearly stops, creating annuli growth rings on the horn. The rate at which the horn grows in length steadily declines after 3.5 years of age, after about 8.5 years growth rings become less defined and their reliability to determine age drops dramatically. Often times if you are close enough, you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. If you know the horn is broomed and heavy at the end then the second growth ring you see is most likely at 2.5 years old. The 2.5 yr and 3.5 year rings are often the most prominent with the 3.5 yr old ring being the deepest because it is associated with the ram's first rut. The ear will usually point to this ring on a mature ram. If only one prominent ring is seen it is probably a 2.5 year old ram. By locating the 3.5 yr old ring you can determine or at least estimate the age of the ram by adding a year for each subsequent annuli growth ring. Disease Issues: Bighorn sheep are highly susceptible to infection from respiratory pathogens. Between 30-70% of the herd can die if they become infected, and lambs born into the herd can continue to die after an outbreak. They usually become infected through contact with domestic sheep or goats. These domestic animals carry the disease but aren't affected by it. While you are out scouting and hunting please report any domestic sheep or goats in bighorn habitat to the local DWR office.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Sheep habitat is found between 3700'and 6000'. Hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters end up walking dozens of miles and traversing thousands of feet in elevation prior to harvesting their ram. As with most bighorn sheep habitat, there are steep impassible canyons and an abundance of cliffs. Be very careful scaling cliffs. It is advised that you bring extra rope and climbing gear to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is very handy on this unit to not only mark sheep and routes but also places where you can get through the ledges as they are relatively rare. Hunters can sometimes spend hours hiking along trying to find a way through the ledges and wasting time and energy. Bring plenty of water, there is very little on the unit. Carry a good survival kit and a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp, where you are hunting, and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Temperatures can swing dramatically in November, be prepared for all weather conditions, pay attention to the weather forecast and use common sense. Generally, plan on cold nights with mild days and little to no snow accumulation. Snow and bad weather is always possible in November. Be cautious of flash flooding during rain and thunder storms.

The information on this webpage is meant to help guide you to areas that are likely to have sheep based upon harvest and observations, as well as other information to help you be successful on your hunt. As with many other desert sheep units, sheep are spread out over large expanses of habitat, often making them difficult to locate. Plan on scheduling enough time for a lot of scouting and hunting.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Suggested Hunting Areas: Higher unit densities of desert bighorns based upon harvest and observations- San Rafael Reef north of I-70, Calf Mesa, Cane Wash, Virgin Springs, The Wedge, and South Coal Wash. Lower density areas- Salt Wash, Eagle Canyon, Buckhorn Wash, Saddle Horse, McCarty, Wood Canyon. Sheep often use cliff bands and the grassy benches between them, the rims of canyons, and the canyon bottoms. They are also often seen in the slick rock areas. Scouting Tips: It's good to be familiar with the area and understand if you have what it will take to find and harvest a mature ram before applying for this permit. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a good spotting scope. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Older rams generally will not move into the area where the ewe groups are until the rut begins in late October. Hunting generally gets better the later you go with more mature rams showing up by November. Rams move a lot in November between ewe groups, so a single group of ewes and lambs can attract different rams from day to day. Behavior: The peak of the rut tends to be the week of Thanksgiving or just prior to it. Rams will be moving from group to group looking for ewes. It is difficult to glass up rams but sometimes you can hear them butting heads as they compete with other rams to breed with the ewes. This can sound like a rifle firing through the canyons if you're close enough. Sheep are generally active throughout the day in November but activity is highest in morning and evening. Bighorn sheep can go long periods without drinking water, acquiring moisture from vegetation that they eat. Bighorn will generally avoid the flat mesa tops where there is tree cover, but not always. Sheep use precipitous canyons and plateaus where the topography is steep with rough rocky outcrops. Between canyon ledges are often wider grassy slopes and shelves where sheep feed and which are corridors to other canyon layers and escape routes. Desert bighorn sheep have cloven hooves with harder sides/edges and softer inner pads. This adaptation allows them to quickly traverse steep rocky terrain to avoid predation. They are good at hiding under tight ledges and rocks. Horn Growth: Both rams and ewes have horns. Mature ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Mature ewes and yearling rams have similar curl; however, a ewe horn is thin and a yearling ram horn is much heavier especially at the base. 2.5 year old rams begin to have a pronounced curl, and rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. The best way to recognize mature trophy class bighorn rams is to look for horns closer to a full curl with horn mass, particularly out near the end of the horn. Mature rams 6 years and older have thicker heavier bases and the horns are thicker out near the ends only because older rams 'broom off' the thinner tips. During the rut horn growth nearly stops, creating annuli growth rings on the horn. The rate at which the horn grows in length steadily declines after 3.5 years of age, after about 8.5 years growth rings become less defined and their reliability to determine age drops dramatically. Often times if you are close enough, you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. If you know the horn is broomed and heavy at the end then the second growth ring you see is most likely at 2.5 years old. The 2.5 yr and 3.5 year rings are often the most prominent with the 3.5 yr old ring being the deepest because it is associated with the ram's first rut. The ear will usually point to this ring on a mature ram. If only one prominent ring is seen it is probably a 2.5 year old ram. By locating the 3.5 yr old ring you can determine or at least estimate the age of the ram by adding a year for each subsequent annuli growth ring. Disease Issues: Bighorn sheep are highly susceptible to infection from respiratory pathogens. Between 30-70% of the herd can die if they become infected, and lambs born into the herd can continue to die after an outbreak. Bighorn sheep usually become infected through contact with domestic sheep or goats. These domestic animals carry the disease but aren't affected by it. While you are out scouting and hunting please report precise locations and numbers of any domestic sheep or goats in bighorn habitat to the local DWR office.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Sheep habitat is found between 4200' to 7900' on this unit. Hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters end up walking dozens of miles and traversing thousands in elevation prior to harvesting their ram. As with most bighorn sheep habitat, there are steep impassible canyons and an abundance of cliffs. Be very careful scaling cliffs. It is advised that you bring extra rope and climbing gear to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is very handy on this unit to not only mark sheep and routes but also places where you can get through the ledges as they are relatively rare. Hunters can sometimes spend hours hiking along trying to find a way through the ledges and wasting time and energy. Bring plenty of water, there is very little on the unit. Carry a good survival kit and a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp, where you will be hunting, and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Temperatures can swing dramatically in November, be prepared for all weather conditions, pay attention to the weather forecast and use common sense. Generally, plan on cold nights with mild days and little to no snow accumulation. Snow and bad weather is always possible in November. Be cautious of flash flooding during rain and thunder storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: Most general areas occupied by bighorn sheep on the Zion unit can be found in Zion National Park (ZNP), Canaan Mountain, and the Barracks. Densities are currently higher inside ZNP however good numbers of sheep exist on public lands open to hunting on the Cannan Mountain and Barracks areas. Hunting is not allowed inside the park boundaries. This bighorn sheep unit has been over population objective so capture and transplant efforts have been accomplished over the past few years. This population was re-established in the early 1970's and was not hunted until 2009. The Zion unit is a highly popular and coveted area to hunt bighorn sheep due to trophy quality, access, and scenic areas to hunt. The Barracks is the area where the Virgin River flows from Mt Carmel, UT into ZNP. Access to this area can be found south of Mt Carmel where sheep can be found close to private lands on the east end. Bighorn are commonly observed on BLM lands from Bay Bill and Merwin Canyons west into the Poverty Wash area to the ZNP boundary. Access from SR9 can also be found in the Poverty area and east of Mineral Gulch. The south side of the canyon can be accessed through Elephant Gap. The Canaan Mountain area is located near Hildale, UT. Hiking access can be found in Short Creek where hunters can focus on Canaan Mountain and South Mountain. This species lives in extreme rugged habitat that can have extreme weather conditions. Be prepared to hike in this type of country and spend a lot of time with your binoculars.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Harvest locations can vary by hunter abilities and preferences. Migration Patterns: Bighorn sheep seem to limit movements in the hottest times of the year with trips to watering areas highly documented. Space use increases as rutting behaviors begin. Scouting Tips: Most hunters spend a substantial amount of time becoming familiar with maps of this area and spend time prior to the hunt to locate areas with sheep. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential to bighorn sheep hunting. Find a high point, get comfortable, and spend time glassing to locate sheep. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens but can offer great insight at any time of the year. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Behavior: Peak rutting behavior appears to occur in September and October, but may begin as early as July. There is more water available on this unit than one would think. Be aware of small seeps and springs and look for tracks since sheep may use watering areas regularly.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Roads may be washed out by heavy rains and an ATV may be most useful to access many areas. Much of this area is inaccessible during wet conditions so watch weather forecasts. A 4WD vehicle is highly recommended. Cellular phone coverage is spotty and the biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms WILL cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Pine Valley, Virgin River unit has a small population of sheep numbering approximately 100 sheep. Most years there are only two ram permits on for this hunt. This is a shared population on with Arizona and the hunt coincides with Arizona's hunt. Their is a lot of movement of sheep across the state line. There are no developed camp grounds in this area. Camping on BLM land is limited to 14 days in any one location.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Sheep can be found 91 in the Scrub Peak, Cedar Pockets and Bull dog Canyon area. Make sure you have good optics. Setting up at key vantage points and glassing large chunks of country should help you find pockets of sheep to set up stocks on. You can expect to find rams in the 150-160 class. Several 165 rams have been harvested over the past ten years. Landownership in the this area is almost 100% BLM lands. You will be hunting along the Utah/Arizona state line and it is not marked in any way. Use a GPS and land marks to know where you are in relation to the state line at all times.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: As with most sheep habitat the terrain is extremely rugged. Make sure you are ready physically and have good hiking boots. Cell phone service is spotty. Make sure friends and family know where you are hunting and when to expect you to return. Carry plenty of water. Day time temps are still very warm for this November-December hunt time frame. Hunting in pairs is a good idea.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Day time temps area still into the 70's, expect the night time low's down into the 20-30's. Occasional short rain showers are possible.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is rugged and vast bighorn sheep country and will be a very hard and physical hunt, be prepared. This unit encompasses some of the most beautiful and remote scenery that Utah has to offer, but most of it is very difficult to access. This is a small population of sheep, with the most recent population estimate of ~70 sheep in 2023. Mandatory online harvest reporting is required.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Suggested Hunting Areas: All of the large canyons along the Colorado River and their tributaries can be good areas to locate bighorn. Sheep, Dark, Lost, Young's, Lean-To, Bowdie, Palmer, and Gypsum canyons can all be good areas to check. Scouting Tips: It is good to do pre-season scouting to learn the country. However, it is very hot on this unit during the summer months so plan accordingly. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a spotting scope. The unit is dry and rocky/cliffy. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Some of the larger, mature rams will move in with these ewe groups in late October. Do not be overly alarmed if you don't see many mature rams during the summer, they will start looking for the ewe groups in late October as the rut begins. Hunting generally gets better the later you go. The peak of the rut tends to be the mid-late November. Rams will typically move between multiple ewe groups, so it is not uncommon to see different rams with the same group of ewes across multiple days. Sheep will be active throughout the day and are good at finding spots just out of sight. Be patient and let your optics cover visible miles, but make sure to check various vantage points. Behavior: The month of November is during the bighorn sheep rut. Rams are moving between groups of ewes during this time. Rams will butt heads to establish dominance, so it can be helpful to occasionally stop and listen for the sound of butting heads as it can be a good tool for locating sheep that are otherwise difficult to see. Bighorn sheep will not be as tied to water in November as it is generally more available that time of year. They tend to be found on the steep open cliffs and mesa tops and are occasionally feeding on the flat canyon bottoms or benches. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl, even young rams will have a pronounced curl. Mature ewes and yearling rams have similar curl; however, a ewe horn is thin and a yearling ram horn is much heavier especially at the base. The best way to recognize mature bighorn rams is to look for horn mass, particularly out near the tip of the horn. Younger rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. Mature rams that are 6 years and older tend to have thicker horns out near the tips, and thicker bases. Often times if you are close enough you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. The first deep and prominent annuli on a rams horn working from the tip back towards the base is most often the 3.5 yr old ring as it is associated with the ram's first rut. Disease Issues: Bighorn sheep are highly susceptible to infection from respiratory pathogens. Depending on the virulence of respiratory pathogen strain, infection can lead to all age die-offs with continued lamb recruitment suppression for years following an outbreak. Bighorn sheep usually become infected through contact with domestic sheep or goats. These domestic animals carry the bacterium but aren't typically affected by it. This unit has tested positive for Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae, the bacterium most often associated with pneumonia outbreaks in bighorn sheep populations. If you notice any disease symptoms (coughing, sneezing, nasal discharge) While you are out scouting/ hunting please report to the local DWR office.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This unit is steep and rough with very little to no cell coverage. As in most bighorn sheep habitat, hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters will cover many rugged miles and climb/descend thousands of feet in elevation. Be careful working through cliff bands. It can be easy to get yourself onto a ledge with no way beyond that spot, it is advised that you bring extra rope to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is also recommended on this unit. Bring plenty of water as it can be warm in November and there may be very little water on the unit. An InReach can be a useful type of satellite messaging if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in November are variable on this unit. Generally, plan on cold nights with mild days and little to no snow accumulation. Most of the occupied bighorn sheep habitat occurs at lower elevations between 4200 and 6000 feet where snow generally doesn't accumulate. Snow and bad weather is always possible in November. Be cautious of flash flooding during rain storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Dirty Devil bighorn sheep population was last surveyed in 2022 on a 3 year interval. We surveyed a total of 158 sheep; 53 rams, 73 ewes, and 32 lambs. The projected population is 263 sheep. Numbers have improved over the last decade from a low count of 60 sheep in 2014. Lamb production hit a low in 2008 at 10 lambs per 100 ewes but has increased slowly to 44 lambs per 100 ewes in 2022. The ram to ewe ratio increased substantially in 2022 at 73 rams per 100 ewes somewhat due to finding 39 sheep along the upper two-thirds of the unit boundary along the Colorado River in Cataract Canyon and below the Canyonlands National Park boundary. This is a very difficult area to hunt because the canyon bottom is not safely accessibile from the top rim of the canyon. Some hunting has been done with watercraft traveling up river but it is not advised as a water craft was lost in the rapids. As with many other desert sheep units, sheep are spread out over large expanses of habitat, often making them difficult to locate. Plan on scheduling enough time for a lot of scouting and hunting.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Suggested Hunting Area: Higher unit densities of desert bighorns based upon harvest and observations- Poison Springs Canyon, Marinus, Stair and Butler Canyons. Lower density areas- Larry's canyon, Gibex Point, Twin Corral, and Sam's Box canyons, and along the Dirty Devil below Sams Mesa and along Happy Canyon. Sheep often use cliff bands and the grassy benches between them, the rims of canyons, and the canyon bottoms. They are also often seen in the slick rock areas. Scouting Tips: It's good to be familiar with the area and understand if you have what it will take to find and harvest a mature ram before applying for this permit. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a good spotting scope. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Older rams generally will not move into the area where the ewe groups are until the rut begins in late October. Hunting generally gets better the later you go with more mature rams showing up by November. Rams move a lot in November between ewe groups, so a single group of ewes and lambs can attract different rams from day to day. Behavior: The peak of the rut tends to be the week of Thanksgiving or just prior to it. Rams will be moving from group to group looking for ewes. It is difficult to glass up rams but sometimes you can hear them butting heads as they compete with other rams to breed with the ewes. This can sound like a rifle firing through the canyons if you're close enough. Sheep are generally active throughout the day in November but activity is highest in morning and evening. Bighorn sheep can go long periods without drinking water, acquiring moisture from vegetation that they eat. Bighorn will generally avoid the flat mesa tops where there is tree cover, but not always. Sheep use precipitous canyons and plateaus where the topography is steep with rough rocky outcrops. Between canyon ledges are often wider grassy slopes and shelves where sheep feed and which are corridors to other canyon layers and escape routes. Desert bighorn sheep have cloven hooves with harder sides/edges and softer inner pads. This adaptation allows them to quickly traverse steep rocky terrain to avoid predation. They are good at hiding under tight ledges and rocks. Horn Growth: Both rams and ewes have horns. Mature ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Mature ewes and yearling rams have similar curl; however, a ewe horn is thin and a yearling ram horn is much heavier especially at the base. 2.5 year old rams begin to have a pronounced curl, and rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. The best way to recognize mature trophy class bighorn rams is to look for horns closer to a full curl with horn mass, particularly out near the end of the horn. Mature rams 6 years and older have thicker heavier bases and the horns are thicker out near the ends only because older rams 'broom off' the thinner tips. During the rut horn growth nearly stops, creating annuli growth rings on the horn. The rate at which the horn grows in length steadily declines after 3.5 years of age, after about 8.5 years growth rings become less defined and their reliability to determine age drops dramatically. Often times if you are close enough, you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. If you know the horn is broomed and heavy at the end then the second growth ring you see is most likely at 2.5 years old. The 2.5 yr and 3.5 year rings are often the most prominent with the 3.5 yr old ring being the deepest because it is associated with the ram's first rut. The ear will usually point to this ring on a mature ram. If only one prominent ring is seen it is probably a 2.5 year old ram. By locating the 3.5 yr old ring you can determine or at least estimate the age of the ram by adding a year for each subsequent annuli growth ring. Disease Issues: Bighorn sheep are highly susceptible to infection from respiratory pathogens. Between 30-70% of the herd can die if they become infected, and lambs born into the herd can continue to die after an outbreak. They usually become infected through contact with domestic sheep or goats. These domestic animals carry the disease but aren't affected by it. While you are out scouting and hunting please report any domestic sheep or goats in bighorn habitat to the local DWR office.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Sheep habitat is found between 3700'and 6000'. Hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters end up walking dozens of miles and traversing thousands of feet in elevation prior to harvesting their ram. As with most bighorn sheep habitat, there are steep impassible canyons and an abundance of cliffs. Be very careful scaling cliffs. It is advised that you bring extra rope and climbing gear to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is very handy on this unit to not only mark sheep and routes but also places where you can get through the ledges as they are relatively rare. Hunters can sometimes spend hours hiking along trying to find a way through the ledges and wasting time and energy. Bring plenty of water, there is very little on the unit. Carry a good survival kit and a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp, where you are hunting, and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Keep abreast of the weather forecast. Be prepared for inclement weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The highest densities of bighorn on the Escalante, East unit can be found within a few miles along the shorelines of Lake Powell and the Escalante river; however sheep can also be found well into the Grand Staircase Escalante National Monument. This herd has received several transplants in past years to augment the existing population so observing a sheep with a GPS collar and/or an ear tag is possible. Bighorn are often observed near shore of Lake Powell in canyons east of the Escalante River. Some high use areas include areas surrounding Steven's Canyon and Long Canyon. This species lives in extreme rugged habitat that can have extreme weather conditions. Be prepared to hike in this type of country and spend a lot of time with your binoculars. Due to limited access by motorized vehicles in this unit, the closest bighorn sheep are still several miles from roads. Be prepared to spend several miles on foot to access the bighorn in the area.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Harvest locations can vary by hunter abilities and preferences. Proportion of mature rams in a particular area is highly correlated with accessibility. The easier access areas receive higher hunting pressure and therefore have fewer mature rams available than the areas more challenging to access. If an accessible area by vehicle and hike trip is desired, focus on the areas by the Middle Moody trailhead or Coyote Gulch trailhead. If a hunt by boat is desired, focus efforts near the Escalante River and north of the lake. Any of these areas can offer a great backpack trip with great scenery. Be prepared to hike in difficult terrain regardless of access method. Migration Patterns: Bighorn sheep seem to limit movements in the hottest times of the year with trips to watering areas highly documented. Space use increases as rutting behaviors begin. The sheep on this unit are known to move great distances in a short amount of time if pressured or in search of resources. Scouting Tips: Scouting is critical to success on this unit. Most hunters spend a substantial amount of time becoming familiar with maps of this area and spend time prior to the hunt to locate areas with sheep. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential to bighorn sheep hunting. Find a high point, get comfortable, and spend time glassing to locate sheep. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens but can offer great insight at any time of the year. Plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and other water sources in the more arid areas of the unit. Behavior: Peak rutting behavior appears to occur in October and November. There is more water available on this unit than one would think. Be aware of small seeps, rock tanks and springs and look for tracks since sheep may use watering areas regularly.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Escalante, East unit offers some truck and ATV access which is highly dependent on weather. Roads are often washed out by heavy rains and an ATV may be most useful to access many areas. Much of this area is inaccessible during wet conditions so watch weather forecasts. A 4WD vehicle is highly recommended. Cellular phone coverage is spotty but a call or text can usually be made if you are in a spot where you can see Navajo Mountain which is the big rounded mountain on the south side of Lake Powell. The biologist suggests handheld radios and even a satellite communication device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms WILL cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The bighorn on the Escalante, West unit can be found anywhere between the Hole in the Rock road and the Escalante river; however, the sheep often prefer to hang around the canyons west of the Escalante river. This herd has received several transplants in past years to augment the existing population so observing a sheep with a GPS collar and/or an ear tag is possible. Bighorn are often observed in and along the canyons west of the Escalante River. Some high use areas include Davis Gulch, Fiftymile Creek, and Indian Creek. This species lives in extreme rugged habitat that can have extreme weather conditions. Be prepared to hike in this type of country and spend a lot of time with your binoculars. Due to limited access by motorized vehicles in this unit, the closest bighorn sheep are still several miles from roads. Be prepared to spend several miles on foot to access the bighorn in the area.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Harvest locations can vary by hunter abilities and preferences. Proportion of mature rams in a particular area is highly correlated with accessibility. The easier access areas receive higher hunting pressure and therefore have fewer mature rams available than the areas more challenging to access. Most of the sheep in the unit can be accessed by vehicle from the Hole in the Rock road followed by a hike east towards the Escalante River. Although it may appear to be a short, flat walk on a map, it's still anywhere from a 3-7 mile hike over rolling slick rock hills in hot temperatures. Make sure you are prepared for the weather and bring lots of water. Carefully watch for sheep as you make your way out to the lake. The flatter terrain makes for an easier hike, but also gives sheep an advantage to spot you coming from a long ways away. Migration Patterns: Bighorn sheep seem to limit movements in the hottest times of the year with trips to watering areas highly documented. Space use increases as rutting behaviors begin. The sheep on this unit are known to move great distances in a short amount of time if pressured or in search of resources. Scouting Tips: Scouting is critical to success on this unit. Most hunters spend a substantial amount of time becoming familiar with maps of this area and spend time prior to the hunt to locate areas with sheep. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential to bighorn sheep hunting. Find a high point, get comfortable, and spend time glassing to locate sheep. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens but can offer great insight at any time of the year. Plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and other water sources in the more arid areas of the unit. Behavior: Peak rutting behavior appears to occur in October and November. There is more water available on this unit than one would think. Be aware of small seeps, rock tanks and springs and look for tracks since sheep may use watering areas regularly. Sheep tend to like hanging out around the rims of the canyons that come off the west side of the Escalante River.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Escalante, West unit offers some truck and ATV access via the Hole in the Rock road which is highly dependent on weather. Roads are often washed out by heavy rains and an ATV may be most useful to access many areas. Some of this area is inaccessible during wet conditions so watch weather forecasts. A 4WD vehicle is highly recommended. Cellular phone coverage is spotty but a call or text can usually be made if you are in a spot where you can see Navajo Mountain which is the big rounded mountain on the south side of Lake Powell. Handheld radios and even a satellite communication device for safety are highly recommended. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms WILL cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt was established to address overall elk population numbers, and to help landowners experiencing damage to hay fields in the county.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the hunting season elk will be found at high elevations where heavy timber is bordered by open faces where they feed. Glassing during early morning and evenings is critical to find these groups of elk. Elk are almost never observed close to roads on this unit. It is imperative that hunters get off the roads either on foot or by horse or mule if they wish to observe cows. Many elk in the area are located on the east slope of the Bear River Range west of Garden City, Round Valley, Randolph and Woodruff. Much of the unit is private property, so be sure to secure permission before accessing these properties. Many of the landowners will allow access but will charge a trespass fee.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Elk are usually not found near roads. Be prepared to hike or ride to observe elk. Make sure you are in good physical condition, harvesting and processing an elk can be physically demanding.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is variable, so check the local forecast and be prepared for likely conditions.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The intent of this hunt is to harvest elk while they are on winter ranges and hopefully harass elk and keep them out of haystacks at low elevations. Hunting is generally poor until there have been several snowstorms. When there has been significant snowfall on the winter range, elk can be found at low elevations across the Gordon Creek WMA. Elk are often found on public lands near the Gordon Creek fields at the upper reaches of the Consumer's Road as well as on Cedar, Telephone, Horse, Wiregrass, and Long Benches. On years where there is little snow, hunting is much more difficult. Elk will remain at as high an elevation as possible on this unit. Much of the higher elevation transitional habitat is on private lands near Scofield Reservoir. During these light winters, hunters can have some moderate success by hunting the Ford Ridge Road off of SR-6 at the top of Price Canyon as well as hiking up some of the tributaries of Gordon Creek such as Bob Wright, Second Water, and Corner Canyons.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: It will be winter. Plan for cold weather, bad roads, steep canyons, and spotty cell coverage. Four wheel drive and tire chains are highly recommended.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect winter conditions. The main highways (ie. SR-6, SR-96, SR-122, and the Consumer's Road near Helper will be plowed. Most of the dirt roads will not be plowed during the winter months. Some years much of the winter range can be accessed with a truck, while others you will need a snowmobile.

hunt_bio_general_information: The intent of this late season cow elk hunt is to harvest elk while they are on the winter range and reduce the overall population while also discouraging elk from using nearby farms and haystacks. On years when snowfall levels are low elk will generally remain at higher elevations and not migrate down to lower winter ranges as expected. This is especially the case in the Stump Flat and Danish bench areas south of SR31 and north of SR29.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is a late season hunt. Success improves substantially once there is substantial snow in the valley. Hunt success is generally poor when there is no snow as elk remain at high elevations where access is rather difficult. On years where it snows, good hunting locations include the benches south of the town of Hiawatha, the benches south of the ghost town of Mohrland, as well as several locations south of Huntington Canyon. When there is very little snow, hunters can try their luck taking the Mohrland Road to the top of Gentry Mountain or taking SR-31 to higher elevation hunting areas such as the Nuck Woodward Canyon Road. These areas will have very little vehicle access.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a late season hunt. Expect winter conditions: very cold weather, snowy roads, steep canyons, and poor cell coverage. Hunters should dress for very cold conditions. 4 Wheel Drive Vehicles are necessary. It is highly advised that you pack a set of tire chains with you
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: See above. Expect winter conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a general season antlerless elk hunt that coincides with the spike bull hunt during the month of October. Expect large numbers of sportsmen afield. Hunt success is generally good during this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are several thousand elk that spend the summer and fall months on this part of the unit. Most people hunt along North Skyline Drive as well as the areas north and south of the Skyline Coal Mine along highway 264. These are areas with a high percentage of public lands that hold elk. The major tributaries of Scofield Reservoir will all hold elk. These include; Gooseberry, Silver, C Canyon, Straight Fork of Fish Creek, and Pondtown drainages. There are roads that go down Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge that access the Pondtown area but most of the other canyons are roadless. Sportsmen also find elk in Bennion Creek and in the Starvation Creek drainage. There are two roads just above the Skyline Coal mine along SR-264 that access other portions of the mountain. A county road going north will access Bean and Granger Ridges. The road to the south accesses Trough Springs Ridge. This area had a significant wildfire in 2014 that has benefited elk. There are some isolated smaller populations of elk on public lands in the Ford Ridge area that is accessed from SR-6 near Colton.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell coverage is poor. The weather can change to winter like conditions suddenly in October.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: October weather is highly variable. Snow is possible as much of the good hunting occurs at high elevations near 9000 feet. When fall snowstorms occur, many of the roads become very muddy and slippery. Expect mild days and cold nights even when weather conditions are good.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Pahvant has many steep and rugged areas. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. There is a main road across the top of the mountain with few ATV trails. Most of the ATV trails will be found on the southern half of the unit which also has the large tracts of private land. Many of the canyons have hiking trails that can help in accessing areas away from main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk can be found at all elevations. They will have seen pressure from other hunts and your chances of locating elk will increase by walking out ridges and glassing into the different canyons.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreationists. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. Storms can make many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage can be good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather can change quickly. It is possible to see rainstorms as well as large snow storms during this hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: This can be a great hunt, especially if Colorado gets any snow accumulation. Elk that spend the summer and fall in Colorado will pull down onto the Utah portion of the Dolores Triangle to winter. Large herds of elk are often seen during this time. Be cautious of private property, as there are a few good sized ranches on the unit that do not want hunters on their property. If you do get into a large herd of elk, try to pick out a single cow and stick with her until she goes down, do not start flock shooting.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: This unit is winter range for elk that summer in the Glade Park and Pinon Mesa areas (unit 40) of western Colorado. CDPW biologists estimate the population of unit 40 at 2500-3500 elk. The number of elk that winter in the Dolores Triangle unit is dependent upon winter severity. Winter population numbers have typically varied between 300 and 700 elk. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in mid November, many of the elk will be on the subunit by then and it will give you a chance to see how many elk you can expect on your hunt. The subunit is not large and elk scatter across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is primarily when elk feed and can be found out in open meadows. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas Dolores Triangle Subunit: Steamboat Mesa - Habitat treatments and fire have occurred in the area, draws a decent number of elk to the area in winter, good place to glass. Ryan Creek/Granite Creek - Rugged canyon rims, limited access, good place for bulls latter in the year. Ryan Park - Great area for elk (cows and bulls), good road and many places to glass for game. Little Dolores - Can hold large herds of elk, good place to glass, bulls and cows found latter in the year.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell phone service is very limited on this unit. It is a good idea to let someone know where you are and when you will return. I would recommend having a four-wheel drive vehicle during this hunt, with tire chains or a tow strap, just in case. Late season snow storms can settle in on this unit, causing some roads to be impassible.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have snow storms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash flooding in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This can be a very fun hunt for everybody, especially if we get some snow during the hunt. Cow elk are very social, and tend to be bunched up in groups throughout the year. When you do find a herd of cows, pay special attention to which elk you are shooting at and stick with that one. Do not start flock shooting if she doesn't go down immediately.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the La Sal Mountains typically migrate from the West to the East and North. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near the JB Ranch CWMU, or near the Utah/Colorado border. Elk also migrate off of the high mesa tops, into lower elevation valleys throughout the unit. Scouting Tips: Start scouting prior to your hunt, in September. The elk probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see how many cow elk you can expect to see on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most feeding takes place in meadow openings. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains Subunit: Bar-A Creek - Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge - This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek - No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Dark Canyon - Higher elevation, borders some private lands, one good main road with several two-track roads splitting off, great camping, good place to glass for elk on the early season hunts. La Sal Pass - Lots of places to glass for elk, rolling meadows with timbered North facing slopes and large aspen stands, not a lot of cows, but does hold a good number of bulls. North/South/Polar Mesas - These mesas are typically best for the late hunts, great for ATV's, good place for late season hunts.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sal unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is managed for a total wintering population of 700 elk. Hunts on this unit are typically very low success. Large amounts of snow will typically increase hunter success.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: There are more elk on the Anthro unit in the winter than there are in the summer and early fall. Many elk migrate from surrounding units to winter on the Anthro. Some elk come all the way from the Strawberry Reservoir area. The migration is typically elk coming from the West to winter further East. This migration can start as early as October, after the rut. There is, however, a fair amount of resident elk scattered across the entire unit, even on the desert parts on the East half of the unit. Scouting Tips: The unit is large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. There are many springs and guzzlers on the unit and these are typically the best places to find elk during the summer and fall. This is a general season hunt and is very difficult, success rates are really low. If you plan on hunting this unit, scouting is a must. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most spike bulls are with cow and calf herds during the hunts. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. There is a lot of pressure put on these elk during the general season hunts, this will push the elk towards private land or areas with difficult access or terrain. After opening morning spend your time hunting the thick timber canyons or large aspen stands. Road hunting is not a very effective method of hunting during the general season. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas Anthro Unit from West to East: Indian Canyon - can only hunt the East side of Highway 191, unless you have the January hunt. Not great during the early seasons, but can be a great place during the later seasons. Steep hillsides, and big canyons. Great place to glass. Cottonwood Ridge - difficult access, better hunting on the late hunts, the best areas are the highest elevation. Sowers Canyon - good access, many large canyons to glass. During the earlier hunts the far South end of the Canyon is best. The entire canyon is good during the late hunts. Wire Fence Ridge - plenty of road access. Large aspen stands near the top of the ridge, there are also several steep hillsides that have been burned and these areas are great during late summer and early fall. Large sage brush flats, great area to hunt on the later hunts. Nutters Ridge - Main road access for the Anthro Mountain portion of the unit. Very similar to Wire Fence, good aspen stands up high and several water troughs and springs. The far North end of this ridge is currently being drilled heavily for oil, avoid these areas. Jeep Trail - good access, a few good aspen stands and burned areas. The far North end of this ridge also has had substantial drilling activity, with many new roads, elk will avoid these areas. There have been several habitat treatments done in this area. Alkaline/Choke Cherry area - Really open area up high, several springs and guzzlers in this area as well. The open areas can hold many large herds of elk in the late fall and wintert. Lots of road access on small secondary ridges. Gilsonite Area - Lower elevation area. Lots of pinyon/juniper and sage brush draws. There are several guzzlers in this area. Most of the elk will be near these water sources on the early hunts. In order to hunt this area scouting is a must. Good road access. This area is best when there is deep snow in the high elevation areas.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Hunt takes place in December, expect cold temperatures and snow.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt targets the elk herds that move down lower in elevation during the winter and that frequently cross Hwy 44. Habitat is mostly thick pine trees with a few clearings. Visibility is low, making this a harder hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move back and forth across Wyoming and Utah state lines. Majority of the elk are up high in elevation during the summer months and will move down in elevation towards Wyoming or Flaming Gorge Reservoir during the winter. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the high country earlier than normal. Scouting Tips: During this season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is low due to dense trees. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October and does not impact this hunt. Where to find elk: Elk are found throughout much of the unit. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the North Slope, Greendale: Good areas to look for elk include Hwy 44, Trail Creek, Eagle Creek, and Swett Ranch areas.

hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically from year to year. Be prepared for snow, cold, and wind. There is usually snow on the ground by November in the higher elevations

hunt_bio_general_information: The Panguitch Lake elk herd is currently managed for 1,100 wintering elk across the unit. Recent surveys and estimates suggest the population is approximately 1,700, which requires several cow elk hunting opportunities to reduce the herd back to objective. This cow elk hunt overlaps with the general spike bull elk hunt. Some elk will have begun migratory movements toward winter range but some elk may still be found on summer ranges. Distribution of elk may range from forested habitats in Sidney Valley and Red Desert to 5 Mile Mountain west of Panguitch. On the northern end, elk may be found in oak, mountain mahogany, and Pinyon/Juniper habitats in the Cottonwood area east to Sidney Peak and Little Creek Peak. Due to the overlap with the general spike bull elk hunt and 200 cow elk permits, expect to see other hunters. Always remember to wear orange and be respectful of other hunters.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Elk can be found across the unit at this time of year. There are some segments of the herd on the east side that may be using lower elevation pinyon/juniper. Portions of the herd will remain on summer range as long as winter conditions do not force them to move. Many elk will be in transition ranges between summering and wintering areas. Elk may move distances of up to 30 miles during this hunt so be prepared to cover a lot of ground to locate elk. This unit offers substantial cover for elk to remain hidden and hunters should be prepared to hunt forested area's along with the burn. Migration Patterns: Migratory movements generally begin in late September and October but some elk will remain in summer range during this hunt. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars will be helpful. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points and hiking trails. Behavior: Elk may still be showing rutting behaviors and it is common to hear bulls bugling during this hunt. This will be useful in locating cows so it is not a bad idea to be familiar with calling elk.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Panguitch Lake unit offers substantial truck and ATV access. Cellular phone coverage within this hunt boundary is generally good but there are areas within the hunt boundary with little or no coverage. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, as well as winter weather conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This can be a very fun hunt for everybody, especially if we get some snow during the hunt. Cow elk are very social and tend to be bunched up in groups throughout the year. When you do find a herd of cows, pay special attention to which elk you are shooting at and stick with that one. Do not start flock shooting if she doesn't go down immediately.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the San Juan limited entry unit typically migrate from West to East and also South. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the public land elk will winter on or near Dry Mesa, Salt Creek Mesa and Bridger Jack Mesa. Elk also migrate off of the high mesa tops, into lower elevation valleys throughout the unit and can also be found in rugged canyons like Montezuma Canyon. Scouting Tips: Start scouting prior to your hunt in September. The elk probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see how many elk you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads, access points and watering holes. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is primarily when elk are out feeding in open meadows. This is also when most rutting activity takes place. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas for the San Juan limited entry subunit: Abajo Mountain - Higher elevations include large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding, lower elevations contain oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, good camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. North Elk Ridge - A good area for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, limited clearings for glassing, camping, nice roads, several different draws, canyons and mesa tops to hunt. South Elk Ridge - Good roads on mesa tops, limited access to rugged canyons, great area for pack-in hunts (Dark Canyon).
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the San Juan unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a great opportunity to have an any bull permit along with a cow permit to really capitalize on putting meat in the freezer. The archery hunt is extremely difficult on this general season unit, and usually averages around 10% success. The south slope is covered with large areas of lodge pole pine. Elk prefer these areas to bed down in, but it this habitat provides very little feed. Concentrate efforts on small parks next to large stands of lodge pole pine.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a General Season hunt and has a considerable amount of hunting pressure. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The Uintah Mountain range can provide a remote hunt with many hunters but there are fewer elk compared to limited entry areas. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for elk. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. Road access is allowed on the majority of the unit. Migration Patterns: Elk on this unit migrate down in elevation during the winter and tend to stay on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. During this hunt it is not uncommon to find bulls right at timberline. Elk Rut: The elk rut usually occurs from mid-September to mid-October. Listen for bugles, and use cow calls to attract other elk. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Vernal: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. There is a variety of habitat to hunt during the any weapon hunt. There is pinyon/juniper, sage brush savanna, thick lodge pole pine, and areas above timber line. The larger openings on the forest are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and rocky terrain. During the hunts most of the elk on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with conifer. I would recommend trying to locate remote watering holes or wallows, and hunt feeding areas. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks River is the western unit boundary, steep terrain. Paradise Park - Higher forest terrain, steep forested canyons. Mosby Mountain - High aspen forest, with large sagebrush bowls, excellent habitat. Red Cloud Loop Rd - Long road that starts in Dry Fork Canyon (west of Vernal). It takes you all the way through the Vernal unit, and comes out on Hwy 191. Taylor Mountain - Great vantage points. Excellent area to glass and locate animals from far distances. Colton Ranger Station - Aspen/conifer mix forest. Lime Stone, Little V, and Range Study - These areas are east of Hwy 191 and border a limited entry deer and elk unit. Diamond Mountain.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit consists of approximately 35% private property and public hunters should not expect access. Most years cow elk will be spread throughout the unit, including in the higher elevations on Diamond, during this hunt. Roads on this unit become very muddy and oftentimes impassable if there is any precipitation. Four wheel drive is strongly advised. The private property is posted and a GPS showing private/public property boundaries is recommended. Even though the unit has private property, there is still 65% public land that is huntable. Don't expect to gain access to hunt the private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move up and down in elevation throughout the year. During normal winters, elk will move down off the rim to the north and south. In dry years, elk will stay on the top of Diamond through the winter. Scouting Tips: During this season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Behavior: Like other wildlife, elk are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Elk can move long distances in short periods of time, especially if they are disturbed by vehicles or people. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October and does not affect this hunt. Where to find elk: Elk can be found throughout the unit during the hunting season; however the majority of the cows will be moving to lower elevations. Roads also become impassable due to mud and snow drifts. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Diamond Mtn Unit: Good areas to look for cow elk include Diamond Rim to the South, Wild Mountain, Top of Crouse Canyon, Marshall Draw, Warren Draw, and Mail Draw.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt can be very extreme. Be prepared for snow and cold temperatures. There is usually snow on the ground by the end of November. Inversions are also a typical occurrence on this unit during the winter.

hunt_bio_general_information: Most elk are south of State Route 21 which bisects the unit east to west. There are a some elk north of 21 but most are south. Elk are found on all mountain ranges except for the Black Hills between Cedar City and Minersville. Elk use all habitats from the bottom of the valleys to the top of the mountains. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Please be respectful of private lands and other hunters.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Antlerless elk can be found throughout the unit. More elk reside in the central portions of the unit on and surrounding the Indian Peaks Range. Elk can be found from the bottoms of the valleys in the open sagebrush to the top of the mountain in the Pinions and Mahogany. The Southwest Desert unit is a very large unit. It can be a difficult hunt. You may have days without seeing an elk because the density is low. To increase your chances of seeing elk it is best to find water in good elk habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few elk. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline/Hamlin Valley - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some larger blocks of private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. This area also has a few larger blocks of private land. South Wah Wah Rang e- BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range - BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Jockeys and Shaunties -BLM and SITLA lands located west of Minersville SW of Milford. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.
