hunt_bio_general_information: The Pahvant has many steep and rugged areas. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. There is a main road across the top of the mountain with few ATV trails. Most of the ATV trails will be found on the southern half of the unit. There are some ATV trails that start in low elevation areas and go part way up several canyons. Many of the canyons have hiking trails that can help in accessing areas away from main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is a great unit to hunt elk. There are many really nice bulls harvested off this mountain every year. This hunt takes place during the peak of the rut and can be a great time to locate many different bulls. Water is limited on the mountain and finding water sources away from main roads can be a productive for finding elk. Elk can be found across the entire unit. Get out on ridges and glass into some of the deep canyons. Many canyons north of Chalk Creek are great places to locate bulls.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreationists. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. After storms, many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage is good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: September is a great time to be on the mountain. There is a chance for rainstorms during this hunt.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Pahvant has many steep and rugged areas. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. Bulls can be found all the way from Ebbs canyon on the North to Dog valley and Three creeks on the South. On this late hunt especially plan to spend a lot of time using optics in order to locate elk. The bulls will be mostly solitary or in small groups and can be tough to find.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The pahvant is steep; especially where you're going to find the elk. Be physically prepared for intense hiking and know your own physical limitations.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Plan for cold weather and snow. Depending on the year you could be chasing elk on bare ground or in 3 feet of snow.

hunt_bio_general_information: This can be a great hunt, especially if Colorado gets any snow accumulation. Bulls that spend the summer and fall in Colorado will pull down onto the Utah portion of the Dolores Triangle to winter. 370" class bull are often seen during this time. Be cautious of private property, as there are a few good sized ranches on the unit that do not want hunters on their property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: This unit is winter range for elk that summer in the Glade Park and Pinon Mesa areas (unit 40) of western Colorado. CDPW biologists estimate the population of unit 40 at 2500-3500 elk. The number of elk that winter in the Dolores Triangle unit is dependent upon winter severity. Winter population numbers have typically varied between 300 and 700 elk. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in mid November, many of the elk will be on the subunit by then and it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The subunit is not large and elk scatter across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. With this hunt occurring latter in the year, after the rut, the bulls are generally found together in bachelor groups. Smaller bulls are typically found with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas Dolores Triangle Subunit: Steamboat Mesa - Habitat treatments and fire have occurred in the area, draws a decent number of elk to the area in winter, good place to glass. Ryan Creek/Granite Creek - Rugged canyon rims, limited access, good place for bulls latter in the year. Ryan Park - Great area for elk (cows and bulls), good road and many places to glass for game. Little Dolores - Can hold large herds of elk, good place to glass, bulls and cows found latter in the year.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell phone service is very limited on this unit. It is a good idea to let someone know where you are and when you will return. I would recommend having a four-wheel drive vehicle during this hunt, with tire chains or a tow strap, just in case. Late season snow storms can settle in on this unit, causing some roads to be impassible.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have snow storms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash flooding in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a great unit for the opportunity to harvest a bull elk . Typical harvested bulls on the unit score around 310" to 330", but a few bigger bulls are taken each year. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. Portions of the unit are extremely steep. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the La Sal Mountains varies, depending on weather conditions. Elk will typically migrate off of the high mountain and mesa tops, into lower elevations throughout the unit. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open and in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains Subunit: Bar-A Creek - Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge - This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek - No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Dark Canyon - Higher elevation, borders some private lands, one good main road with several two-track roads splitting off, great camping, good place to glass for elk on the early season hunts. La Sal Pass - Lots of places to glass for elk, rolling meadows with timbered North facing slopes and large aspen stands, not a lot of cows, but does hold a good number of bulls. North & South/ Beaver/Polar Mesas - These mesas are typically best for the late hunts, great for ATV's, good place for late season hunts. Slaughter Flat & Pole Cyn. - West side of the mountain. Good places to look for bulls on the late season hunt. Upper Castle Crk. - North side of the mountain. Good place to look during the late season hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sal unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe is a popular unit for hunting and outdoor recreation. There is ample public land with good road/trail access. Valley floors start between 5,000 - 6,000 feet with some of the peaks reaching near 11,000 ft in elevation. Habitat types include sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Monroe unit has long been considered a great unit to hunt elk. Good numbers of Mature bulls, beautiful scenery, and good access makes it a popular place to hunt. It is managed for an average age of harvested bull of 6.5-7yrs. Early Any Weapon season: Elk use the entire Monroe unit. During the Early Any Weapon season the rut is in full swing. Bulls are usually very vocal, especially early in the morning. By this time, due to the rut and hunting pressure, some of the elk have started using the mid elevation oak and pinyon/juniper habitats. Most of the bulls are with or at least near the cow herds. A good number of elk have also began to move south on the unit. The southern part of the unit will have increased numbers of elk during this season. Warm temperatures common during this time of year sometimes keep elk in the cooler canyon. Generally there are no other hunts during this season. As a result, hunters enjoy a quality hunt with little pressure from other hunters. Good areas to hunt: The central part of the unit is the most popular place for elk hunters for several reasons: There is really good camping and access, the terrain is mild, and the largest part of the elk herd resides there during the archery hunt. Elk can be found across the entire central part of the unit. Just about every meadow and canyon may have elk in them. Many people hunt this large area consisting of gentle terrain between the Dry Creek ranger station and the Koosharem ranger station. There are several large tracts of private property here. Consult maps to avoid conflicts with Private ground. Hunters should not overlook the many side canyons that lead from the top of the plateau down to the foothills. Elk use these because of the good feed and also they get less pressure as there are fewer roads. During this season there are generally significant numbers of elk using the agricultural fields near Koosharem, Greenwich, and Monroe. If you ask, many of these landowners may grant permission to hunt on their property or at least pass through. Generally the elk move onto public ground during daylight hours so they are accessible. Good numbers of elk also use the north end of the mountain. Elk can be found near Hunter's Flat, Big Lake, Magleby pass, and Monument peak. There are several sections of private ground in this area so be sure to know where you are. Make sure to check the mid-elevation areas. A few elk have now moved down to the south end of the unit during this hunt. Elk will be on the Forshea Mountain area where the thick aspen stands are. There are also small groups of elk stretching from the Forshea to the Langdon mountain area. Migration Patterns: Though most of the elk that spend the summer on Monroe also stay there for the winter. A significant number also migrate south to the Mt. Dutton unit. This movement usually begins in September and elk trickle south through November. Because of this, do not count on bulls being is the same place you may have scouted them in during the summer. Also, many elk now use the mid-elevation areas that have fewer roads and less pressure. Scouting Tips: June is a great time to begin scouting, as elk are less wary and there will be less people on the mountain. Elk will still be growing their antlers but will be easier to locate. The elk may move before this hunt but you will have an idea of what is in the area. A scouting trip just before the season opens will tell you what areas the bulls and cow herds are using. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for effective and efficient scouting in this area. Other Information: Hunters enjoy a high harvest rate on the Monroe unit. Hunters are usually able to locate quite a few mature bulls during scouting and hunting trips. This unit typically produces good mature bulls though not as many really large bulls as some nearby units that have more difficult terrain and access.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, cold and high temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions. During some seasons very warm temperatures may occur. Hunters should be prepared to cool meat quickly to avoid wasting meat.

Valley floors start between 5,000 - 6,000 feet with some of the peaks reaching near 11,000 ft in elevation. Habitat types include sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Monroe unit has long been considered a great unit to hunt elk. Good numbers of Mature bulls, beautiful scenery, and good access makes it a popular place to hunt. It is managed for an average age of harvested bull of 6.5-7 yrs. Late Any Weapon season: Elk use the entire Monroe unit. During the Late Any Weapon season generally the bulls have separated from the cow herds. Though bulls may occasionally bugle they are generally quiet. Long range glassing is important for finding the bulls on this hunt. Many of the bulls spend this season high on ridges far from roads. A fair number of elk have left the unit by migrating south to Mt. Dutton. The bulls will be spread out across the entire unit in small bachelor groups. If snows are deep most of the elk will be forced off of the flatter terrain on the top of the unit and will be on south facing slopes. If snows are light they could be anywhere. Generally there are no other hunts during this season. As a result, hunters enjoy a quality hunt with little pressure from other hunters. Good areas to hunt: The Monroe unit is a long mountain unit running north and south with the top being a plateau with more gentle terrain. Many of the bulls in November live along the rim and the side canyons of the plateau. Bulls really tend to like ridges with thick mahogany. North end - Hunter's Flat, The Circle, Bear Valley, and Little Creek. East side - Drainages west of Burrville and Koosharem, including: Blue Peak, Indian Peak, upper Box Creek. Also check the steep canyons south of Greenwich between Brown's canyon and Pine canyon. South End - This end will have bulls on the edges of the Forshea. There is a lot of pinyon/juniper on the extreme south end that holds a few bulls. Also, the country between Dry Creek and Twin Peaks will hold bulls. West side - Good places to find groups of bulls include Marysvale Peak area, Hunts lake, and the roadless drainages east of the town of Monroe. Migration Patterns: Though most of the elk that spend the summer on Monroe also stay there for the winter. A significant number also migrate south to the Mt. Dutton unit. This movement usually begins in September and elk trickle south through November. Because of this, do not count on bulls being is the same place you may have scouted them in during the summer. Also, many elk now use the mid-elevation areas that have fewer roads and less pressure. Though there are plenty of bulls on the unit this time of year, realize that there are not as many as there were in earlier seasons. Scouting Tips: Bulls will likely not be where you found them in the summer or early fall. The best way to scout for this hunt is the several days just before the hunt. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for effective and efficient scouting in this area. Other Information: Hunters enjoy a high harvest rate on the Monroe unit. Hunters are usually able to locate quite a few mature bulls during scouting and hunting trips. This unit typically produces good mature bulls though not as many really large bulls as some nearby units that have more difficult terrain and access. Monroe is managed for an average age of harvest of 6.5-7 yrs.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, and cold temperatures. Storms can cause muddy or snow-packed road conditions. Temperatures can be very warm during the early seasons. Hunters should be prepared cool meat quickly.

hunt_bio_general_information: This elk herd has seen a reduction in cow numbers the past several years. This unit is currently below the bull age objective. This is a tough hunt as bull elk move across state lines to find cows. 330+ size bulls are rare. This unit also sees a lot of tourism due to the Green River and Flaming Gorge Reservoir. There is a Landowner Association in this unit and the majority of the private property is towards Colorado and Wyoming state lines. There was a fire this summer on the north and east sides of Goslin Mountain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move back and forth across state lines quite regularly. Cow elk are sensitive to hunting pressure. Success rates on this unit vary widely by year depending on where the elk are. Utah, Wyoming, and Colorado coordinate the opening of the Any Weapon hunt so elk can't seek refuge in other states. Scouting Tips: In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot. Visibility on this unit is high due to the lack of trees. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Behavior: Like other wildlife, elk are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. If it's a dry year, they will be more concentrated around water sources, and these can sometimes be hunted successfully. On average precipitation or wet years, elk won't be as concentrated around water. Elk can move long distances in short periods of time, especially if they are disturbed by vehicles or people. Elk can be called in close for a shot during the rut. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October and is typically going during this hunt. Where to find elk: Elk are found throughout much of the unit. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, guzzlers, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the North Slope, Three Corners: Good areas to look for elk include Bare Top, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, Bender Mountain, Dutch John Mountain, and Clay Basin.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Panguitch Lake elk herd is currently managed for 1300 wintering elk across the unit. Recent surveys and estimates suggest the population is approximately 1200. Substantial summer range exists on the Markagunt Plateau which is heavily forested. There are also several mid-elevation areas across the unit that bull elk will use as summer range. Elk occupy most all suitable habitat throughout the unit. The unit had a significant burned in 2017 and has opened alot of new habitat for ELK, look for elk in the burn.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Nursery groups of cow elk can be observed generally very early in the morning or right before sunset. During warmer times of the day, elk will be staying cool in the forested areas and will be more difficult to observe. Focus on areas with high densities of aspen near water sources. Look for elk in the burn. Migration Patterns: All elk in this hunt boundary will migrate but these movements are generally not observed until late October and November. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars will be helpful. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points and hiking trails. Behavior: Elk will be on summer range and will begin to rut in September with cooler weather patterns.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Panguitch Lake unit offers substantial truck and ATV access. Cellular phone coverage within this hunt boundary is generally good but there are areas within the hunt boundary with little or no coverage. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, as well as warm weather conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake/Thousand Lake unit is a very popular hunting area. Elevation ranges from some peaks above 11,600 feet to some valley floors near 5,000 feet. There are all types of vegetation and terrain. The good scenery, camping, fishing, and hunting draws many people to the area every fall. The Fish Lake unit has a large herd of 5,600 elk. It is manages for a 5.5 to 6 year average age of harvest. In 2015 the average bull was just under 6 years old. hunt_bio_general_information: This is one of the best bull elk limited entry units in the state. The unit is managed for a 7.5 to 8 yr. old bull, which is what is being harvested, so we have an older age class of bulls in the population, although it can be a tough hunt. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. The Elk Ridge portion of the unit is flat and thick with vegetative cover and visual opportunities are limited. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the San Juan unit varies, depending on weather conditions. Typical migration goes from high elevations in the summer and early fall to low elevations in the winter and early spring. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Dry Mesa, Salt Creek Mesa, Bridger Jack Mesa, Milk Ranch Pnt., Peter's Point and Devil's Cyn. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads, access points and watering holes. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas for the San Juan limited entry subunit: Abajo Mountain - Higher elevations include large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding, lower elevations contain oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, good camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. North Elk Ridge - A good area for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, limited clearings for glassing, camping, nice roads, several different draws, canyons and mesa tops to hunt. South Elk Ridge - Good roads on mesa tops, limited access to rugged canyons, great area for pack-in hunts (Dark Canyon).
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the San Juan unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the East part of the Wasatch Mountains typically migrate from west to east on Currant Creek and Avintaquin subunits and east to west on the Wasatch West subunit. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Tabby Mountain WMA. On the Wasatch West portion of the unit winter along Heber Valley, Wallsburg WMA, and along the Wasatch front. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many large herds of cows and calves will be up high and in the open. They may not be in the exact same area during the hunt, but they will be in the same general areas. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most spike bulls are with cow and calf herds during the hunts. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. There is a lot of pressure put on these elk during the general season hunts, this will push the elk towards private land or areas with difficult access or terrain. After opening morning spend your time hunting the thick timber canyons or large aspen stands. Road hunting is not a very effective method of hunting during the general season. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas Currant Creek Subunit: CO-OP Creek - Just North of Strawberry Reservoir, large aspen stands, great camping, nice road, a lot of elk. Currant Creek Drainage - This entire area is great for elk, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands, great access, camping, nice road, several different draws or canyons to hunt(Layout Canyon, Big Dry Hollow, Low Pass Creek, Race Track), can hold large herds of elk North Fork Deep Creek/Water Hollow - very few roads, great area for horseback hunts, land managed by UDWR, borders private land in many spots, great area for elk. Wildcat WMA - UDWR land, borders private, lots of roads, not as many elk, West Fork Duchesne - Big area, road access, limited ATV access, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands. Tabby Mountain WMA - the North slope is best, the entire WMA great spot for the late season hunts, UDWR land, great for ATV's Recommended areas Avintaquin Subunit: Reservation Ridge - big area, road on the divide, great area for glassing(especially on the late season hunts), not as many elk as Currant Creek Strawberry Peak Area - Highest peak on Avintaquin, great access to roadless areas(Slab Canyon and Cow Hollow), great area for glassing Long Ridge - low density for elk, but can hold some elk, great glassing area, good access to roadless area (Lion Hollow), best on the late season hunts, a couple of nice burn areas, steep and rough terrain Lake Canyon, Right Fork of Indian Canyon, Skitzy WMA - not good areas for the early hunts, good areas for the late season hunts, not a lot of cows, but does hold a lot of bulls Recommended area on Wasatch West subunit: Strawberry Reservoir -All canyons around the reservoir have elk in them. Try Clyde Creek, Squaw Creek, Horse Creek, Indian Canyon, Chipman Creek, Poison Ridge, French Hollow, Buffalo Canyon, and Willow Creek. Strawberry Ridge - The ridge road is rough, in some places on ATV have access. This is a great place to glass and listen for elk. Sheep Creek - Try hunting the Waters along the Rays Valley road. Each of the Waters (first through sixth) has a trail head. Try hunting Halls Fork and Yellow Jacket areas. Diamond Fork/Hobble Creek - Try hunting the upper sections, elk will move into the lower sections later in the season. Mt. Timpanogos - There is a herd of around 200 elk in this area. Try looking around Cascade Springs, the top of American Fork Canyon, and the west side above Grove and Battle Creek. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

The Forest has been actively managing across the forest to meet resource objectives through vegetation treatments and prescribed fire management. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: ATTENTION-The US Forest is planning on a few prescribed burns this fall that might interfere with some hunt areas. Please be aware. The Heber-Kamas Ranger District is proposing to treat 3,300 acres with active fire in three operational areas occurring in Summit and Wasatch Counties. These areas are in the Provo watershed 10 miles east of Kamas and in the West Fork watershed 20 miles southeast of Heber City. Operations are planned to begin August 21, 2023, and will continue as conditions allow. The operation will require some area and road closure for public safety, active fire management will occur primarily during the daytime but also could occur at night to increase resource objectives. The Forest Service has established a Wildfire Crisis Strategy for dramatically increasing fuels and forest health treatments. The 10-year Wildfire Crisis Strategy (WCS) is built around the scale of the problem, which estimates that 50 million acres in addition to what we currently treat on an annual basis need fuels and forest health treatment to address the growing wildfire crisis. The goal of the project is to reduce wildfire risks to communities and natural resources by restoring and maintaining healthy, resilient fire-adapted forests. Approximately 382,000 acres (44%) of the Wasatch landscape is classified as high or very high fire hazard, posing a considerable threat to the function of vital watersheds, plant and wildlife habitat, recreational opportunities, and private property. The Forest has been actively managing across the forest to meet resource objectives through vegetation treatments and prescribed fire management. The Forest will continue to use all available tools to continue managing the resources meet the goals in the WCS. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers

hunt_bio_general_information: This is one of the best elk hunts in the state of Utah. Most hunters are able to look over or locate multiple mature bulls. The Beaver mountain range provides great habitat for elk. You can find and hunt elk in all elevations on the mountain. I would suggest hunting the areas where you like to hunt. The Beaver Mountains are so large that it can be difficult to cover every area. Some hunters find it best to scout drainage and hunt that drainage until they are ready to move on. I would suggest bringing extra water, tires, and fuel. The Beaver offers a challenging landscape. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. A lot of the canyons and ridges have roads or ATV trails to provide access. There are plenty of areas to hike and get away from the main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of hunters choose to hunt the canyons and draws surrounding the higher elevation areas during the muzzleloader hunt. The areas around Big Johns flat and Big Flat hold large amounts of elk. There are canyons and areas surrounding those areas where you can get out and hike to get away from people. There is plenty of water on the mountain for the elk. However as you hike you can find several unmarked springs. These springs may be useful if the weather is hot and dry. The northern areas of the unit have recently been through an extensive burn. As the burned area reestablishes vegetation it attracts large amounts of elk. Migration Patterns: You will find elk from one end of the Beaver to the other. The elk will start feeling pressured toward the end of the archery hunt with increased rifle hunters scouting for their upcoming hunt. During the winter months the bulls prefer to stay in the highest elevations. They will locate wind swept south slopes and wait out the winter. The cows and calves will migrate to lower elevations. After the calving season you can find large herds of elk at higher elevation in grassy meadows. Once the rut begins the bulls begin to herd up smaller herds of cows and the elk seem to spread out through the whole Beaver Range. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting elk in this area. Scouting is most effective late-summer to early fall. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of the bulls. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are several recovering burned areas that have produced large amounts of grass that is excellent for elk. Elk spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs. Scouting during the summer is effective for learning the areas where you want to hunt. I would not expect to see the same elk on the same ridge during the summer and also in the fall. The elk do tend to move before the rut. I would focus scouting efforts during the first of September. Behavior: The elk seem to prefer bedding down in the dark conifer timber during the day. Towards the evening the elk will start to work their way onto the burned faces and points of the ridges. Once the bulls shed their velvet they will start to break up from their winter and summer bachelor herds. They will usually water at least two times a day. It is not unusual for elk to graze through the night. As the hunt progresses and if colder weather moves in, the elk will start to come into the rut. Before they start to herd the cows up the bulls are very susceptible to cow elk calls. I have had success calling bulls in from far distances in the unit with the use of a cow call in early September. As elk get closer to the rut they will become more vocal and will start to round up small herds of cows. The larger bulls will usually try to keep their cows away from contending bulls. It is normal to have one herd bull and other bulls surrounding the cows at a distance. During this hunt it is effective to hunt water holes early on the hunt. Later in the hunt it is more efficient to call and locate the bulls and try to get them to come to cow calls.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Beaver Mountains has a moderate bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Southern Regional Office as soon as possible (435-865-6100).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and high temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: Most hunters plan on spending five days hunting in this remote area. There are plenty of water sources so don't plan on bringing much water in with you. Some hunters who do not have much horse experience camp at the trail heads and hike in and out every day. There are several guides and outfitters who work in this area. I would plan on a very challenging and rewarding hunt. Not many hunters can say they have killed a trophy bull in the true back country like this unit can provide. Currently there is no cattle grazing in this area, to allow stream bank restoration, and let the landscape heal after the massive fire. There are native Colorado cutthroat trout in most of the streams. There are 30-40 wild horses in this area. I have seen anywhere from 30-70 bison on this unit. It is not uncommon to see black bears in this area. There is usually plenty of feed for horses, most sportsman hobble their horses; for a few hours a day. This area is patrolled quite frequently by DWR personnel. Keep this in mind when you are transporting your game. Try to make it easy to access the permit and tag on the animal.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The roadless area has four main drainages: West Willow Creek, She Creek, Little Creek, and East Willow Creek. All of these drainages are good for camping. The ridges that separate the drainages are: Went Ridge, and Little Creek Ridge. There is a spring on Little Creek Ridge called Three Springs that has good drinking water. This is a popular elk hunting area. Other popular areas to find elk are: Santio Knolls, One Eye Canyon, Rivoguts Canyon, Fish Creek, and Dry Fork Canyon. The elk are found more on the tops of the ridges and come down on the faces and in the canyons to feed and drink. Most archery hunters have the most success early in the hunt sitting remote water holes. As the hunt progress the elk start to rut and become easier to spot and stalk. Migration Patterns: During the archery hunt I would expect to see large herds of cows, calves, and spike bulls. The bulls will start breaking up from their bachelor herds. If there isn't much pressure in the bottom of the canyons I would expect to see elk coming out in the evenings to drink from the creeks. You will find elk from one end of the roadless area to the other. The elk will start feeling pressured towards the end of the hunt with increased rifle hunters scouting for their upcoming hunt. Little Creek Ridge consistently holds a lot of elk. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting elk in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of the bulls. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are several recovering burned areas that have produced large amounts of grass that is excellent for elk. Elk spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs. There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area. Behavior: Once the bulls shed their velvet they will start to break up from their winter and summer bachelor herds. They will usually water at least two times a day. It is not unusual for elk to graze through the night. As the hunt progresses and if colder weather moves in, the elk will start to come into the rut, or breeding season. Before they start to herd the cows up the bulls are very susceptible to cow elk calls. I have had success calling bulls in from far distances in the unit with the use of a cow call in early September. As elk get closer to the rut they will become more vocal and will start to round up small herds of cows. The larger bulls will usually try to keep their cows away from contending bulls. It is normal to have one herd bull and other bulls surrounding the cows at a distance.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The Biologist suggests handheld radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs roadless area has a high bear population. I recommend keeping a clean camp and putting your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeast Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or local the local dispatch center (435 789-4222). The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. The trails are very steep and challenging. Every year sportsmen kill horses and mules in the roadless area. I would suggest bringing horses that are in good physical condition. It is not uncommon to have thunderstorms, flash floods and have trails wash out. If it rains hard it makes it difficult to navigate the trails, and the access roads. Tire chains can come in very handy.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat. I would plan on hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Manti is the largest elk herd in Utah and has stable elk numbers. Elk are distributed fairly evenly across the good habitat on the unit. Elk typically remain at high elevations during the muzzleloader hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: For the most part the elk will not show any migratory behavior during the archery, muzzleloader, and early rifle hunts. These elk will remain on summer ranges at elevations generally above 8,000 feet. Bulls will begin to migrate by the Late Season Any Weapon Hunt. Most bulls tend to move down in elevation on to steep ridges predominated by mountain mahogany shrubs. About 90% of the elk move east to winter and spend the winter months on the ridges west of SR-10 Scouting Tips: You can not go terribly wrong on this unit. There is excellent access to most of the unit. A popular route to learn the unit is Skyline Drive. Skyline Drive runs along the spine of the mountain range and provides access to most of the high elevation habitat on the entire unit. Learn country! There are over 12,000 elk on this mountain so there are small groups of elk with bulls in nearly every canyon with good habitat on the mountain. Listen for bugling activity and cow calls to locate elk. Also listen for domestic sheep. There are an abundance of sheep that will still be on the mountain during the September hunts. If you can hear sheep in the canyon below you, it is best to move to the next canyon as elk and sheep are rarely found in the same vicinity it seems. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Glass the open south facing slopes where elk like to feed or small meadows near the canyon bottoms. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended Areas to look on the Central Mountains Manti Unit Upper Fish Creek and it's tributaries. The tributaries include Gooseberry Creek, Silver Creek, C Canyon, and the Straight Fork. This is a roadless area on the north end of the unit. This area typically holds a lot of elk and had some prescribed fires recently that has improved elk habitat. It can be accessed from North Skyline Drive on the west or from Scofield Reservoir on the east. The bottom two miles of Upper Fish Creek is privately owned and in a CWMU Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge These ridges have roads going down them. They are northwest of Scofield Reservoir. The bottom 2 miles of these ridges are privately owned. This is excellent habitat in the Pondtown Creek drainage on the north end of the unit. It is best accessed from North Skyline Drive. Trough Spring Ridge This is accessed off of SR-264 southwest of the town of Scofield. It is just above the Skyline Coal Mine. This is the ridge on the east side of Electric Lake. There are some small pockets of private land that are posted well but the majority of the acreage is Forest Service. Much of this ridge burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 which has improved the elk habitat in this area. Gentry Mountain. This is accessed from SR-10 just north of the town of Huntington at Huntington Reservoir. Part of this mountain is privately owned and part of it burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 Ford Ridge (Late Rifle Hunters Only) This area is the top of a steep canyon overlooking Spring Canyon west of Helper. It holds bachelor groups of bulls in the fall and winter. There are numerous private lands around so be very careful of where you are. There is ample public lands also. West of Skylin

hunt_bio_general_information: The Pahvant has many steep and rugged areas. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. There is a main road across the top of the mountain with few ATV trails. Most of the ATV trails will be found on the southern half of the unit. There are some ATV trails that start in low elevation areas and go part way up several canyons. Many of the canyons have hiking trails that can help in accessing areas away from main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is a great time to be on the mountain. Once the rut starts elk tend to scatter a little more and can be found across the entire unit. Deep canyons away from roads are great places to locate elk. There are many ridges and peaks that offer excellent glassing opportunities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreationists. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. After heavy rain storms, many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage is good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather can change quickly. Be prepared for all different types of weather. In general though, this is a great time to be on the mountain.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a great unit for the opportunity to harvest a bull elk . Typical harvested bulls on the unit score around 310" to 330", but a few bigger bulls are taken each year. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. Portions of the unit are extremely steep. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the La Sal Mountains varies, depending on weather conditions. Elk will typically migrate off of the high mountain and mesa tops, into lower elevations throughout the unit. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open and in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains Subunit: Bar-A Creek - Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge - This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek - No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Dark Canyon - Higher elevation, borders some private lands, one good main road with several two-track roads splitting off, great camping, good place to glass for elk on the early season hunts. La Sal Pass - Lots of places to glass for elk, rolling meadows with timbered North facing slopes and large aspen stands, not a lot of cows, but does hold a good number of bulls. North/South/Polar Mesas - These mesas are typically best for the late hunts, great for ATV's, good place for late season hunts.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sal unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe is a popular unit for hunting and outdoor recreation. There is ample public land with good road/trail access. Valley floors start between 5,000 - 6,000 feet with some of the peaks reaching near 11,000 ft in elevation. Habitat types include sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and aspen/conifer. It is currently managed for an average age of harvested bulls of 6.5-7 yrs.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Monroe unit has long been considered a great unit to hunt elk. Good numbers of Mature bulls, beautiful scenery, and good access makes it a popular place to hunt. Muzzleloader season: Elk use the entire Monroe unit. However, during the Muzzleloader season the rut is in full swing. Bulls are usually very vocal, especially early in the morning. By this time, due to the rut and hunting pressure, some of the elk have started using the mid elevation oak and pinyon/juniper habitats. Most of the bulls are with or at least near the cow herds. A good number of elk have also began to move south on the unit. The southern part of the unit will have increased numbers of elk during this season. The general season deer muzzleloader hunt generally overlaps with this hunt. Expect a bit more hunting pressure because of this. Good areas to hunt: The central part of the unit is the most popular place for elk hunters for several reasons: There is really good camping and access, the terrain is mild, and the largest part of the elk herd resides there during the archery hunt. Elk can be found across the entire central part of the unit. Just about every meadow and canyon may have elk in them. Many people hunt this large area consisting of gentle terrain between the Dry Creek ranger station and the Koosharem ranger station. Hunters should not overlook the many side canyons that lead from the top of the plateau down to the foothills. Elk use these because of the good feed and also they get less pressure as there are fewer roads. During this season there are generally significant numbers of elk using the agricultural fields near Koosharem, Greenwich, and Monroe. If you ask many of these landowners may grant permission to hunt on their property or at least pass through. Generally the elk move onto public ground during daylight hours so they are accessible. Good numbers of elk also use the north end of the mountain. Elk can be found near Hunter's Flat, Big Lake, Magleby pass, and Monument peak. There are several sections of private ground in this area so be sure to know where you are. Make sure to check the mid-elevation areas. More elk have now moved down to the south end of the unit during the muzzleloader hunt. Elk will be on the Forshea Mountain area where the thick aspen stands are. There are also small groups of elk stretching from the Forshea to the Langdon mountain area. Migration Patterns: Though most of the elk that spend the summer on Monroe also stay there for the winter. A significant number also migrate south to the Mt. Dutton unit. This movement usually begins in September and elk trickle south through November. Because of this do not count on bulls being is the same place you may have scouted them in during the summer. Also, many elk now use the mid-elevation areas that have fewer roads and less pressure. Scouting Tips: June is a great time to begin scouting as elk are less wary and there will be less people on the mountain. Elk will still be growing their antlers but will be easier to locate. The elk may move before the Muzzeloader hunt but you will have an idea of what is in the area. A scouting trip just before the season opens will tell you what areas the bulls and cow herds are using. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for effective and efficient scouting in this area. Other Information: Hunters enjoy a high harvest rate on the Monroe unit. Hunters are usually able to locate quite a few mature bulls during scouting and hunting trips. This unit typically produces good mature bulls though not as many really large bulls as some nearby units that have more difficult terrain and access.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, cold and high temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions. During some seasons very warm temperatures may occur. Hunters should be prepared to cool meat quickly to avoid wasting meat.

hunt_bio_general_information: This elk herd has seen a reduction in cow numbers the past several years. The average age is currently below objective. This is a very tough hunt as elk move across state lines to find cows and has very low success. 330+ size bulls are rare. This unit also sees a lot of tourism due to the Green River and Flaming Gorge Reservoir. There is a Landowner Association in this unit and the majority of the private property is towards Colorado and Wyoming state lines. There was a fire this summer on the north and east sides of Goslin Mountain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move back and forth across state lines quite regularly. Cow elk are sensitive to hunting pressure. Success rates on this unit vary widely by year depending on where the elk are. Scouting Tips: In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot. Visibility on this unit is high due to the lack of trees. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Behavior: Like other wildlife, elk are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. If it's a dry year, they will be more concentrated around water sources, and these can sometimes be hunted successfully. On average precipitation or wet years, elk won't be as concentrated around water. Elk can move long distances in short periods of time, especially if they are disturbed by vehicles or people. Elk can be called in close for a shot during the rut. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October and doesn't usually affect this hunt. Where to find elk: Elk are found throughout much of the unit. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, guzzlers, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the North Slope, Three Corners: Good areas to look for elk include Bare Top, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, Bender Mountain, and Dutch John Mountain.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable or very muddy.

Substantial summer range exists on the Markagunt Plateau which is heavily forested. There are also several mid-elevation areas across the unit that bull elk will use as summer range. Elk occupy most all suitable habitat throughout the unit. The unit had a significant burned in 2017 and has opened alot of new habitat for ELK, look for elk in the burn.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Nursery groups of cow elk can be observed generally very early in the morning or right before sunset. During warmer times of the day, elk will be staying cool in the forested areas and will be more difficult to observe. Focus on areas with high densities of aspen near water sources. Look for elk in the burn. Migration Patterns: All elk in this hunt boundary will migrate but these movements are generally not observed until late October and November. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars will be helpful. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points and hiking trails. Behavior: Elk will be on summer range and will begin to rut in September with cooler weather patterns.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Panguitch Lake unit offers substantial truck and ATV access. Cellular phone coverage within this hunt boundary is generally good but there are areas within the hunt boundary with little or no coverage. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, as well as warm weather conditions. Early winter storms are possible. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake/Thousand Lake unit is a very popular hunting area. Elevation ranges from some peaks above 11,600 feet to some valley floors near 5,000 feet. There are all types of vegetation and terrain. The good scenery, camping, fishing, and hunting draws many people to the area every fall. The Fish Lake unit has a large herd of 5,600 elk. It is manages for a 5.5 to 6 year average age of harvest. In 2015 the average bull was just under 6 years old. This unit can produce a few really large bulls, but in general you can expect to see a fair number of medium sized, mature bulls with a chance at some larger ones. On the earlier hunts many elk can find refuge on private property which can be frustrating.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Early Rifle: Elk are generally concentrated in the higher elevations during the early rifle hunt (above 8,000 ft.). The bulk of the herd tends to be in the higher elevations in the north/central part of the unit. Some good places to look are High Top Plateau, Mtn. Terrel, Mtn. Marvine, Mtn. Hilgard, Gooseberry area, Niotche, and UM Plateau. There are some elk on the Thousand Lake portion of the unit but they can be difficult to find. The elk will not be as easy to find as they were earlier in the year. During this hunt the rut is in full swing. Locating bulls by their bugles early and late in the day and even at night is a good strategy. These elk hear a lot of bugles and can be difficult to call in. A few more elk may have moved down into the oak brush habitats during this hunt, so don't overlook it. Muzzleloader: This hunt also occurs during the elk rut. Bulls are still vocal but a little more wary as they have already been hunted. Try locating bulls with bugles or cow calls but don't expect many to come into the calls. After locating the elk try stalking to get into range. The majority of the elk will still be in the areas they used during the early season, though some movement may have occurred. The elk will be sticking close to the trees or not even leaving cover if ample feed exists under the trees. This hunt overlaps with the muzzleloader buck deer hunt, so there will be other hunters in the field. Migration Patterns: From late October to early November many of the elk on the unit move to lower elevations. A large number of the elk head east to their wintering grounds on Mytogi, Last Chance, Red and Clear Creeks, Tidwell Slopes and Thousand Lake. Some elk will move south off of the unit onto the Parker Plateau. On the rest of the unit the elk drop down to lower elevations all around the unit. Scouting Tips: To see a lot of bulls, late June and July are great times to scout while elk are using the open meadows and hillsides. Many of these bulls will have moved by the time the hunting seasons arrive but you will get a good idea of what caliber of bulls are in the area. Good binoculars and spotting scope help you cover a lot of ground. One last trip just before your hunt will let you know where the elk are. For the early hunts concentrate on the conifer/aspen habitats and for the later hunt hit the oak brush/pinyon, mahogany areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a Large area and cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Fish Lake unit has a healthy bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting seasons. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, and both hot and cold temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions. The Archery and early rifle season can be very warm. Be prepared to get meat to a locker quickly or be prepared to cool meat as fast as possible to avoid spoilage.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is one of the best bull elk limited entry units in the state. The unit is managed for a 7.5 to 8 yr. old bull, which is what is being harvested, so we have an older age class of bulls in the population, although it can be a tough hunt. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. The Elk Ridge portion of the unit is flat and thick with vegetative cover and visual opportunities are limited. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the San Juan unit varies, depending on weather conditions. Typical migration goes from high elevations in the summer and early fall to low elevations in the winter and early spring. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Dry Mesa, Salt Creek Mesa, Bridger Jack Mesa, Milk Ranch Pnt., Peter's Point and Devil's Cyn. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads, access points and watering holes. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas for the San Juan limited entry subunit: Abajo Mountain - Higher elevations include large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding, lower elevations contain oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, good camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. North Elk Ridge - A good area for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, limited clearings for glassing, camping, nice roads, several different draws, canyons and mesa tops to hunt. South Elk Ridge - Good roads on mesa tops, limited access to rugged canyons, great area for pack-in hunts (Dark Canyon).
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the San Juan unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The elk on this unit are doing well, with nice bulls being harvested the past several years. Habitat on Diamond Mountain consists of sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, pine, aspen, and lower elevation desert scrub. This unit contains a Landowner Association and consists of about 35% private property. The private property is posted and a GPS showing private/public property boundaries is recommended. Even though the unit has private property, there is still 65% public land that is huntable. Public hunters should not expect to be allowed to hunt the private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move up and down in elevation throughout the year. During normal winters, elk will move down off the rim to the north and south. Bull elk will typically stay up higher in elevation in more inaccessible places. In dry years, elk will stay on the top of Diamond through the winter. Scouting Tips: In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Behavior: Like other wildlife, elk are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. If it's a dry year, they will be more concentrated around water sources, and these can sometimes be hunted successfully. On average precipitation or wet years, elk won't be as concentrated around water. Elk can move long distances in short periods of time, especially if they are disturbed by vehicles or people. Elk can be called in close for a shot during the rut. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October. Where to find elk: Elk are usually found in the higher elevations of the unit during the hunting season. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, guzzlers, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Diamond Mtn Unit: Good areas to look for elk include Wild Mountain, Top of Crouse Canyon, Marshall Draw, Warren Draw, and Mail Draw. Most of the ridges on this unit are public land and are accessible through public lands, although not always easily.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable or very muddy.
