hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Old Woman Plateau Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located east of the junction between Salina Creek and Meadow up Salina Creek. There are really three parts to this CWMU. The north part has high elevations of 8600 feet in the south and 8400 feet in the north. Spring Canyon is the major drainage ranging from 7600 feet to 8400 feet. There are four (4) small parts (7400 feet to 7800 feet) of the Unit up the South Fork of Rock Canyon and Saddle Horse Canyon. Southeast of these four parcels over Emigrant Pass (7800 feet) is the south part of the Unit. The high point on this south part is 8200 feet. Coal Mine Creek, 7600 feet to 8100 feet, cuts the south part of this Unit on the westside. Mill Hollow, 7000 feet to 8200 feet, cuts the northeast corner of this south part. The most common elevation is 8100 feet but ranges from 6900 feet to 8800 feet with an elevation difference of 1900 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7600 feet and 8200 feet an elevation difference of 600 feet. The majority of the Old Woman Plateau Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is composed of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) is another common land cover type. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) and Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) complete the dominant land cover mix. One of the Old Woman Plateau Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SALINA (427557), is about 4.6 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. SALINA has thirty-one (74) years of records, 1923 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.48 inches, but it can be as high as 6.67 inches or as low as 0.43 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 12 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 2.8 inches but can be as high as 18.0 inches. FALL temperature at SALINA averages 49.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 102.0 degrees F. or as low as -8.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 48 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 4 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Preston Nutter Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located northeast of Sunnyside, Utah. Higher elevations range from 9700 feet in the south to 9800 feet in the north. Then in the northwest corner elevation reaches 10000 feet. Range Creek cuts this high area, ranging from 9200 feet to 9900 feet. Cottonwood Canyon moving from west to east ranges from 9400 feet to 8000 feet, Jack Creek in like manner ranges from 9600 to 8100 feet. Flat Canyon (7300 feet to 9600 feet) and Summer-house Canyon (7400 feet to 9000 feet), also cut the Unit on the eastside. The most common elevation is 8600 feet but ranges from 6800 feet to 10000 feet with an elevation difference of 3200 feet. Fifty-five percent (55%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7900 feet and 9000 feet an elevation difference of 1100 feet. Almost half of the Preston Nutter Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit is covered by Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). This Sagebrush Steppe is confined to to the westside of the unit. A quarter of the unit is covered by Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22), and is dominant on the west side of the unit. The final quarter of the unit is covered with a combination Forest, Woodland, Pinyon-Juniper, and Grassland, Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (28), Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Jiniper Woodland (36), Rocky Mountain Subapline Dry-Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland, and Southern Rocky Mountain Montane-subalpine Grassland (71). One of the Preston Nutter Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SUNNYSIDE (428474), is 7.2 km southwest of the southwest edge of the CWMU. SUNNYSIDE has eighty-three (83) years of records, 1905 - 1988. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 4.13 inches, but it can be as high as 7.39 inches or as low as 1.66 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day with precipitation greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 12.6 inches but can be as high as 31.0 inches. FALL temperature at SUNNYSIDE averages 49.2 degrees F. but can be as high as 89.0 degrees F. or as low as 8.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 30 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is located southwest of Grouse Creek. Habitat types include open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and irrigated and non-irrigated agricultural fields.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has opened private land for public use to help compensate the public for having public land in the CWMU. Here is a link to a map showing "trade lands" in CWMUs https://wildlife.utah.gov/cwmu.html . The majority of the elk will use higher elevations of the CWMU through the summer months and move lower into irrigated agricultural fields towards the end of summer. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk west out of the country and into Nevada earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Scofield Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located northeast of Scofield Reservoir. The southwest boundary is Scofield Lake State Recreation Area. The Price River flowing from Scofield Reservoir is close to the Unit's south boundary and is part of the Unit's east boundary. The Price River ranges from 7100 feet to 7600 feet. The highest elevations are on a ridge running northwest to southeast on the western side of the Unit. Elevations on this ridge range from 8600 feet in the north, reaching a maximum a around 9000 feet, before decreasing again to 8600 feet. In the north Woods Canyon cuts the entire length of the Unit, ranging from 7500 feet to 8400 feet. The ridge just north of Woods Canyon reaches between 8500 and 8600 feet. On the eastside of the Unit are six small drainages running west to east, ranging from 7100 feet elevation to 8700 feet. The most common elevation is 8200 feet but ranges from 7200 feet to 9100 feet with an elevation difference of 1900 feet. Fifty-four percent (54%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7700 feet and 8400 feet an elevation difference of 700 feet. Just about half of the Scofield Canyons Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit is covered with Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). These Sagebrush Steppe areas are more prominent on the east and west sides of the unit. A good part of the middle and western parts of the unit are covered by Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). The middle also shows areas of Rocky Mountain Gamble Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). Also, in the middle Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32) and Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38) add to the forest and woodland character. There are some Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) areas on the east side, west and south border. One of the Scofield Canyons Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SCOFIELD DAM (427724), is 0.3 km south of the south edge of the CWMU. SCOFIELD DAM has forty-three (43) years of records, 1948 - 1991. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.48 inches, but it can be as high as 6.98 inches or as low as 0.76 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 17 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 17.2 inches but can be as high as 61.5 inches. FALL temperature at SCOFIELD DAM averages 40.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 86.0 degrees F. or as low as -22.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 67 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Scofield West Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is a long narrow CWMU located west, northwest and southwest of Scofield Reservoir. It is basically a series of higher elevations cut by canyons running west to east. In the north the higher elevations are around 8100 feet, in the middle elevations reach 8500 feet and in the south elevations rise to 9300 feet. In the north Starvation Creek cuts the Unit ranging from 7200 feet to 8000 feet. Moving south Bear Creek cuts the unit ranging between 7600 feet and 7700 feet. Fish Creek only cuts the Unit for a short distance around 7600 feet elevation. Tucker Canyon also cuts the Unit a short distance, ranging from 7900 feet to 8400 feet. The next three canyons are long canyons and cut the Unit for a short distance of their total length, Woods Canyon (7900 feet to 8400 feet), Winter Quarters Canyon (7900 feet to 8300 feet), and Green Canyon (8300 feet to 9200 feet). The most common elevation is 8100 feet but ranges from 7300 feet to 9600 feet with an elevation difference of 2300 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 8000 feet and 8800 feet an elevation difference of 800 feet. A good forty percent (40%) of the Scofield West Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is covered with Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Over twenty-five percent (25%) is occupied by Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). With the addition of Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41), over eighty-four (84%) of the CWMU is accounted for. One of the Scofield West Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SCOFIELD DAM (427724), is 4.2 km east of the east edge of the CWMU. SCOFIELD DAM has forty-three (43) years of records, 1948 - 1991. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.48 inches, but it can be as high as 6.98 inches or as low as 0.76 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 17 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 17.2 inches but can be as high as 61.5 inches. FALL temperature at SCOFIELD DAM averages 40.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 86.0 degrees F. or as low as -22.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 67 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Skull Crack Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is south of Causey Reservoir. Part of the Weber - Morgan County line forms the boundary of this Unit in the southeast, the Unit overlaps this boundary in the south. Highest elevation is the west is 7700 feet elevation, rising to 8200 feet in the middle of the Unit, then dropping again to 8000 feet elevation. Many small drainages drop off to the north and west. The Pete Nelson Hollow, ranging from 6400 feet to 8000 feet is one of these drainages. Skull Crack (5800 feet to 8000 feet), Mill Hollow (5800 feet to 8000 feet), Mill Canyon (5600 feet to 7300 feet), Magpie Canyon (5400 feet to 7800 feet), Quarry Hollow (5300 feet to 6600 feet), and Sheep Herd Creek (5700 feet to 8000 feet) are other small drainages on the Unit. The most common elevation is 8100 feet but ranges from 5100 feet to 8200 feet with an elevation difference of 3100 feet. Forty-nine percent (49%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6000 feet and 7400 feet an elevation difference of 1400 feet. The Skull Crack Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) has a mixture of two (2) land cover types with strong contribution from a third. Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) is the most common, but Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrsuh Steppe (62) is almost as common. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is also very common. Another common type is Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23). Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32) and Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30) contribute minor amounts to the Forest and Woodland character of the unit. One of the Skull Crack Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY (424135), is about 1.3 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY has thirty-one (31) years of records, 1976 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 5.74 inches, but it can be as high as 12.30 inches or as low as 1.36 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 10.2 inches but can be as high as 31.0 inches. FALL temperature at HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 56 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Soldier Summit Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) extends from Gilluly, Utah to Soldier Summit, down to Colton along State Highway 6. The Unit includes land on both sides the Highway 6 with most of it to the south of this highway. Higher elevations range from 8200 feet to 8400 feet in the north. On the eastside of Soldier Summit the White River ranges from 7100 feet to 7400 feet elevation. On the west Soldier Creek ranges from 6500 feet to 8100 feet. One of the Soldier Summit Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SOLDIER SUMMIT (427959), is about 0.25 km from the edge of the CWMU in the middle. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Strawberry Ridge Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is west of Woodruff, Utah and west of Birch Creek Reservoir. In the west the Unit starts at a high elevation of 8500 feet, then moving east drops down to Woodruff Park, around 7800 feet, then rises again to Strawberry Ridge, 8100 feet in the west to 7600 feet in the east. Birch Creek cuts the unit on the north side of Strawberry Ridge and runs nearly the length of the Unit, ranging from 6900 feet to 8400 feet. On the south side of the Strawberry Ridge is Walton Canyon. This canyon contains State Highway 39 and ranges from 7300 feet to 8000 feet elevation. The most common elevation is 7700 feet but ranges from 6900 feet to 8600 feet with an elevation difference of 1700 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7600 feet and 7900 feet an elevation difference of 300 feet. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Pahvant Ensign Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is divided into two parts, the west part and the east part. The west part is located southwest of Kanosh, Utah, and the east part is more directly south of Kanosh. On the north and west part of the west Unit the boundaries are hard surface roads. The highest elevations on the west part are in the extreme south, 6600 feet. This elevation drops into Dog Valley around 5700 feet. Then the elevation rises again to 6400 feet before dropping down into White Sage Flat, 5000 feet. Another rise in elevation to Six Mile Point (5400 feet) and higher to 5900 feet before dropping down to about 5000 feet just outside of the town of Kanosh. The east part of the Unit is much smaller. The east part is northwest and northeast of Gardner Hollow Reservoir (8300 feet). On the east part the highest elevations are at 9000 feet on the east unit border. hunt_bio_general_information: There are elk on this CWMU seasonally. It appears they like the southeastern side of the unit. They will water in Willow Creek, and walk up the canyons on to the CWMU to bed down. There are elk that water in Hill Creek on the west side of Little Pack Mtn. It is an extremely arid part of the Book Cliffs. The main water sources are Willow Creek and Hill Creek. There are a few water developments on the CWMU.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There is a chance early in the season to find bulls bachelored up pre-rut. They will be susceptible at certain water holes on the unit. Once they start to rut I suggest locating them with a good bugle and attempt to get inside their bubble and continue bugling to get the bull irritated enough to come within range. Elk densities on the unit can fluctuate drastically depending on the time of year. The southern end of the unit has more pinyon and juniper trees. This habitat provides excellent cover for bedding. You can locate their trails that lead down into willow Creek where they will feed and drink.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: his is a remote area and you will not always have cell phone reception. I would make sure you have good tires, and emergency equipment with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: I would prepare for fair to cold weather conditions. The roads can be affected by rain and snow. There is a fair amount of oil field traffic that helps keep the roads open.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Avintaquin Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located southeast of Duchesne, Utah about 30 km. The major feature of the CWMU is the Avintaquin Canyon and Avintaquin River. The Avintaquin River ranges from 6400 feet to 6800 feet on the unit. At 6800 feet the river splits into the West Fork Avintaquin River (6900 feet to 6800 feet) and the South Fork Avintaquin River (7100 feet to 6800 feet). Minnie Creek is another major drainage on the CWMU. Minnie Creek flows from the west to the east entering at 7100 feet and merging with the West Fork Avintaquin River at 6800 feet. On the Avintaquin Canyon CWMU 7300 feet is the most common elevation. However, elevation ranges from 6400 feet to 8400 feet, a difference of 2000 feet. Fifty-five percent (55%) of the unit's elevation ranges from 6400 feet to 7300 feet, a difference of 900 feet. The Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) is the most common cover type, nearly 50%. The only other cover type that takes up much area is the Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Most of this cover type is on the west side of the unit. Together the pinyon-juniper woodland and the sagebrush steppe account for 70% of the cover. One of the Avintaquin Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SOLDIER SUMMIT (427959), is about 39.0 km from the edge of the CWMU in a southwest direction. SOLDIER SUMMIT has one hundred nine (109) years of records, 1893 - 2002. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.09 inches, but it can be as high as 7.56 inches or as low as 1.27 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 16 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.3 inches but can be as high as 33.3inches. FALL temperature at SOLDIER SUMMIT averages 40.5degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -20.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 71 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Sharp Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is about 5 km southeast from Porcupine Reservoir in south Cache County. Almost all of the CWMU is in Cache County, but a small section in the southeast is in Weber County. The CWMU's name sake, Sharp Mountain rises to 9100 feet. Porcupine Ridge in the north is 8500 feet and in the south higher elevations are around 8300 feet. Davenport Creek in the south ranges from 6000 feet to 7400 feet on the unit. In the north Porcupine Creek ranges from 7400 feet to 8800 feet on the unit, and in the, east La Plata Canyon ranges from 7000 feet to 7900 feet. Much of the Sharp Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit is covered (32%) with Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). This Sagebrush Steppe is not concentrated in just one area but is spread throughout the CWMU. Similarly, Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) covers 29% of the CWMU and is spread throughout the unit too. Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38) covers 7% of the unit, and Inter-Mountain Basins Mountain Mahogany Woodland and Shrubland (44) covers 5% of the unit. The Woodland Complex is spread throughout the unit, but the Mahogany Woodland and Shrubland is more concentrated in the southwest part of the unit. One of the Green Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, LOGAN FARM (425194), is about 8.8 km northwest from the northwest edge of the CWMU. LOGAN FARM has thirty-nine (39) years of records, 1989 - 2008. There will also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 5.3 inches but can be as high as 15.5 inches. During the FALL, 47 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit has a population estimate of ~160 mountain goats. This is a difficult and physically demanding hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Most of the mountain goats in this unit can be found near Loafer Peak, Bald Mountain, and Mount Nebo above or near 11,000 feet. Scouting trips are highly recommended. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Mountain goat hunting requires a lot of glassing in cliff faces and "Bollies." Mountain goats do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. Some areas they stay fairly consistently all year while others they move quite far. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Goats do have areas they like and stay in the same general area but they can simply walk over the ridge and be gone for a day or two. What they can hike in minutes can take you all day. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in the cliffs or on rocky ridge tops, etc... occasionally move down into the trees so don't overlook those areas too. Mature Billies often like to hang out in very steep, rocky, cliffs by themselves or in small groups of two and threes. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep are open and green where they find better feed. Nannies and kids are usually in larger groups of five to fifty. Billy vs. Nanny: It is very difficult to tell the difference between a billy and a nanny mountain goat from a distance. Please review the Rocky Mountain Goat Hunt Orientation packet to learn how to properly identify mountain goats https://dwrapps.utah.gov/wex/examBorder.jsp?content=loginForm.jsp&formstat=0 . There are also other informational resources including this video produced by the Rocky Mountain Goat Alliance https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J8gUaMx8G7I While permits are either sex permits, hunters are encouraged to take billies and avoid harvesting a nanny with a kid.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Mountain goat habitat on this unit is very remote and hard to access. Appropriate precautions should be taken. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Mountain goats live in very steep, cliffy, treacherous terrain. Do not shoot a mountain goat in an area where you cannot safely retrieve it. You may need to wait until it moves to a safer spot before you can harvest the animal.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind, and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges where mountain goats live. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until through the first week on October. It is recommended that hunters do not wait until the very end of the hunt to go out hunting. At high elevations, there is a very real chance of a snowstorm that will not melt out until spring after the first week of October.

The Uinta Mountains goats hair up quite quickly after shedding their winter coats. Billies shed first in the summer and also hair back up first in the fall. I recommend against waiting until the very end of the hunt to have good hair for the cape. I would suggest the end of September and first few days of October to be a great time to hunt the Uintas for a good cape on a goat. Mountain goats on this unit occasionally move down into the trees so don't overlook those areas. Mature Billies often like to hang out in very steep, rocky, cliffs. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep and with rubble rock or green patches in rock where they find better feed. You can often guess whether it's a billy or a nanny just by the habitat it's in. Goats on the Chalk Creek/Kamas unit migrate very little during the winter. Goats can be found at or above 9000' in elevation throughout most of the year on this unit. Mountain goats can be found throughout the hunt on Bald Mountain, Notch Mountain and Haystack, as well as the Whiskey Lake area.

hunt_bio_general_information: 100% of the mountain goat habitat in this hunt unit is within the High Uintas Wilderness Area where motor vehicles are prohibited and access is difficult and remote. Mtn. goats live in very steep, cliffy, treacherous terrain. Do not shoot a mtn. goat in an area where you cannot safely retrieve it. You may need to wait until it moves to a safer spot before you can harvest the animal. Wasting of wildlife is not excusable simply because you chose to shoot it in a location you couldn't safely get to. Where to find mountain goats: Access to almost all of the mountain goat habitat is by foot or horseback only and is very remote. Mountain goat hunting is very physically demanding. Mountain goats live in steep cliffy areas, usually above tree line. Hunting can be very difficult, particularly in this hunt unit. Mountain goats are usually found in small groups or by themselves scattered across the cliff faces and the "bollies" between drainages and across the summit of the Uintas. Goats are well distributed in cliffy habitat across the entire unit. Goats are found in every drainage. Mountain goat rut:The mtn. goat rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not really affect the hunt. Recommended areas in the High Uintas Central:Goats are found across the spine of the Uintas. Billies in particular seems to prefer the spine of the Unitas. The Red Castle Peak area is probably the most popular area to hunt on this unit because there are almost always goats in the area. To the east of Red Castle, Flat Top Mtn also always has good numbers of goats along both sides up in the cliffs. On the South Slope, there are always mtn goats on the east side of the Lake Fork drainage but those areas can be difficult to access due to lack of trails on the Lake Fork side. There are goats from Swasey's Hole to Garfield Basin too. Another popular area is Swift Creek area and Yellowstone Canyon. Further east in the Uinta Canyon drainage, the Krebs Creek area has been popular, and up high on the sides of Mt. Emmons and above the Chain Lakes Basin.

Some areas they stay fairly consistently all year while others they move quite far. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep and with rubble rock or green patches in rock where they find better feed. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The Biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents but bear incidents in the Wilderness area have been rare in the past. Mtn. goats live in very steep, cliffy, treacherous terrain. hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. hunt_bio_general_information: Land Ownership: Moose habitat is primarily public land. Population Objective: 500 Current Population Estimate: 350
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Most moose are seen near rivers, streams, ponds, or lakes, focus your efforts near these areas. Later in the fall they will move into thick, brushy areas of oak brush and mahogany. Moose are very spread out on these subunits, so it is important to cover a lot of area. It is a great place to camp in the summer to scout and learn the roads and trails. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find moose. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Moose are typically a solitary animals. Recommended areas Wasatch West Subunit: American Fork Canyon- The canyon road takes you from the mouth of AF canyon east to Heber City. This area has a lot of moose. Look around Casacade Springs area. Strawberry Reservoir- Look along all streams feeding into Strawberry Reservoir, such as Strawberry River, Coop Creek, Mud Creek and Indian Creek and Trout Creek. These areas are not a high density area. Salt Lake County- All canyons on the east side of the valley have moose in them, such as Big and Little Cottonwood Canyons, Mill Creek, and Lambs Canyon. You can hunt with any weapon east on I-15 for cow moose. Other canyons to look in- Squaw Peak road, Right Hand Fork of Hobble Creek, Diamond Fork, Sheep Creek and Tie Fork. Not a lot of moose in these areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Always be sure of your target. Don't shoot from roads. Do not keep a loaded gun in your vehicle
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until through the first week on October.

hunt_bio_general_information: Nearly 90% of this unit is on private property. Hunters should have written permission to hunt private land prior to applying for this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Moose are very large animals and difficult to haul long distances. They are often found near or in water. Do not shoot if you cannot retrieve the animal where it may go down, such as in a lake or stream. Choose your shot wisely; you may have to wait for it to move to a better location. Migration Patterns: Moose do not show a definite migration pattern on this unit.. They are not as dependent on water sources during the winter months. Snow depth also does not seem to affect where they are located. Scouting Tips: Scouting trips are highly recommended in order to become familiar with the area. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Plan to spend a lot of time hiking in areas away from human disturbance. Bull Moose can move long distances, especially during the rut when they are in search of cows so you may not see the same moose on different scouting trips. Behavior: Like other wildlife, moose are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. They are often found in mountain riparian areas, near lakes and streams, with willows or aspen. During the rut, bulls and cows will call to attract mates. This can be useful in finding bulls in the thick vegetation. Moose rut: The moose rut usually runs during September and October. Where to find moose: Moose can be found throughout the higher elevations of this unit, mainly on private property. Written permission to hunt private land is recommended prior to applying for this hunt. During the hunt, moose will generally be found along streams and in aspen stands, but they may also be found in conifer stands moving between areas. Recommended areas: High elevation riparian and wet meadow habitat types, away from human disturbance.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past in this unit. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Moose can be unpredictable and dangerous if you encroach into their space. Females can be protective of young and may charge if they perceive you as a threat. Males can be defensive, especially during the rut.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning if you're crossing high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Occasionally a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit encompasses low desert to high mountain terrain. Moose are found on both sides of Flaming Gorge Reservoir, with the majority found in the higher elevations west of Flaming Gorge Reservoir. This unit is a general season deer unit and the West Daggett subunit is a general season elk unit; this area is heavily utilized during these other hunts with many people camping out during the seasons.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Moose are very large animals and difficult to haul long distances. They are often found near or in water. Do not shoot if you cannot retrieve the animal where it may go down, such as in a lake or stream. Choose your shot wisely; you may have to wait for it to move to a better location. If you cannot retrieve the moose, do not shoot; this is not an excuse for wasting game. Migration Patterns: Moose do not show a definite migration pattern on the North Slope. They are not as dependent on water sources during the winter months. Snow depth also does not seem to affect where they are located. Scouting Tips: In the Uintas, locating a bull moose is the hardest part of the hunt. Scouting trips are highly recommended so you become familiar with the unit and know the size of bull you will most likely harvest. Take your fishing pole along and enjoy the mountain lakes and streams. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Bull moose can move long distances, especially during the rut when they are in search of cows so you may not see the same moose on different scouting trips. Moose do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. When the rut starts, a bull moose may move many miles in one day so don't count on finding the same bull in an area on consecutive days. Behavior: Like other wildlife, moose are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time, they are found in mountain riparian areas near lakes and streams, most often where there are willows or aspen. During the rut, bulls and cows will call to attract mates. This can be useful in finding bulls in the thick vegetation they are often in. Bulls are sometimes attracted to thrashing willows if they think it's another bull. You may be able to use this trick to lure them into a different area for a better shot. Moose rut: The moose rut usually runs during September and October. Where to find moose: The majority of the moose are found on the West Daggett portion of the unit. It is generally higher in elevation and has more water than the 3 Corners side. During the hunt, moose will generally be found along streams and in aspen stands, but they may also be found in conifer stands moving between areas. These units are heavily utilized by hunters during these seasons with many people camping out on public lands. This is a tough hunt due to low moose densities.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Moose are very large animals and difficult to haul long distances. They are often found near or in water. Do not shoot if you cannot retrieve the animal where it may go down, such as in a lake or stream. Choose your shot wisely; you may have to wait for it to move to a better location. If you cannot retrieve the moose, do not shoot; this is not an excuse for wasting game. Migration Patterns: Moose do not show a definite migration pattern on this unit. They are not as dependent on water sources during the winter months. Snow depth also does not seem to affect where they are located. Scouting Tips: In the Uintas locating a bull moose is the hardest part of the hunt. Scouting trips are highly recommended so you become familiar with the unit and know the size of bull you will most likely harvest. Take your fishing pole along and enjoy the mountain lakes and streams. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Bull moose can move long distances, especially during the rut when they are in search of cows so you may not see the same moose on different scouting trips. Moose do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. When the rut starts, a bull moose may move many miles in one day so don't count on finding the same bull in an area on consecutive days. Most of the time, they are found in mountain riparian areas near lakes and streams, most often where there are willows or aspen. During the rut, bulls and cows will call to attract mates. This can be useful in finding bulls in the thick vegetation they are often in. Bulls are sometimes attracted to thrashing willows if they think it's another bull. You may be able to use this trick to lure them into a different area for a better shot. Moose rut: The moose rut usually runs during September and October. hunt_bio_general_information: This is a Once in a lifetime hunt. The quality of the bulls on this unit is average. Moose can be found during this hunt anywhere across the unit from the highest elevations in the Wilderness area to the lowest along the Duchesne River corridor. Hunters should be aware of Ute tribal lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. Moose are found primarily along stream corridors and near lakes and ponds. They can also be found in forested areas and brushy areas away from water. This unit includes the South Slope portion of the High Uintas Wilderness Area. The wilderness can provide a remote hunt with very few hunters but moose can be hard to locate. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine with little understory vegetation. Road access on the remainder of the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Moose on this unit can be found almost anywhere during the hunt. This herd generally move down in elevation for the winter. Most of the moose winter on Ute Tribal Lands or on lower elevation slopes on Forest Service lands. They also winter in river bottoms etc... Some moose are found on ridgetops and fairly high elevation during the winter. Moose rut: The moose rut on this unit usually peaks the end of Sept. and early Oct. The rut is usually dropping off by the end of the hunt. Some hunters are successful calling in bulls during this hunt, but most bulls are harvested simply by spot and stalk style hunting. During the rut, bull moose will cover a lot of ground looking for cows that are in heat. Finding a bull in one canyon does not mean he will still be there the next day when they really get rutty. When on the rut and looking for cows, bulls will often make a low grunting noise while they travel. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Yellowstone: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. The Wilderness Area can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but is very tough to hunt and it can be hard to locate moose. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine with little understory. Moose in the wilderness are generally found near lakes and along the stream corridors. During the hunt, most of the moose are found near water but can be also be found in brushy or timbered areas. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit): Mirror Lake Hwy - Hwy 150 is the west boundary of the hunt, closest to the Wasatch front Soapstone/Iron Mine - good road access, closer to the Wasatch Front North Fork of the Duchesne - limited road access Log Hollow - must cross tribal Lands to access, rough roads Rock Creek - paved road access, steep areas, be aware of tribal boundary Bear Wallow - steep terrain, be aware of tribal boundary Lake Fork/Moon Lake - paved road access, some private property to be aware of Yellowstone - rough roads, be aware of tribal boundary 77 Flat/Burnt Mill - gravel roads, a little flatter area, be aware of tribal boundary Dry Gulch - very rough road, steep terrain, be aware of tribal boundary on the east Uinta Canyon - tribal lands down low, steep terrain Painter Basins - wilderness area, very remote Elk Horn Loop - gravel roads that go almost to the summit of the Uinta Mountains, lots of opportunity to scatter out, good access to the high country Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks River is the eastern unit boundary, steep terrain

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Most moose are seen near rivers, streams, ponds, or lakes, focus your efforts near these areas. Later in the fall they will move into thick, brushy areas of oak brush and mahogany. Moose are very spread out on these subunits, so it is important to cover a lot of area. It is a great place to camp in the summer to scout and learn the roads and trails. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find moose. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Moose are typically a solitary animal, groups of bulls are uncommon until late fall and winter. Bull moose can, and will travel long distances during the rut in search of cows. This is important to know, because areas where you saw bulls in the summer might not be where they will be in the fall, however areas where you saw cows in the summer may be good places to find bulls during the rut. Moose rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting middle of September, with the peak of the rut being the end of September through the middle of October. There should be rutting activity throughout the entire hunting season. Areas to Hunt: Recommended areas Currant Creek Subunit: Currant Creek Drainage - This entire area is great for moose, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands, lots of ponds, creeks, streams, and lakes. Great access, camping, nice road, several different draws or canyons to hunt(Layout Canyon, Big Dry Hollow, Low Pass Creek, Race Track), can hold moose. North Fork Deep Creek/Water Hollow - very few roads, great area for horseback hunts, land managed by UDWR, borders private land in many spots. Wildcat WMA - UDWR land, borders private, lots of roads, highest density of moose on the subunit. West Fork Duchesne - Big area, road access, limited ATV access, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands, lots of water. Tabby Mountain WMA - the North slope is best, ponds on top, UDWR land, great for ATV's. Red Creek Drainage - Great area for moose, some private property, lots of SITLA property that is open for hunting, anywhere along the Red Creek is good for moose. Strawberry River - The entire river corridor East of Strawberry Reservoir. Area is thick and can be difficult to spot moose. Primarily land managed by the UDWR Recommended areas Avintaquin Subunit: Reservation Ridge - Big area, road on the divide, great area for glassing, not as many moose as Currant Creek. Strawberry Peak Area - Highest peak on Avintaquin, great access to roadless areas(Slab Canyon and Cow Hollow), not a lot of moose in these areas. Long Ridge - Great glassing area, areas South of Long Ridge along creeks and near ponds. Not a high density area. Recommended areas Wasatch West Subunit: American Fork Canyon - The canyon road takes you from the mouth of AF canyon east to Heber City. This area has a lot of moose. Look around Casacade Springs area. Strawberry Reservoir - Look along all streams feeding into Strawberry Reservoir, such as Strawberry River, Coop Creek, Mud Creek and Indian Creek and Trout Creek. These areas are not a high density area. Salt Lake County - All canyons on the east side of the valley have moose in them, such as Big and Little Cottonwood Canyons, Mill Creek, and Lambs Canyon. You can hunt with any weapon east on I-15 for OIAL hunts. Other canyons to look in - Squaw Peak road, Right Hand Fork of Hobble Creek, Diamond Fork, Sheep Creek and Tie Fork. Not a lot of moose in these areas, but big bulls have been seen in the past. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is cut east-west by Dry Creek and north-south by State Road 68. Dry Creek starts at about 7200 feet and flows east and then south and exits the Unit at about 4400 feet. The higher elevations are on the west below Snow Basin Ski Resort. Then with a moderate slope the terrian slopes to the southeast and drops down into the Dry Creek cut before exiting the Unit. The most common elevation is 5800 feet but ranges from 5000 feet to 8500 feet with an elevation difference of 3500 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5700 feet and 7600 feet an elevation difference of 1900 feet. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is the dominant land cover type on the Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). There are many large patches of Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23) dispersed among the Gambel Oak, as are smaller patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are patches of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) on the west side, more in the middle of the Unit are patches of Rocky Mountain Lower Montane Riparian Shrubland (79), and scattered about are patches of Recently Burned (116) areas. There are some minor areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) scattered about. One of the Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, PINE VIEW DAM (422424), is about 3.6 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. PINE VIEW DAM has twenty-seven (72) years of records, 1935 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 7.33 inches, but it can be as high as 16.43 inches or as low as 1.52 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 15 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is also 2 days with precipitation greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 13.7 inches but can be as high as 49.5 inches. FALL temperature at PINE VIEW DAM averages 46.2 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 48 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Beaver Hollow Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is just east of the right extension of Lost Creek Reservoir. Towards the northeast corner are extensive areas of Recently Burned (116) land cover. Distributed among the Sagebrush Steppe are patches of Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) and Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has opened private land for public use to help compensate the public for having public land in the CWMU. Here is a link to a map showing "trade lands" in CWMUs https://wildlife.utah.gov/cwmu.html . The Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is west and north of Causey Reservoir. Beaver Creek and State Highway 39 forms the west boundary and Elk Ridge forms the east boundary. The Unit consists of a main ridge which is about 8000 feet in the north dropping to 6700 feet in the south before it drops into Water Hollow. From this main ridge the Unit drops into Beaver Creek (5600 feet to 6600 feet). On the eastside the unit drops in to Dry Bread Hollow (6000 feet to 7200 feet) before rising up to Elk Ridge (7600 feet to 7900 feet). The most common elevation is 6800 feet but ranges from 5500 feet to 7900 feet with an elevation difference of 2400 feet. Fifty-four percent (54%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6000 feet and 7300 feet an elevation difference of 1300 feet. There are three (3) main land cover types and one (1) land cover type that dominates the Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). First, there is the Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Then there are the Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) and Rocky Mountain Gamble Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) in about equal amounts. In lesser amounts is Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland(23). One of the Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY (424135), is about 11.0 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY has thirty-one (31) years of records, 1976 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 5.74 inches, but it can be as high as 12.30 inches or as low as 1.36 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 10.2 inches but can be as high as 31.0 inches. FALL temperature at HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 56 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) takes up parts of Weber, Morgan and Rich counties, with Rich county having the most area. The higher points on the Deseret CWMU are along Horse Ridge (8500 feet). On the west the Unit drops away to about 6400 feet in the south and 8000 feet in the north. On the eastside of Horse Ridge the Unit makes a less steep drop, dropping down to around 6400 feet in the north and 6800 feet in the south along the Utah - Wyoming state border. The most common elevation is 6400 feet but ranges from 6000 feet to 8700 feet with an elevation difference of 2700 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6800 feet and 7800 feet an elevation difference of 1000 feet. The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is much larger than other CWMUs in Utah, therefore land cover is more diversified. About half (50%) of the land cover on the Deseret CWMU is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Towards the northeast and at lower elevation, there are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Steppe (66). Thet higher elevations on the west of the Unit, mixed with Sagebrush Steppe are extensive areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). At lower elevations towards the northeast are several patches of Agriculture (114) land. At minor extents are Southern Rocky Mountain Montane-Subalpine Grassland (71), Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48), and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane shrubland (41). One of the Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, WOODRUFF (429595), is about 10.5 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Durst Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located north of Morgan, Utah and Interstate Highway 84. Because Durst Mountain is near the Unit's west boundary elevation only drops to 8700 feet in the west. To the south it drops down to 5200 feet, and to the east and north it decreases to 7600 feet. Other Forest and Woodland types are Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23), Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30), and Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (28). hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Three C Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is southeast of Heber City. The highest elevation is in the southeast at near 9900 feet. This high elevation decreases to 7200 feet in the northwest. Crooked Creek is one of the drainages that cuts the Unit. It ranges from 6600 feet to 8700 feet. Center Creek is another drainage that cuts the Unit. It ranges from 6400 feet to 8600 feet. The most common elevation is 8000 feet but ranges from 5800 feet to 9900 feet with an elevation difference of 4100 feet. Fifty-three percent (53%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7000 feet and 8700 feet an elevation difference of 1700 feet. The Three C Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is somewhat divided in half. On the west half the land cover is dominated by Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). Whereas, the east half is dominated by Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23), Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (28), and Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) add to the Forest and Woodland character of the Unit. Rocky Mountain Subalpine-Montane Riparian Shrubland (77) and Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland support the Shrubland character. One of the Three C Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HEBER (423809), is 4.6 km northwest of the northwest edge of the CWMU. HEBER has one hundred sixteen (116) years of records, 1892 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.92 inches, but it can be as high as 10.14 inches or as low as 0.50 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 18 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.9 inches but can be as high as 29.5 inches. FALL temperature at HEBER averages 46.6 degrees F. but can be as high as 98.0 degrees F. or as low as -21.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 57 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located just south of the Idaho - Utah state-line with State Highway 150 forming much of the east boundary. The high elevation is around 9100 feet. The Hayden Fork (7800 feet to 8400 feet) and the West Fork (7800 feet to 9000 feet) of the Bear River cut the Unit on the east. Two major drainages flowing into the Bear River and its forks are Mill City Creek (8400 feet to 9200 feet) and Deer Creek (8300 feet to 9100 feet). On the west side of the Unit, Yellow Creek, ranging from 7700 feet to 8800 feet, cuts the unit. The most common elevation is 8900 feet but ranges from 7500 feet to 9600 feet with an elevation difference of 2100 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 8100 feet and 8900 feet an elevation difference of 800 feet. The Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) land cover is dominated by two (2) types in almost equal proportions, Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) and Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Rocky Mountain Subalpine-Montane Riparian Shrubland (77) is also a prominent land cover type on the Unit. There is also a large patch of Rocky Mountain Lodgepole Pine Forest (29) in the southeast corner that contributes to the land cover mix. One of the Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, COALVILLE (421590), is about 14.2 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. COALVILLE has thirty-four (34) years of records, 1974 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.71 inches, but it can be as high as 7.09 inches or as low as 1.68 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 19 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.8 inches but can be as high as 32.0 inches. FALL temperature at COALVILLE averages 43.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 87.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 61 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Wallsburg Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located east of Wallsburg, Utah. The higher elevations are on the east side of the Unit, ranging from 8900 feet in the south to 8400 feet in the north. Maple Creek or Maple Canyon cuts the Unit in the southwest, ranging from 6200 feet to 8400 feet. In the north Boomer Canyon cuts the Unit, ranging from 7000 feet to 8400 feet. Near forty percent (40%) of the Wallsburg Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). This Aspen Forest and Woodland is all on the eastside of the unit. On the westside of the unit it is a mixture of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed MontaneShrubland (41). One of the Wallsburg Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, DEER CREEK DAM (422057), is 12.1 km west of the west edge of the CWMU. DEER CREEK DAM has forty-nine (49) years of records, 1959 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.54 inches, but it can be as high as 7.69 inches or as low as 0.60 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 4.4 inches but can be as high as 30.0 inches. FALL temperature at DEER CREEK DAM averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 97.0 degrees F. or as low as -12.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 54 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

The Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is east of East Canyon Reservoir and southwest of Porterville, Utah. The Unit highpoint is around 8000 feet. This highpoint is in the southeast part of the unit. The elevation in the north decreases to 6000 feet, in the south it decreases to 7600 feet, in the west 6600 feet and in the east 5800 feet. Hardscrabble Creek divides this Unit starting at 7600 feet in the south, then exiting the Unit in the northeast corner at 5400 feet. The most common elevation is 6600 feet but ranges from 5400 feet to 9300 feet with an elevation difference of 3900 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6700 feet and 8100 feet an elevation difference of 1400 feet. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is the dominant land cover type on the Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Management Units (CWMU). This Shrubland is more dominant in the central and north parts of the Unit, than in the south. Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) is also a prominent feature of the Unit scattered through the shrubland. There are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) scattered on the Unit. Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30), Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), and Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23) add to the Forest and Woodland character of the Unit. One of the Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, CITY CREEK (421446), is about 6.2 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. CITY CREEK has fifty-three (53) years of records, 1955 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 6.94 inches, but it can be as high as 10.80 inches or as low as 2.38 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 24 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 5 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is also 1 day where the precipitation and be greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 18.6 inches but can be as high as 56.0 inches. FALL temperature at CITY CREEK averages 49.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 92.0 degrees F. or as low as 2.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 34 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is located northeast of Grouse Creek near Lynn. Habitat types include open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, sub-alpine forest, and irrigated and non-irrigated agricultural fields.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The majority of the moose will use higher elevations of the CWMU through the summer months. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the moose out of the country earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for moose and then working to get close for a shot or stalking moose through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Moose are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Moon's Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located west of Hanna,Utah. The highest elevation on the east side starts about 8400 feet and increases to 8800 feet before dropping down into several drainages, but it rises again to 8200 feet on the west side of the Unit. In the north, the West Fork of the Duchesne River, ranging from 7200 feet to 7600 feet, cuts the Unit. In the south, Sand Creek, ranging from 6800 feet to 8000 feet, cuts the Unit. On the west side, Little Sand Creek, ranging from 7500 feet to 8000 feet, cuts the unit. The most common elevation is 8000 feet but ranges from 6700feet to 8800 feet with an elevation difference of 2100 feet. Fifty-seven percent (57%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7500 feet and 8100 feet an elevation difference of 600 feet. Over half of the land cover on the Moon's Ranch CWMU is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). This cover type is generally distributed over the entire unit. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) and Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) are the next largest contributors. Several hundred hectares each of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) and Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland round out most of the land cover types. One of the Moons Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HANNA (423624), is 0.5 km east of the east edge of the CWMU. HANNA has forty-two (42) years of records, 1952 - 1994. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.35 inches, but it can be as high as 4.43 inches or as low as 2.52 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 10 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inches of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inches, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inches of prercipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 2.2 inches but can be as high as 5.0 inches. FALL temperature at HANNA averages 63.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 78.0 degrees F. or as low as 5.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 23 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: ****IMPORTANT NOTICE-PLEASE READ*** On September 12, 2023 a tamarisk removal project will begin in the Willow Creek drainage of the Book Cliffs and run for approximately 10 weeks. Hunters should be advised that work will be conducted with chainsaws and they may be heard for a short distance from the project location. Please plan accordingly and if you have further questions, contact the Vernal UDWR office: (435)781-9453. The Book Cliffs antelope population has been steadily declining since 1998. It could be from a combination of drought, predation, and interspecific competition. It is a still a good place to draw a permit. It is such a large area that hunter competition is really low. I would put a significant effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime antelope habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources, placing trail cameras, and selecting a site for a ground blind. Unless it rains which has been a rare occurrence, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day. Spot and stalk techniques are effective as well. The pronghorn are used to vehicle traffic because of all the oil and gas production in the area. They rely on their eye sight and speed to avoid predation. As long as they don't see anything out of the ordinary they are fairly docile, and calm.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of hunters choose to hunt close to the Seep Ridge Road on the north end of the unit. After the road crosses the White River you are on the unit. Once you cross the river and are off of Tribal land I would start focusing your efforts there. There are several wide open flats with folding hills that antelope prefer. The Glen Bench Road is the first major road that takes you back to the east. I wouldn't be deterred from all of the oil field traffic. The oil field workers spend a lot of time driving through prime antelope habitat, and can provide some great scouting tips. On the west side of the unit there is a large open area called Wild Horse Bench. It is a popular place for antelope, elk, wild horses, livestock, and some deer. I have seen antelope in this area, but it is a large area and sometimes they are difficult to locate. I don't think it receives very much hunting pressure. Winter Ridge is an area with sparse antelope, but receives very little hunting pressure. Migration Patterns: The Book Cliffs antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. During the past decade of drought, the poor maintenance condition of many of these artificial water sources limited their effectiveness. Repairs have been made and are continuing. Natural gas and oil production is rapidly increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I have seen antelope shade up during the day under the large tanks on oil well pads. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas on the northern part of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope in the Book Cliffs is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice. The Book Cliffs has a high bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or call the local dispatch center (435 789-4222).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.
