hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is in the southeast part of Duchesne County, about 10.5 km from Duchesne, Utah. Higher elevations are in the southwest corner of the unit (6300 feet). Antelope Creek that cuts the CWMU ranges from 5300 feet to 5800 feet. Pleasant Valley in the east ranges from 5300 feet to 5800 feet. The most common elevation is 5500 feet but ranges from 5300 feet to 6300 feet with an elevation difference of 1000 feet. Fifty (50%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5600 feet and 6100 feet an elevation difference of 500 feet. About thirty-six perecent (36%) of the Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Colorado Plateau Mixed Low Sagebrush Shrubland (50), located on the westside of the unit. Another thirty-four percent (34%) is Inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58), located mostly on the eastside of the unit. Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (66), Inter-Mountain Basins Greasewood Flat (82), and Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Grassland (76) also figure into the mix. One of the Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, DUCHESNE (422253), is about 6.0 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. DUCHESNE has eighty-three (92) years of records, 1906 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.57inches, but it can be as high as 6.21 inches or as low as 0.25 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 3.1 inches but can be as high as 17.1 inches. FALL temperature at DUCHESNE averages 46.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 93.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 49 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Zane Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located southwest of Lund, Utah. This mostly flat Unit ranges from 5100 feet in the south to 5300 feet in the north. Mountain Spring Wash the only substantial drainage cuts the unit also ranges from 5100 feet to 5300 feet. The most common levation is 5200 feet but ranges from 5100 feet to 5400 feet with an elevation difference of 300 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5200 feet and 5300 feet an elevation difference of 100 feet. Much of the Zane Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is dominated by Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). Most of this Sagebrush shrubland is in the northwest part. Inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58) is dominate in the southwest part, extending into the southeast. Patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Shrub Steppe (67) occur across the unit, but there are large areas on the eastside of the Unit. In the middle of the Unit, are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Grassland (76). One of the Zane Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, LUND (425247), is about 7.8 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. LUND has sixty-seven (67) years of records, 1900 - 1967. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 1.97 inches, but it can be as high as 4.37 inches or as low as 0.03 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 7 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 5 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 1.1 inches but can be as high as 7.0 inches. FALL temperature at LUND averages 50.3 degrees F. but can be as high as 104.0 degrees F. or as low as -9.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 47 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 5 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Parker offers great opportunity to view and hunt pronghorn. The area of this hunt boundary that contains the highest densities of pronghorn is located roughly west and south of Loa and Bicknell. The pronghorn also use a smaller area north of Loa. Animals can occasionally be found on the west side of the unit in John's Valley crossing back and forth between the Parker and Mt Dutton units.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn on this unit love timbered areas! During the warmer weather they will lounge in small meadows in the aspen and spruce forests on the south and east portions of the Parker plateau. As hunting pressure increases on this unit, the pronghorn will also use the trees for security cover. Pronghorn can be found in the more traditional open areas of the Parker, but the greatest densities are found higher up along the tree lines. Access to these areas in a vehicle is limited. The pronghorn on the Parker are also wary of motorized vehicles and will go to great lengths to avoid them. It may be profitable for hunters to plan on walking away from roads and vehicles to glass for animals. There are many water sources on the Parker and pronghorn like to use these sources. They are accustomed to drinking every day and locating water sources and waiting in blinds for animals to show up is a good hunting strategy. Mature bucks are most likely to be found with larger herds of does and fawns but are frequently off on their own as well. Be prepared to seek out the highest densities of animals at a much higher elevation than one might expect.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit and the terrain is very similar throughout the Parker plateau. It is very easy to become disoriented. There is limited cell service in the area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions and check weather forecasts often. Late summer and early fall monsoonal rains can make roads incredibly muddy and impassible roads. Drive these roads with extreme caution, otherwise you may get vehicles stuck.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is also known as the Rattlesnake Unit. Bighorn sheep populations have been stable in this area for several decades. Permit numbers have not changed dramatically over this time period. The unit boundary is relatively large however, the vast majority of the occupied bighorn sheep habitat is in the western third of the unit from Thompson west to Green River.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Over 80% of the bighorn sheep observed on this unit are found within 2 miles of the Green River. Sheep use the first 2 to 3 cliff bands above the river and the grassy benches between them. The core area where most sheep live can be found between Tushar Canyon north to Rattlesnake Canyon. Lower densities of bighorn sheep can be found north of Rattlesnake Canyon to the tribal boundary in Coal Creek. Lower densities of bighorn can also be found east of Tushar Canyon along the Book Cliffs to as far east as Thompson. Generally no bighorn sheep are found anywhere on the unit east of the town of Thompson. Scouting Tips: It is good to do pre-season scouting to learn country. However, it is very hot on this unit during the summer months so plan accordingly. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a spotting scope. This unit looks a lot more like desert bighorn sheep habitat than Rocky Mountain bighorn habitat. It is dry and cliffy. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Many of the larger harvestable rams will not move on to public lands and be available for harvest until the rut begins in late October. Do not be alarmed if there are no big rams in the summer. They will show up by November. Hunting generally gets better the later you go. The peak of the rut tends to be the week of Thanksgiving. Find groups of ewes and lambs and often times a new ram will be with the ewe group each day as rams are moving alot in November between ewe groups. A way to cover lots of ground is to hike up on top of a canyon and glass the other side while having someone else hike the other side of the canyon and look back across the canyon toward you. Behavior: The month of November is during the bighorn sheep rut. Rams are moving from group to group looking for ewes. Rams can also be observed butting heads. It is advised to occasionally stop and listen for the sound of butting heads it can be a good tool for locating sheep that are otherwise difficult to see. Sheep are generally active throughout the day in November but activity is highest in morning and evening. Bighorn sheep will not be as tied to water in November as it is generally more available that time of year if it has snowed. Bighorn will generally avoid the flat mesa top areas where there is any sort of tree cover. They tend to be found on the steep open cliffs and are occasionally are feeding on the flat canyon bottoms or benches. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Many young rams will have a pronounced curl. The best way to recognize mature trophy class bighorn rams is to look for horn mass particularly out near the tip of the horn. Younger rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. Mature rams 6 years and older tend to have thicker horns out near the tips, and thicker bases. Often times if you are close enough you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut runs during late October and extends through early December with the peak being around Thanksgiving. Where to find Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep: Recommended areas: Highest density areas are Tushar Canyon, the Canyon above Swaseys Beach, the canyon above the Rock House, and Butler Canyon. Hike up through the first cliff band and hunt the upper cliff layers within 2 miles of the river and you will generally see sheep in these canyons.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This unit is steep and rough with very little cell coverage. As in most bighorn sheep habitat, hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters end up walking dozens of miles and climbing thousands of feet prior to harvesting their ram. As with most bighorn sheep habitat, there is an abundance of cliffs. Be very careful scaling cliffs. It is advised that you bring extra rope to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is very handy on this unit to not only mark sheep and routes but also places where you can get through the ledges as they are relatively rare. Hunters can sometimes spend hours hiking along trying to find a way through the ledges and wasting time and energy. Bring plenty of water. It can be warm in November and there is very little water on the unit. Water in the Green River is plentiful but is tough on most portable water filters as it generally runs pretty muddy. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in November are variable on this unit. Generally, plan on cold nights with mild days with little snow accumulation. Most of the occupied bighorn sheep habitat occurs at lower elevations between 4200 and 6000 feet where snow generally doesn't accumulate. Snow and bad weather is always possible in November. The roads can get icy as they rarely see sunlight in these dark canyons.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The majority of sheep stay in the same general areas throughout much of the year. During summer months, sheep concentrate on the north end of the mountain range in conjunction with natural water availability. During the late fall and winter, sheep begin to spread south across the range. Miners Basin and Desert Peak hold the highest densities of sheep, but sheep will range in high densities south to Big Pass and to the military boundary. Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep are found in steep rocky terrain. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your bighorn sheep. If you cannot safely retrieve the bighorn sheep, do not shoot. Once the rut starts, the rams will be begin to move to where the ewes are. Scouting is a good way to see what size of ram you can expect to harvest. Sheep are most active in mornings and evenings. Using a spotting scope works well to find sheep in the steep rocky areas. Scores for sheep from the Newfoundlands have typically been in the 150s-160s. We are going to start providing more opportunity in this hunt so those scores may be lower in the future.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage on this hunt unit is spotty. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and hunt, and when you will return. Roads around the mountain can become very slick and muddy when wet, and access roads are rough and can cause tire damage. This unit is very isolated and is very far from the nearest services. The closest services are in Wendover, Utah/Nevada, Grantsville, or Snowville. Munitions from the active military base may be present on public property. If found, do not touch! Take a GPS location and report what you found.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, and wind. Typically by this hunting season, any precipitation that is received is freezing rain or snow and temperatures regularly fall below freezing at night. Be very cautious of lightning while scouting and hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Any precipitation will cause the roads to become very slick and muddy.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit has spectacular scenery with many tourists, fishermen, and campers utilizing the area during the summer months. Many visitors to this area travel here specifically to view bighorn sheep. This hunt allows hunters to scout and hunt from land or from a boat. This unit is small with a low sheep population. Many of the mature rams congregate in 1 to 2 groups most of the year. Herd numbers have been declining and older rams have been dying before being harvested. Hunters should expect a class III or 3/4 curl (score 140-150) type ram.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep are found in steep rocky terrain. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your bighorn sheep. If you cannot safely retrieve the bighorn sheep, do not shoot. Scouting Tips: The bighorn sheep stay fairly consistently in the same general areas throughout much of the year. Once the rut starts, the rams will be begin to move to where the ewes are. Scouting is a good way to see what size of ram you can expect to harvest. Scores for sheep on Bare Top are usually in the 140s-150s and are 5.5-6.5 years old. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in steep terrain, but they occasionally move down to the shoreline or up on top of Bare Top where it's flat. Mature rams seem to hang out more in steeper cliffs than ewes. Ewes with lambs prefer areas that are a little less steep and where they can find better feed. Bighorn sheep will usually go to water at least once a day. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut runs during November. Where to find Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep: Bighorn sheep like steep cliffy areas because it provides an escape from predators. You can find them on grassy flats or near the shoreline when they are eating or come down to drink. Recommended areas: There are a couple of areas that the sheep use regularly. These areas include Hideout, Boars Tusk, along the Flaming Gorge Reservoir shoreline and along the Green River below the dam to Little Hole. Hunters that access the area by boat tend to have better success and satisfaction.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The majority of sheep stay in the same general areas throughout much of the year. One exception is a group of bighorn sheep that migrate to the High Uintas during the summer. They move to the High Country starting in June and come back down to lower elevations along Sheep Creek and Lodgepole Creek by November when the rut starts. Location of harvest: Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep are found in steep rocky terrain. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your bighorn sheep. If you cannot safely retrieve the bighorn sheep, do not shoot. Scouting Tips: The bighorn sheep stay fairly consistently in the same general areas throughout much of the year. Once the rut starts, the rams will be begin to move to where the ewes are. Scouting is a good way to see what size of ram you can expect to harvest. Sheep are most active in mornings and evenings. Using a spotting scope works well to find sheep in the steep rocky areas. Scores for sheep from West Daggett are usually in the 140s-160s and are 5.5-6.5 years old. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in steep terrain, but they occasionally move down to the shoreline. Mature rams seem to hang out more in steeper cliffs than ewes. Ewes with lambs prefer areas that are a little less steep and where they can find better feed. Bighorn sheep usually go to water at least once a day. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut runs during November. Where to find Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep: Bighorn sheep like steep cliffy areas because it provides an escape from predators. You can find them on grassy flats or near the shoreline when they are eating or come down to drink. Recommended areas: There are a couple of areas that the sheep use regularly. These areas include Sheep Creek, Phil Pico, Red Canyon, Dowd Mountain, Carter Creek, and along the Flaming Gorge Reservoir shoreline. Sheep from the High Uintas may come down occasionally and use the area around Hoop Lake if they don't travel all the way to Sheep Creek.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, and wind. Typically by this hunting season, any precipitation that is received is snow and temperatures regularly fall below freezing at night. Be very cautious of lightning while scouting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: u>Location of harvest: The core area where most bighorn reside and are harvested is along the lower Price River and lower Green River in Gray Canyon. Probably 75% of the harvest occurs here. There are small concentrations of sheep near Lila Canyon where people can harvest sheep. Sheep can be found down along the river and canyon bottoms all the way up through the cliffs to the top. It is rare to find sheep on the juniper covered mesas on the top. The confluence of the Price River and Green River tends to have the highest concentrations of sheep. There are no known sheep north of Rabbit Valley along the Green River so I wouldn't spend much time there. Bighorn observations in lower Range Creek are also quite rare. Common spots where sheep are found from south to north include Blue Castle Canyon, Long Canyon, Short Canyon, Sand Knolls Canyon, the lower Price River, and Jenny Canyon. Sheep can also be found on Bighorn Mountain and along the face of the Book Cliffs facing SR-6 as far north as Sunnyside. Scouting Tips: It is good to do pre-season scouting to learn country. However, it is very hot on this unit during the summer months so plan accordingly. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a spotting scope. This unit looks a lot more like desert bighorn sheep habitat than Rocky Mountain bighorn habitat. It is dry and cliffy. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Many of the larger harvestable rams will not move in with the ewes and be available for harvest until the rut begins in late October. Do not be alarmed if there are no big rams in the summer. They will show up by November. Hunting generally gets better the later you go. The peak of the rut tends to be the week of Thanksgiving. Find groups of ewes and lambs and often times a new ram will be with the ewe group each day as rams are moving alot in November between ewe groups. If you need to get a feel for how to judge a ram, it is advised that you go to the town of Sunnyside during the summer months. From April to September each year there is occasionally a group of 5 to 10 rams that reside in the east part of town and can be viewed at close range ( Behavior: The month of November is during the bighorn sheep rut. Rams are moving from group to group looking for ewes. Rams can also be observed butting heads. It is advised to occasionally stop and listen for the sound of butting heads it can be a good tool for locating sheep that are otherwise difficult to see. Sheep are generally active throughout the day in November but activity is highest in morning and evening. Bighorn sheep will not be as tied to water in November as it is generally more available that time of year if it has snowed. Bighorn will generally avoid the flat mesa top areas where there is any sort of tree cover. They tend to be found on the steep open cliffs and are occasionally are feeding on the flat canyon bottoms or benches. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Many young rams will have a pronounced curl. The best way to recognize mature trophy class bighorn rams is to look for horn mass particularly out near the tip of the horn. Younger rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. Mature rams 6 years and older tend to have thicker horns out near the tips, and thicker bases. Often times if you are close enough you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut runs during late October and extends through early December with the peak in late November
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is very remote, very steep, insanely rugged country. There is little to no cell coverage in most of the bighorn sheep habitat. As in most bighorn sheep habitat, hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters end up walking dozens of miles and climbing thousands of feet prior to harvesting their ram. As with most bighorn sheep habitat, there is an abundance of cliffs. Be very careful scaling cliffs. It is advised that you bring extra rope to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is very handy on this unit to not only mark sheep and routes but also places where you can get through the ledges as they are relatively rare. Hunters can sometimes spend hours hiking along trying to find a way through the ledges and wasting time and energy. Bring plenty of water. It can be warm in November and there is very little water on the unit. Water in the Green River is plentiful but is tough on most portable water filters as it generally runs pretty muddy. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a very remote, very rugged hunt unit. Access is very difficult and will often require either a multiple day float trip down Desolation Canyon or long hikes which will require a descent of several thousand feet to the river bottom.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There is a good population of bighorn sheep in this area of approximately 70 to 100 sheep. This resource has been underutilized so this hunt was created to provide sportsmen with an opportunity to exclusively hunt this area. Most of the sheep reside between Rockhouse Canyon on the North to Flat Canyon on the south with the highest concentrations of sheep near the mouth of Jack Creek. There are lots of layers to the canyon so sheep can be difficult to locate. There are also a few more trees in the canyon than in most bighorn sheep habitat. Most sheep tend to be in the bottom several layers of the canyon closer to the river, but they are occasionally seen on the ridgetops as well. Main access points are Cottonwood Ridge and the Peters Point wellpads accessed from the Nine Mile Canyon road. This will overlook Jack Creek from the north and will give you a good access point to hop in to the canyon. A second way is to continue driving to Cedar Ridge which is south of Jack Creek. There are locked gates on this road so your walk to the river will be much longer but it will be your closest access point to all points south of Jack Creek. You can reach lower Horse Bench (near Rockhouse Canyon) with an ATV by taking a trail from the Sand Wash boat ramp that crosses Nine Mile Creek and goes up on Horse Bench. The final access point would be floating the river. This takes 4 days and roughly 90 miles and can be a bit tricky at low water levels and a bit cold. Please consult the Price BLM office for permitting and regulations regarding float trips on Desolation Canyon.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The general area you will be hunting is called Desolation Canyon. It is appropriately named. You will be in the middle of nowhere. There is no cell coverage, no people, and no real roads to speak of. Make sure people know where you are and when you will return. Be very careful in attempting to navigate through the countless ledges in the canyon. Do not go down through something you don't feel you can get back up. This is a very deep canyon where the sun rarely shines in some portions. Some slopes may have snow and be slick. If you are planning to float the river, make sure you have an experienced oarsman and all of the correct equipment. The river will be running low in November and be rather technical. There are several Class 3 and 4 rapids along the 90 mile float trip required.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Highly variable. November is a volatile month. Prepare for winter-like conditions and be pleasantly surprised if the weather is nice. The main access road in to the area on Cottonwood Ridge will remain open even if the snow piles up but most of the side roads will not. There is the possibility that the river could freeze up in late November if it got really cold. Generally the slow parts of the Green River do not freeze until mid to Late December.

hunt_bio_general_information: Bighorn sheep on this unit are California Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep. The population is still growing and expanding. The Unit is a classic Great Basin mountain range. The terrain is steep and rocky. This unit has had several wildfires in the past decade, creating good bighorn habitat. The higher elevations have a mix of aspen and conifer forests. The mid elevations are juniper woodlands, and burned areas with grass. The lowest elevations are sagebrush and desert scrub.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The unit has an estimated 100 bighorn sheep. Most of the bighorns are on the very north end of the Stansbury Mountains, from Muskrat Canyon and north. There are a handful of bighorns further south on the west slope of the Stansbury Mountains. The unit produces rams in the 140 to 150 inch range. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting bighorns in this area. Most hunters use the few roads to access the base of the mountain and use binoculars and spotting scopes to locate bighorns. Once a ram is located, they hike up after it. The rams will be fully in the rut during the hunt. Rams can move long distances during the rut trying to locate ewes. There are several recovering burned areas that are excellent for bighorns. There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The locations where bighorn sheep occur are very steep and rocky, with many cliffs. Come prepared in very good physical shape. Plan on hiking in very steep terrain. Snow can make hiking in the steep rocky terrain very difficult. There are very remote location with a few areas having limited access. Cellular phone coverage is fair over most this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. Handheld radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Snowstorms can cause muddy and slick road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: Rocky Mountain Bighorn sheep are scattered from Alpine on the north to Springville on the south. Population estimates for sheep on the unit is 90+ animals.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Rocky Mountain Bighorn can be found above Alpine in the old burn, in American Fork Canyon, Mt. Timpanogos, Rock Canyon and above Springville on the north end. Sheep can also be found in places in between. Rams are on the move during the hunt looking for ewes to breed. Spend time looking pre-season for sheep. Most sheep can be found on the mountain face.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Areas where Rocky Mountain Bighorn sheep hang out in is steep and rocky. Where good boots and where gloves bring lots of water to drink. Be prepared for rain and snow at this time of year. Carry cell phone for emergency.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is usually good at this time of year, but prepare yourself for bad weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The bighorn population in this unit typically fluctuates between approximately 40 and 60 animals. Even in November sheep can be found near 11,000 feet. This is a very rugged and physically demanding hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep are found in steep rocky terrain. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your bighorn sheep. If you cannot safely retrieve the bighorn sheep, do not shoot. Scouting Tips: The bighorn sheep stay fairly consistently in the same general areas throughout much of the year. Once the rut starts, the rams will be begin to move to where the ewes are. Scouting is a good way to see what size of ram you can expect to harvest. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in steep terrain, but they occasionally move down to stream bottoms to water. Ram vs. Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut peaks in November. Where to find Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep: Bighorn sheep like steep cliffy areas because it provides an escape from predators. Recommended areas: Willow Creek to North Creek near Mona, Bald Mtn, and basins near Nebo Peak are good spots to start looking.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Bighorn sheep live in steep, rugged, and cliffy areas. Use precaution while climbing and hunting these areas.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: This hunt takes place the month of November. This area can be very snowy and cold this time of year.

hunt_bio_weather_considerations: This time of year can be cold with possible rain or snow storms.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: For the Northern Region, there should be more turkeys than last year. Turkeys have responded to the conditions favorably and we have been seeing birds spread out across the Region. With how the winter is going so far, we are expecting high over-winter survival with more production anticipated this coming spring and an increase in numbers again next year. Look to find turkeys during the hunts in the following locations: Cache County: Paradise, Blacksmith Fork Canyon, Richmond; Box Elder County: Sawtooth National Forest, Pilot Mountain, along the Bear River corridor, Coldwater WMA; Weber County: Ogden Valley, Hwy 39; Morgan County: Mountain Green, Morgan. _______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Turkey populations across central Utah are looking good this year. There are some great areas to hunt turkeys, and most areas with suitable habitat support huntable turkey populations. In particular, here are a few areas to keep in mind when hunting turkeys in central Utah: Diamond Fork Canyon Provo Canyon Hobble Creek Spanish Fork Canyon Payson Canyon Mona Bench East Tintic Mountains Sheeprock Mountains Turkeys can also be found in the canyons east of Tooele and most canyons in the Oquirrh Mountains. As always, be mindful of property ownership and obtain documented permission from landowners in order to hunt on private property. Turkey populations in the Southeastern region of Utah appear to be doing well. Two consecutive mild winters and good brood production has led to steady increases in populations in most areas. This should lead to improved hunting conditions this spring. Merriam's turkeys can be found in the Ponderosa pine habitats of the La Sal and Abajo mountain ranges, while Rio Grande turkeys tend to be found along riparian areas of the major rivers and tributaries in the region including the Green, Colorado, Dolores, San Rafael, and Price Rivers. _______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Turkey populations in the Southeastern region of Utah appear to be doing well. Two consecutive mild winters and good brood production has led to steady increases in populations in most areas. This should lead to improved hunting conditions this spring. Merriam's turkeys can be found in the Ponderosa pine habitats of the La Sal and Abajo mountain ranges, while Rio Grande turkeys tend to be found along riparian areas of the major rivers and tributaries in the region including the Green, Colorado, Dolores, San Rafael, and Price Rivers. __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Northeastern Region: The Northeastern Region is in the midst of the third mild winter in a row which has increased turkey survival and resulted in good production. This has led to an increase in turkey numbers across the region. Lower elevation flocks are almost exclusively on private lands but are still the best areas to find turkeys in the Northeastern region. Make sure you have written permission before hunting private lands. A few birds are showing up on Forest and BLM lands due to the milder winters. Locating these birds requires a lot of scouting due to the low numbers. _________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Southern Region: Habitat is looking good right now with slightly earlier green-up than usual. This year is already, dry turkeys will concentrate heavily near permanent/reliable water sources and agricultural fields. Some creek bottoms are already dried up in the southwestern part of the region. Expect birds to be scattered and at higher elevations. Good bird numbers have been seen so far on the early hunt and populations seem to be increasing in the Central and Southern parts of the region. Toms were especially receptive to calls this limited entry season. Central and Southern areas are showing high hunting success rates. The high success rate of the limited entry season may limit the number of toms left over for the general season. The successful early hunters also get friends and family excited about the hunt so expect crowding in the usual roost areas. Birds are being found at higher elevations this year and are spread out. Turkeys will chase the newest, most tender green up so the higher elevations will get more birds as the little bit of snow melts off. The Monroe and Fish Lake areas should produce good turkey hunting. This past winter was very mild so we had very little winter mortality. Elevation movements of turkeys will not be hindered by deep snow this spring so hunters may have to look expand their search areas if they're hunting turkey flocks that migrate. The Wayne County area is still growing some turkeys, but growth is slow due to drought. Hunters should target riparian areas and areas with abundant water, as those locations will have the best food for the turkeys this year, especially with the non-existent winter.

hunt_bio_general_information: Turkey numbers in the northeastern part of the state have decreased a little from previous years, most likely due to the severe drought conditions in Utah that have persisted over the past couple of years. The above-average snowfall this winter - and how long the snow has lasted - has pushed most turkeys onto private property across the south slope of the Uintas. Hunters should target the corridors along the Duchesne River, the Green River and the Ashley Creek drainage, which should all be good areas to hunt turkeys this year. Lower agricultural areas should also have good turkey hunting, but many of these areas are private property, so hunters will need to get written permission from landowners before hunting. There are also pockets of turkeys throughout much of the Book Cliffs area and in the middle and lower areas of several major drainages across the northern and southern slopes of the Uinta Mountains.

Turkeys can also be found on public land in Cache Valley (including Blacksmith Fork Canyon), the Richmond Wildlife Management Area (along Cherry Creek), the Wellsville Range above Wellsville and Mendon, and Walk-in Access areas around Clarkston. Expect to see fewer turkeys in Cache, Weber, Morgan and Summit counties as the severe winter has resulted in higher-than-normal mortality rates. Turkey numbers are better in Box Elder County than the rest of northern Utah because the winter was less severe there than in other counties. In Box Elder County, there are turkeys on the Raft River Mountains near Clear Creek, One Mile Creek, Johnson Creek and Wildcat Creek. There are also turkeys on the Pilot Mountain Range.

hunt_bio_general_information: Turkey populations in the Southeastern region of Utah appear to be doing well. Two consecutive mild winters and good brood production has led to steady increases in populations in most areas. This should lead to improved hunting conditions this spring. Merriam's turkeys can be found in the Ponderosa pine habitats of the La Sal and Abajo mountain ranges, while Rio Grande turkeys tend to be found along riparian areas of the major rivers and tributaries in the region including the Green, Colorado, Dolores, San Rafael, and Price Rivers. Popular areas to find Rio Grande turkeys in this part of the state include along the Colorado and Green rivers, as well as many of their tributaries. These tributaries include the San Rafael River, Price River, Range Creek, Gordon Creek, Huntington Creek, Ferron Creek and Muddy Creek, and many drainages along the southern portion of the Book Cliffs. There is also a sizable turkey population along the Fremont River, between Hanksville and Caineville. Be aware that much of the good Rio Grande turkey habitat in this part of the state occurs on private lands with isolated areas of public land. Hunters should secure written permission prior to hunting on private lands. There is one Walk-in Access property (Wells Property) in the Hanksville area that can provide some limited public access to private lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: See General notes above. Rio Grande turkeys tend to use river bottoms along the major drainages in southeast Utah. Rio Grande turkey densities tend to be significantly higher near agricultural areas. Merriam's turkeys tend to prefer Ponderosa pine habitats that are found throughout the La Sal and Abajo mountains.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Conditions can be very muddy during spring turkey seasons. Many areas in southeastern Utah do not have reliable cell coverage. Be prepared for inclement weather and bad roads.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Spring-like conditions which includes a bit of everything including: snow, rain, wind, and hot. Be prepared for anything and you should be fine. Nights and early mornings tend to be cold. Afternoons can be quite windy during the spring months.

hunt_bio_general_information: Turkey numbers have been low in southern Utah for several years, and populations have declined. However, there were no known turkey die offs during the winter for this part of the state. Turkey hunting on the Panguitch Lake, Mt. Dutton and Paunsaguant areas will be average this year due to the low production over the past four years. Birds will be found in areas with green plants and near streams. Turkey populations on the Beaver, Pahvant and Oak Creek areas are also lower than four years ago. However, populations are still healthy, and birds can be found in most of the major drainages across these ranges. This year, hunters should expect access to be much more difficult due to lingering snow and mud. Turkey hunting on the Monroe and Fish Lake areas is only expected to be fair this spring. Turkey hunting in Washington and Iron counties should be better than it has been the last few years, due to good chick production last year. With the delayed spring conditions, there has been a delay in the breeding season as well. Birds may still be gobbling well into the middle of May in these areas. Turkey numbers have been low on the Boulder/Thousand Lake hunting unit this year. There is some concern that survival may have been poor due to the severe winter conditions. Areas once containing many turkeys have had few to none this year. The hunt may be more difficult this year, due to limited accessibility with lingering snow and low turkey numbers. Turkeys can be found along creeks at lower elevations when spring plants begin to emerge.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Overwinter survival was lower than usual in the Wayne County/Escalante area, though poult production and survival was high this summer. If deep snow conditions persist this winter, hunting near riparian areas will be key as turkeys will congregate there in search of food (green-up occurs faster in mesic areas) and cover.

hunt_bio_general_information: There are two fall management areas in the southeast region where you can hunt. You can see more detailed information and the boundary decription for each area by selecting them below. • Cainville Fremont River Corridor in Wayne County • Cleveland-Elmo Area in Emery County To find information on turkeys and turkey hunting you can search 'turkey hunting' on the utah division of wildlife webpage. Do your homework and make contact with landowners prior to hunting to get written permission to hunt on private property. Some landowners may not allow hunting on, or access through, their property. It's very important that you do not shoot towards livestock, equipment, or structures. Unless you have written permission do not shoot within 600 feet of: • A house, dwelling or any other building • Any structure in which a domestic animal is kept or fed. Please be respectful of private property and consider picking up trash along the way. You are encouraged to acquire a hunting app that clearly identifies public and private land ownership.
